Therefore, Avicenna, wishing to explain the nature of the voluntary motive power found in animals, stated: the motive power—meaning the specific type of voluntary motion found in an animal—consists of the appetitive and irascible powers <note>original: "uirtus appetitiua, & irascibilis"; these refer to the drives for desire and spirited defense/anger</note>. These are controlled by the will. This power moves the animal with a progressive motion <note>walking or moving from place to place</note>, which is distinct from the "natural" motion caused by the dominance of a particular element within the animal <note>natural motion refers to involuntary movements, like a heavy object falling due to the element of 'earth'</note>. Avicenna’s text is clear to those who understand the reasoning, etc.

<margin>G</margin> **AND THE POWER** of motion—specifically voluntary motion—does not act except through the firm cognition of the **ESTIMATIVE POWER** <note>original: "uirtutis existimatiuę"; the faculty that allows an animal to instinctively sense if something is useful or dangerous</note>, because the will and the appetite are never directed toward something unknown. The estimative power, however, organizes and divides information; it judges and discerns truth from falsehood, and good from evil. Therefore, after the estimative power provides this knowledge, the will either desires the object or rejects and recoils from it. **AND THE POWER** of motion in a non-rational animal <note>such as a beast</note> acts as the "end" or goal. This means that in such animals, the other faculties—the external and internal senses—are organized to serve it. As Avicenna explains by example later, the motive power in a non-rational animal is like a prince served by the senses. This is because these senses are only placed in a non-rational animal to refine and improve the causes of voluntary progressive motion. The causes of this motion are the appetitive and irascible powers mentioned before, which are held under the will; and the will, along with its subordinate powers, does not move toward what it does not know. Note that the Reconciler <term>Conciliator: A title for the scholar Pietro d'Abano (c. 1257–1315), who attempted to reconcile the differences between Greek philosophy and Arabic medicine</term> says in Part 10, Problem 15: In the front part of the brain, the perception of external forms occurs through the individual senses. This information is carried like a tribute by "servant parts" to the common sense <note>original: "sensui cōmuni"</note> so it may judge. In this process, the foresight and deliberation of what must be done consists. Therefore, these powers do not result in action until knowledge is acquired from the external senses and from the imaginative and estimative powers—specifically, the knowledge that "this thing is helpful and should be pursued" or "that thing is harmful and should be avoided." Even the power that stores the memory of what is helpful or harmful <note>the memory</note> serves the will. When a non-rational animal remembers that a certain place contains something beneficial or dangerous, the will moves the animal and commands it to either seek or flee that thing. From this, it is clear how the external senses and the faculties of the brain serve the motive power. The motive power does not serve the senses; rather, in a non-rational animal, all other powers are ordered toward the motive power (the appetitive and irascible). Thus, the motive power is the "end" and the "prince" that the other powers serve.

<margin>H</margin> **IN THE SPECIES** that is rational <note>human beings</note>, however, the situation is the opposite: for it was not established in this way, etc. From these words of Avicenna, it appears that in humans and rational animals, the aforementioned motive power—the appetitive and irascible...

# AVICENNA

...are not placed under the control of the will except for the perfection of the rational, intellectual soul. For according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>, all our knowledge has its origin in the senses, as will be better declared below. Therefore, if the external senses <note>sight, hearing, etc.</note> and internal senses <note>memory, imagination, etc.</note> did not transition from potentiality to the actual performance of their operations, the rational intellectual soul would not acquire perfection in intellectual knowledge. Instead, it would remain imperfect, like a **blank slate** <note>original: "tabula rasa"; a tablet that has been scraped clean and has nothing written on it</note> on which nothing is depicted.

<margin>D</margin> Therefore, for the perfection and improvement of the rational intellectual soul which apprehends—that is, the soul which in a well-disposed human is fit to grasp ideas and to engage in rational discourse—it was necessary to place in man a **power** that might move the aforementioned senses and command them. This power ensures they carry out their actions so that, through these acts of the senses, the rational intellectual soul may acquire its understanding and its perfection. Such a commanding and moving power is the **voluntary power**, which includes under it the **appetitive power** <note>desire</note> and the **irascible power** <note>the "spirited" drive often associated with anger or defense</note>. For this reason, the commanding will is directed toward the perfection of the intellectual soul according to Avicenna, and consequently, it is directed toward understanding, which is the perfection of the soul itself. Therefore, the act of the aforementioned will is directed toward the act of the intellect as if toward its own goal. 

Now, according to the Philosopher, the "end" or goal is nobler than the things that exist to serve that goal. For this reason, the voluntary power and its acts are lower in dignity and nobility than the intellectual power and the act of understanding. From these words of Avicenna, the response of the **Thomists** <note>followers of Thomas Aquinas</note> is confirmed; they hold that the intellectual power and the act of the intellect are nobler than the power of the will and the act of willing. Because of this, **blessedness** <note>original: "beatitudo"; supreme happiness or the state of the soul in the afterlife</note> in the next life consists more in the noblest act of the intellect—by which a human is made like unto God Himself—than in the act of the will, which is not as noble as the act of the intellect. 

Furthermore, the words of Avicenna written above also confirm the response to the argument of those who hold that the power of the will and its acts are nobler than the intellectual power and its acts, and that the aforementioned blessedness consists more in the act of the will, etc. For the **Scotists** <note>followers of Duns Scotus</note> argue as follows: the power that commands is nobler than the one which is commanded. But the will commands the intellectual power to understand; therefore, the will is superior and nobler, and the intellectual power is subject to the command of the will. Consequently, the intellect is inferior to the will and not as noble as the will and its acts. 

Those holding the contrary opinion <note>the Thomists</note> respond that the will commands the intellect not for itself, but for the perfection of the intellectual power, just as was said in this chapter: that the motive power and the will were placed in man for the perfection of the intellectual soul and for the act of understanding itself, as has been declared. Therefore, the will is not superior or worthier than the intellect according to Avicenna. 

However, taking the opposite path, it must be said that the appetitive and irascible powers are twofold: namely, **sensitive** and **intellective**. Consequently, there is a certain sensitive will and a certain intellective will. Having established these points, let it be said that through the motive power, which is the appetitive and irascible, toward which are directed...

### ON THE SOUL

...in non-rational animals, the powers of the exterior and interior senses; and in rational animals, the aforementioned **motive power** <note>original: "uirtus motiua"; the capacity to move or be moved by desire</note> itself is ordered toward the perfection of the intellectual soul. Avicenna understood the motive power to consist of the **sensory appetite** and the **sensory irascible power** <note>the drive related to anger or survival</note>, both of which are contained under the sensory will, not the intellectual one. Although, according to Avicenna—for the reasons assigned above—the sensory will in man is ordered toward the perfection of the intellectual soul and is inferior to the intellectual power, nevertheless, the **intellectual appetite** <note>the "intellectual will" or higher desire</note> and the non-sensory will, along with its actions, are nobler than the intellectual power and its acts.

Furthermore, **blessedness** <note>original: "beatitudo"; the state of ultimate spiritual happiness or salvation</note> in the next life consists more in the act of the **will** than in the **intellect**. This is because the aforementioned blessedness, which arises from the union of the soul with God, is perfected more by the act of **love** and **charity** <note>original: "amor et caritas"</note>—which is an act of the will according to Augustine—than by an act of the intellect. The **Good** is the object of the will, which is not drawn toward the unknown; thus, as much as the act of the intellect is focused on the knowledge of the Supreme Good, which is God the Glorious, so much more is the act of the non-sensory will and love focused toward God himself. Through this mediating love and charity, the desired blessedness of the soul is caused, and this blessedness is indeed the true and complete perfection of the intellectual soul. 

If, therefore, the blessedness and perfection of the highest soul is completed by the act of love (which presupposes the act of the intellect), it follows that the act of the intellect is ordered toward the act of love and will. Consequently, the act of the will, appetite, and non-sensory love is nobler than the act of the intellect. 

And since both of the aforementioned opinions face objections and considerations in theology that are not easy to resolve, let such difficulty be left to the theologians. But it is quite a marvel that concerning the **voluntary power** <note>the power of the will</note> and its operation—whether it is nobler or not than the intellectual power and its acts—the most excellent ancient philosophers did not write as extensively or distinctly as they did regarding the intellectual power, its operation, and the other powers of the soul in their own chapters. This is evident in the works of Aristotle and others; and even Avicenna, in this compendium and in the sixth book of his *Natural Philosophy*, does not speak of the will except implicitly, as was shown above where he speaks of the motive power. Since the will is a real power of the soul and not just a concept of the mind <note>original: "ens rationis"</note>, it is therefore a wonder that Aristotle and the other most famous philosophers wrote more implicitly and briefly about the voluntary power and its operation than about the other powers of the soul. However, for the sake of brevity, I leave the derision of this doubt to those who are wiser.

### AVICENNA

*...in many other books. The reason is that an animated body <note>a body endowed with a soul or life-force</note> is more noble than an inanimate body. According to Avicenna, the celestial bodies are the most noble of all bodies in this lower world; therefore, it must be said that the celestial bodies are animated and possess a soul, just as he stated here. Avicenna will further declare below in chapter ten that the first thing created was the **Intelligence** <note>original: "intelligentia"; in this context, a pure, disembodied divine intellect</note>, and after it the **soul**, and then the **celestial body**. And just as there are nine celestial bodies <note>the nine spheres of medieval cosmology, including the planets, the fixed stars, and the "primum mobile"</note>, so too was one soul created in each of them. This soul is their **substantial form** <note>the essential nature that gives a thing its being</note>, which gives existence to each of them, just as the human soul does in human bodies.*

*And because every such soul of the celestial bodies is not perfectly "intellectual in act" <note>meaning it does not possess all knowledge at all times</note> but only "in potentiality"—much like the human soul—it requires help. In difficult and speculative matters, the human soul (according to Christians) is illuminated by the **Holy Spirit**; however, according to Avicenna, it is illuminated by the **Universal Intelligence**. This Intelligence relates to the human intellect as light relates to the power of sight, as is explained in chapter ten of this compendium.*

*Because the soul of every celestial body possesses a **voluntary motive power** <note>original: "uirtus motiua uoluntaria"; the capacity to move by choice</note> and moves its own specific celestial body by its will, and because such a soul is by its nature less perfect than an **abstract intellectual substance** <note>a pure intellect completely separated from any physical body</note>—which understands all things possible to it in actuality—the Soul of the Heaven, being less perfect, does not understand itself in actuality, but only in potentiality. Therefore, the soul of the heaven could err in its cognition and its notions. For this reason, it requires an **abstract Intelligence**, which by its own nature understands perfectly and in actuality to the extent that is possible for it. Thus, this Intelligence flows into the celestial soul a perfect intellectual cognition, by which the soul understands the proper movement of the heaven, ensuring it does not wander from what is appropriate and from what is understood by **God the Most High**.*

*Just as the human soul, in its understanding and in ruling itself and its body, requires the assistance of the light of the Universal Intelligence, so too does the soul of each celestial body require the assistance of the abstract Intelligence assigned to it. Therefore, according to the order of nature, God first created the **Universal Abstract Intelligence**, which is not tied to any specific celestial orb but is common to all higher substances (except God) and to lower substances, as will be explained in chapter ten. After the Intelligence, He created the soul of each celestial body, and finally, He created the celestial bodies themselves. Although these were created simultaneously in an instant, this order of "before" and "after" is based on the priority of nature as understood by the intellect.*

*Therefore, the Heaven—that is, each celestial body—has a soul and life for the reasons mentioned above, according to Avicenna. Yet, it does not possess the power of the **senses**, nor **imagination**, even though it has the motive power. Nor does it have the **nutritive power**, the power of **growth**, or the power of **reproduction**, which three powers are found in animals and plants.*

### Chapter six: on the distinction of the discourse concerning the five senses, and the nature of their perception.

**R**egarding the **power of sight**, philosophers have long disagreed on how its perception occurs. For some of them believed that sight only perceives through rays emerging from the eye and reaching the visible objects; this was the path and position of the philosopher **Plato**. Others, however, believed that a "piercing power" <note>original: "uirtus forantiua"; a technical term for the visual force that was thought to reach out and 'touch' objects</note> reaches the visible objects on its own and perceives them. Still others said that visual perception occurs through the arrival or impression of the **species** <note>original: "species"; here meaning the visual forms or formal likenesses of objects</note> of visible things upon the **crystalline humor** <note>the lens</note> of the eye, by means of a transparent body <note>such as air or water</note> that has been illuminated. This arrival is similar to the way forms or images are impressed in mirrors. Indeed, if mirrors possessed the power of sight, they would perceive the forms or species of things coming to them or being impressed upon them; this was the position of the philosopher **Aristotle**, and it is the discourse that contains the truth.

The falsehood and refutation of the discourse spoken by Plato, however, is manifest. For if rays emerged from the sight and reached the perceived objects, then sight would not need external light; rather, it would perceive or see in the dark or in shadows. Indeed, the air would even be illuminated by the emergence or 
<margin>of those, namely the rays from the eye.</margin>
extramission <note>the act of sending out</note> of these rays in the darkness. However, rays of this kind cannot exist without a "subject" <note>a physical substance to hold the quality of light</note>; either their subject is only the eyes—in which case Plato's claim about their departure from the eye would be false—or their subject is a body other than the eye. For it is necessary that there be something to carry and support them. Whence the ear is struck, and the air enclosed or located in the instrument of the sense of hearing is moved. And the condition of **hardness** was not established except because soft bodies do not strike the air away from themselves with force; rather, the air is scattered or retained in their cavities. And indeed, the condition of **flatness**, or equality, or smoothness—the opposite disposition to roughness—was established because bodies that are not smooth or flat do not strike the air away from themselves entirely or quickly with force. Rather, the air is retained in the openings. And the condition of **rapid concussion** was not established except because when a concussion is soft and slow, the air is not struck out with force. 

An **echo** indeed is caused by the sending or expulsion of the air struck or expelled from two bodies struck or meeting each other, on account of its strong resistance or its vehement encounter with another hard, wide, or hollow body filled with air. Whence the air contained within it prevents the penetration of the struck or expelled air, and the ear is struck a second time after the first striking, according to the original form.

### Declarations on the sixth chapter.

Then Plato’s claim regarding the "exit" of those [rays] will be false.
*It must be known that a ray is a quality. If, therefore, its **subject** <note>In medieval philosophy, a "subject" is the substance or body in which a property—like color or heat—resides</note> were only the eye, and Plato says that the aforementioned ray goes out from the eye to the thing being sensed, then Plato’s claim is false, because then an **accident** <term>accident: a property that cannot exist on its own (like a color or a feeling) but must exist within a substance</term> would move from one subject to another, which is impossible.*
*IF THE SUBJECT of the ray is a body exiting the eye, then the eye would not see everything that is beneath the heavens, because beneath the heavens are air and water, which are **transparent bodies** <term>transparent bodies: literally "diaphanous" bodies, which allow light to pass through</term>, and the penetration of one body into another is not possible. Therefore, the body that is the subject of the ray exiting the eye would not penetrate the air or the water, and thus things existing in the air or water would not be seen. For one body does not penetrate another body unless one of them gives way to the other and one of them is moved locally and leaves its place behind for the other. And even if we were to grant the existence of a **vacuum** <term>vacuum: a space entirely empty of matter, a concept often debated in medieval physics</term> by way of a hypothesis, then that body exiting from the eye would not penetrate the mass of the water except in certain empty spaces of the water, and it would not penetrate a large part of the water where there is no vacuum. Therefore, the eye would see only certain cavities and certain holes into which it penetrates. But this is contrary to experience, for we see to the bottom of deep water, and the eye sees a great...*

# ON THE SOUL

...between two things, not by composing and dividing, but it perceives white [as] not black, and it perceives sweet [as] not black, or not fluid, without composing and dividing. <note>In medieval logic, "composing and dividing" refers to the mental act of forming a proposition—joining concepts (composition) or separating them (division). Here, the author argues that the senses recognize basic differences before the mind even forms a logical sentence about them.</note> And we can say that, just as the sense of sight, knowing white and black, places a difference between them by means of an internal judgment—for instance, the **estimative** <term>estimative: (Latin: *existimatiua*) the faculty, often called instinct, that perceives "intentions" like danger or utility that the five senses cannot see</term> or the **cogitative** <term>cogitative: (Latin: *cogitatiua*) the human version of the estimative power, capable of joining and separating mental images</term>—so the **common sense** <term>common sense: (Latin: *sensus communis*) the internal hub where all five external senses meet to create a unified experience</term>, perceiving diverse sensations of diverse objects, discerns differences between them by means of the estimative or cogitative power, which judges it to be so or not to be so.

<margin>B</margin>
**FURTHERMORE**, there is in the animal a power that composes what is gathered in the common sense, etc. In this part, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian philosopher and physician whose "De Anima" (On the Soul) is being discussed here.</note> after the formative power or common sense, places the imaginative power; afterward, he places the estimative power (or the opinion-forming power) and the cogitative power—which powers, namely the estimative and cogitative, are one and the same, as will be shown below. Finally, he places the **memorative** <term>memorative: (Latin: *memoratiua*) the faculty of memory</term> power. Thus, Avicenna in this chapter does not posit more than four internal powers: namely, the common sense, then the imaginative power, thirdly the estimative or cogitative power, and fourthly the memorative power. And although in the first book of the *Canon* <note>original: *1. canone*; referring to Avicenna’s famous medical encyclopedia, the *Canon of Medicine*</note> in the chapter on the animal powers, he posits according to the philosophers five different powers: first, the common sense; second, the **phantasy** <term>phantasy: (Latin: *phantastica*) the faculty that stores the raw data or "forms" received from the five senses</term>, which preserves the sensed images <note>original: *species sensatas*; the mental "pictures" or forms received from the external senses</note> apprehended by the common sense; third, the imaginative power; fourth, the estimative or cogitative power; and fifth, the memorative power. This last one differs from the phantasy because the phantasy stores only sensed images, whereas the memorative stores sensed images and "unsensed" images <note>original: *species insensatas*; qualities like "danger" or "friendliness" that are felt rather than seen or heard</note> apprehended by the cogitative or estimative power. Nevertheless, Avicenna there in that chapter of the first *Canon* states that according to the physicians, the phantastic power and the common sense are one and the same power. And Avicenna speaks in this same way in this chapter, stating that the common sense preserves sensed images. And because in this treatise he speaks concisely and briefly, therefore in this chapter Avicenna, favoring brevity, speaks more succinctly about these two powers than he did in the first book of the *Canon*. In this chapter, therefore, he posits that the common sense and the phantasy—which preserves sensed images—are only one and the same thing.

<margin>C</margin>
And by this, the meaning of the text is apparent: namely, "**furthermore, in the animal there is a power that composes what is gathered in the common sense**," in the manner stated above, where the sensations of the external senses are terminated and united in the common sense, etc. And it composes and divides, and causes diversity to occur between them or within them, without the forms or images being removed from the common sense. That is, the imaginative power composes and divides sensed images that are gathered in the common sense, and it establishes a difference between them, without those sensed images themselves being removed from the common sense—that is, while those images are still preserved in the common sense. And indeed, sensed images from the external senses do not seem to be able to be gathered in the common sense unless they are preserved there. Therefore, the phantastic power, which preserves the aforementioned sensed images, and the common sense are one and the same, as the physicians maintain.

->### AVICENNA<-

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
<note>The letters C and D in the margins are printer's signatures, used to help binders assemble the book in the correct order.</note>

It should be noted that, although the **imaginative power** <term>imaginative power: (Latin: *uirtus imaginatiua*) the faculty that combines or separates mental images</term> "composes and divides" <note>The phrase "composes and divides" refers to the mental act of joining concepts together (e.g., imagining a "golden mountain") or separating them.</note> just as the **estimative** and **cogitative** powers do, they nevertheless differ. This is because the estimative or cogitative power judges a thing to be certainly so, or certainly not so; it makes a certain judgment <note>original: *iudicium certum*</note> that it is thus, even though such a judgment is sometimes in error. 

However, the imaginative power composes and divides the "species" <note>In medieval philosophy, a "species" is not a biological category but a mental "image" or "likeness" of an object.</note> apprehended by the **common sense**, as well as false species not acquired from the senses. In such composition and division, the imaginative power does not judge the result to be certainly true, nor does it make a certain judgment about what it joins or separates. This happens, for example, when a person imagines themselves to be in a place where they are not, or performing some action; in such an imagination, the imaginative power does not judge for certain that the person is in that place, or that place, or that they are performing that action or another.

**FOR THE** **formative power** <term>formative power: (Latin: *uirtus formatiua*) another name for the retentive imagination, which stores the forms received by the senses</term> formed, or rather received, the image of the sun according to how it was received from the senses, etc. By these words, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose theories on the "internal senses" dominated medieval psychology.</note> intends to establish the difference between the formative power (or common sense) and the **estimative**, **cogitative**, or **opinative** <term>opinative: (Latin: *uirtus opinatiua*) the faculty of forming opinions or beliefs</term> powers. 

For the **common sense** <term>common sense: (Latin: *sensus communis*) the hub where all physical sensations are unified into a single experience</term> receives the image of the sun as it is taken from the sense of sight: namely, according to the size of a round shape that is not very large, as it appears to the eye. But this estimative power judges the sun to be larger than it appears to the sight and the common sense. Therefore, the common sense and the eyes differ in this regard from the estimative power, which judges the reality of the matter. Similarly, a lion sees its prey <note>original: *uenationem*, literally "the hunt" or "the object of the hunt."</note> from a distance and must catch it for food. The lion's eye does not perceive that prey or animal from afar except as a small size—perhaps as small as a little bird. Nevertheless, the lion's estimative power, which makes certain judgments and judges differently than the eye appears to, does not doubt the actual size of that animal. Rather, it judges the size to be greater than what appears to the eye from a distance. Therefore, the lion focuses on that prey and follows the animal seen by the eye to capture it. For this reason, it is clear that the estimative power makes a more certain judgment than what is perceived by the sense of the eye and the common sense.

**WHEN** the **cogitative power** <term>cogitative power: (Latin: *uirtus cogitatiua*) the human version of the estimative power, guided by reason rather than just instinct</term> uses the imaginative power, etc. Note that these three powers, as stated above, are one and the same, yet they differ according to different perspectives. Hence, Avicenna says here that sometimes the estimative power uses the imaginative power according to its own simplicity. 

For example: when the estimative power apprehends a "species of enmity" <note>In medieval psychology, an animal doesn't just see a shape; it perceives an "intention" (like "friend" or "enemy") through the estimative power.</note> drawn out from stored images, the imagination then imagines that such an enemy is huge, or becomes terrifying, or creates other similar imaginations. In its simplicity—that is, without judging it to be certainly so or not so—the estimative power is then called "imaginative." If, however, the **rational power** <note>original: *uirtus rationalis*</note> uses the imaginative power in some intellectual cognition or in some discourse, it is then called "cogitative."

Note that Avicenna did not speak of the **motive power** <term>motive power: (Latin: *uirtus motiua*) the faculty that causes physical movement</term> here because he spoke of it above in Chapter 5, where he said that the moving cause of the animal itself is the appetitive power...

### Chapter Eight: Concerning the nature of the human soul, and the sequence of its origin through to its perfection.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>
*Alheiulani*, that is, similar to *hyle*, that is, to matter. With *alheiule*, that is, with matter.
</margin>
There is no doubt: the species of the "rational animal" is distinguished from the non-rational by a power that can grasp **intelligible forms**, or which can grasp things that can be understood. And this power is indeed named the **rational soul**. It is also customary for it to be called the **material intellect** <term>material intellect: (Latin: *intellectus alheiulani*) the human mind's capacity to receive knowledge, which is initially blank like raw matter</term>, that is, the "intellect in potential," or the **possible intellect**, because of the similarity it has with *hyle* <note>original: *alheiule*, a Latinization of the Greek word *hyle*, meaning primary matter or raw material</note>. 

This power is found in the entire human species, and it does not possess any of the intelligible forms or species by its own nature; rather, they arrive in it in two ways. One way is through **divine infusion** or emanation without instruction and without being acquired from the senses. These are the understandings of **first principles** <term>first principles: fundamental truths that are self-evident and do not need to be proven</term>, such as understanding or agreeing that the "whole" is greater than its "part," and that two opposites cannot exist at the same time in one thing or in one subject. Those who possess a perfect or complete reason share in this kind of formation or understanding. 

The second way is through **acquisition** by means of rational discourse or demonstrative knowledge. This occurs when the **intelligible species** <note>In this context, "species" refers to mental concepts or categories</note> of logical considerations arrive—things like **genus, species, difference, property, and accident** <note>These are the "Five Predicables," the basic building blocks of logic used to define and categorize things</note>—as well as simple and composite statements with various ways of being put together. It also includes true and false composite arguments, and propositions or "premises" which, when formed into **syllogisms** <term>syllogism: a form of reasoning in which a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises</term>, lead to conclusions by the necessity of demonstration, or by the necessity of inductive reasoning, or by persuasive or even sophisticated <note>original: *sophisticae*, referring to sophistry or fallacious reasoning used in academic debate</note> reasoning. 

It also includes the investigation or consideration of natural things, such as **matter, form, privation, nature, place, time, and motion**, as well as the celestial bodies, the elemental bodies, and generation and corruption in an absolute sense, and the essence or the process of becoming...

The distinction between them in terms of forms is like the shared nature of the form—or kind—of Plato and a donkey in the form of life or "animal," and the difference between them, namely that the former is rational and the latter is not rational. **Essential** characteristics in them are like "life" in both. **Accidental** characteristics, however, are like blackness and whiteness. 

And when the soul finds them according to these forms, it sets each of these forms—whether essential, substantial, accidental, shared, or unique—as a single **intelligible** <note>original: *intelligibilem*; something that can be understood by the mind rather than just perceived by the senses</note>, universal kind according to its singularity. With this skill, it extracts or draws out intelligible genera, species, differences, properties, and accidents. 

Next, it arranges these simple concepts <note>original: *intentiones*; in medieval philosophy, an "intention" is a mental concept that "points to" an object</note> into well-ordered or appropriate compositions. Then it arranges them into **syllogistic** <term>syllogistic: a form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises</term> structures, by which those things intended to be concluded are reached, or by which the knowledge of conclusions is attained.

And all these things are present in the soul through the service of the animal power <note>the lower faculties of the soul, such as the senses and imagination</note> and the help of the **universal intellect**, as we shall explain, and through the mediation of the natural disposition which is within it from necessary intelligible principles. And although this power [the rational soul] is assisted by the **sensory power** during the extraction of simple intelligible forms, or when it draws out simple intelligible forms from sensed objects:

<margin>It does not need it (namely, the sensory power).</margin>

nevertheless, the soul does not need that sensory power for the formation of these concepts within itself, nor for their syllogistic arrangement, nor for their certification, nor for the process of verifying their formation, as we shall say later. And whenever the forms or sensory cognitions (which are necessary to it through the aforementioned skill or method) have been impressed upon it, it rejects the service of the sensory powers; rather, it is sufficient by itself for all the operations it desires. 

And just as the sensory powers do not apprehend except through the likenesses or proportions of things perceived, similarly the rational or intellectual power does not apprehend except through the proportion of **intelligibles**. And this "proportion" is indeed the stripping away or separation of the **form** from **matter**, and from those things joined with it.

AND NO intelligible form or species exists within it by itself; rather, they arrive in it in two ways, etc. One of which is **divine emanation** <note>original: *manatio diuina*; the "flowing out" of knowledge from a higher source to the soul</note>, etc. Note: According to Avicenna's opinion, the intelligible species <note>concepts or ideas</note> and intellectual knowledge that come to the soul do not belong to it inherently, but come to the soul in two ways. Indeed, such knowledge is like the knowledge of **first principles** <note>fundamental truths that are self-evident and do not need proof</note>—such as understanding and agreeing that "the whole is greater than its part," etc. For knowledge and understandings of this kind are not obtained through acquisition, nor from the senses and the reasoning that depends on them, but from a power received through divine emanation. For anyone possessing perfect and complete reason immediately grasps these kinds of understandings without logical deduction. Thus, once the terms are known, the intellect agrees with the first principles—that the whole is greater than the part, and that two contraries cannot exist in the same subject at the same time. Therefore, the knowledge and understanding of first principles, etc., comes to the soul not through acquisition from reasoning or demonstration, but comes to the soul from divine emanation. ...received from God and from the universal intelligence is the science and knowledge of **first principles** <note>original: *primis principijs*; these are self-evident truths that do not need to be proven, such as "the whole is greater than its part"</note>, namely that the whole is greater than its part, and similar things. The knowledge of such principles presupposes the knowledge of quantity, which is perceived by the sense. **IT IS SAID** that the "intellect in act" <note>the mind when it is actively thinking</note> is simultaneously the thinking subject and the object being thought. For it is the "thinker" because it is actually thinking, and it is the "thing thought" because the intelligible species—which comes to the intellect and is understood by it—is united with the intellect itself and becomes one single form. In substances that are separate from matter, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> and according to logic, the thinker and the thing thought are the same. Now, the intellectual soul is abstracted from matter, just as the "separate intelligences" <note>angelic or celestial minds</note> are; therefore, the same principle applies. And note that the Arabs <note>referring to Arabic philosophers like Avicenna and Averroes</note> say that just as we see the action of fire in red-hot iron—to the point that we can say the iron and fire have become one single thing—similarly, one single thing is formed from the intelligible species and the active intellect. Therefore, when the "potential intellect" <note>the mind's capacity to learn</note> is brought into action by a certain species and is actually thinking, we then say that the intellect in act is both the thinker and the thing thought. It is the thinker because the very substance of the soul is actively thinking. It is the thing thought because of the intelligible species being understood, which is united with the soul as stated above. And just as iron, when it has been subjected to fire for a long time, becomes glowing and unites with the fire to perform the works of fire, so too the potential intellect, when it is united with the intelligible species of divinity, is united with divinity itself. Or to put it another way: the potential intellect, by understanding divinity in the way it is capable, is united with divinity itself. And sometimes, from this union, it performs divine operations through grace infused by God, and the union of the soul with God, and so on.

<margin>q,</margin>
Regarding this specific point, there is a doubt as to whether in glowing iron (or in its matter) there exists the substantial form <term>substantial form: the essential nature that makes a thing what it is (e.g., "iron-ness" or "fire-ness")</term> of fire, or the substantial form of iron, or the form of fire together with the form of iron. It is clear among philosophers that it is impossible for two substantial forms to exist in the exact same matter at the same time. Therefore, it remains that in the matter of glowing iron there must be either the form of iron or the form of fire. Because glowing iron performs the actions of fire by heating and burning—as experience proves—it follows that the substantial form of fire must be in that matter. On the other hand, it is argued that the form of iron must be in the matter, for the iron remains the same individual thing while it is glowing, before it was glowing, and after it has cooled down. One cannot say it is a different piece of iron, or that a numerically different substantial form of iron replaced the original one during cooling. Cooling by air or water alone is not a sufficient process to introduce a brand-new substantial form of iron into the matter...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "intellect in act," using the analogy of red-hot iron to explain how two things can become unified. This page transitions from that analogy into a deeper physical and metaphysical analysis of whether iron remains iron when heated to a glow.</meta>

-># ON ANIMATED BEINGS #<-
<center>d 3</center>
<meta>catchword: Avicenna</meta>

For anything is not generated from just anything, nor in just any place; rather, iron, gold, and other minerals are generated in a specific mine where the "influence" <note>likely referring to celestial or astrological influence believed to guide the formation of metals</note> for the form of iron or gold prevails. And where a mixture occurs that acquires a "complexion" <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—resulting from the blending of elements</term> from opposing mixing elements acting upon one another, it is through this very complexion that the mixture is rendered fit or prepared to receive the substantial form <note>the essential nature that makes a thing what it is</note> of iron. 

Furthermore, it is evident that if red-hot iron is extinguished in any place without the aforementioned mixture of elements, no new substantial form of iron is "clothed" in the matter through cooling alone, nor is a new piece of iron generated that is numerically distinct from the iron that was previously red-hot. And if it should be argued that, according to the alchemist, true gold and true silver can be made in any place, the answer is that the alchemical art <note>original: "ars archimica"</note> imitates nature. It applies active agents to passive subjects, artificially compounding various mixing elements so that, through artificial heat and the proportions of those opposing elements, nature may complete the process by introducing the substantial form of gold or silver into the mixture—provided it has been prepared by the resulting complexion to receive that form. However, in the extinguishing and cooling of iron, no new mixing of elements occurs; therefore, no new iron is generated by the cooling of red-hot iron.

It must be said, therefore, that in red-hot iron, the substantial form of iron remains the same as it was before it was heated. And when it is said that red-hot iron burns and possesses heat in the highest degree, just like fire, the answer is that although it burns like fire—and indeed burns more strongly than a flame—it does not follow that red-hot iron *becomes* fire, nor that the form of fire exists within the iron. Nor is the heat within it identical in nature to the heat of fire in its highest state. Even though red-hot iron burns more powerfully than a thin, flickering flame, this happens only because of a heat that is actually less intense than the heat of fire, but which exists within a hard and solid mixture that contains more matter than a thin flame does. 

As the Arabs <note>referring to Islamic philosophers like Avicenna and Averroes</note> and other philosophers say: air is "moister" <note>in terms of the quality of humidity</note> than water, yet water, which is denser than air and contains more matter, moistens and wets things more effectively than air. Similarly, red-hot iron, retaining its substantial form as iron, burns more strongly than the flame of a fire, even though the flame's inherent heat is more intense than the heat of the red-hot iron. 

And if it is also argued that wood and other combustibles are ignited and burned, and through that burning are corrupted and lose their substantial form—and that iron is similarly ignited, as experience shows, and through that ignition is eventually consumed and loses its substantial form—it would follow that the substantial form of iron is lost in red-hot iron. Consequently, red-hot iron would not be iron, nor would it have the substantial form of iron, but rather the substantial form of fire. To this, it is answered that wood, because of the "rarity" <note>porosity or low density</note> of its substance, is burned part by part and becomes charcoal; and in that part where it becomes charcoal, the wood is destroyed...

<summary>This page uses the physical properties of red-hot iron to argue that a substance's "substantial form" (its essence) remains even when its qualities change, contrasting natural formation with alchemical processes.</summary>

-># AVICENNA #<-

¶ The substantial form <term>substantial form: the essential nature that makes a thing what it is (e.g., "ironness")</term> of charcoal follows within its matter, and as that charcoal is further burned and turned to ash, the matter of the charcoal then receives the form of ash. This ash is certainly not combustible in the way that charcoal or wood was, because no moisture remains in the ash, nor any substance fit to be kindled or inflamed. However, red-hot iron <note>original: "ferrum ignitum"</note>, because of its density and its great mass, although it is set on fire, nonetheless resists burning and corruption. It does not become charcoal, nor is it turned to ash like wood. Instead, as long as the iron is red-hot, it retains the substantial form of iron. The proof of this is that through its extinguishing and cooling, it remains numerically the same iron that it was before it was heated. Truly, it cannot be denied that red-hot iron—after a long delay in a strong fire—may be diminished in some part. This happens because, by the long and powerful action of the fire, certain subtle, scaly parts <note>referring to iron oxide or "slag" that flakes off</note> are separated from the red-hot iron, whereby the iron is reduced. 

From these points, it is clear that red-hot iron is the same iron it was before its heating; it does not differ from its former state except accidentally, through the heat inherent in the iron and united with it, impressed upon it by the fire. Just as a white cloth is made black by a dyeing agent or a black tincture, yet remains the same substance of cloth that it was before it received the black color and was united with it, so too iron, while it is red-hot, receives an accidental warmth <term>accidental: a quality that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist</term> from the fire. This heat, adhering to the dense iron and united with it, burns, heats, and performs the operations of fire. 

With these premises established, let us clarify the comparison mentioned above: just as red-hot iron is a single thing composed of the substance of iron and the accidental heat impressed by the fire—and the red-hot iron is said to be "united" with the fire by means of that impressed heat—so it is because every agent acts through contact, whether mediately or immediately. Likewise, nothing that is acted upon undergoes an effect or receives an impression from an agent except through the aforementioned corporeal contact, or through a spiritual or virtual <note>acting through power or essence rather than physical touch</note> non-corporeal contact. 

And just as the intellect, when it understands some intelligible object, is said to "suffer" <note>original: "pati"; in medieval philosophy, "to suffer" often means to be passive or to receive an impression</note> from it—because the act of understanding consists in a certain being-acted-upon by the intelligible object—it is said to receive an impression and an "intellection" from it. By means of such a received intellection, which is united with the intellect, the intellect is said to be a single thing composed of the substance of the intellect and the aforementioned act of understanding. Thus, the intellect is said to be united with the intelligible object from which it received the understanding and the "intelligible species" <note>the mental image or concept of the thing being studied</note>. 

In a similar way, the virtuous soul—not immersed in these lower earthly things, but raised to the contemplation of God and ignited by divine love, as was the soul of every prophet and of other saints—receives infused knowledge from God. By means of such infused knowledge, received virtually from God, that soul is said to be united with God. From this very union, the aforementioned soul performs miracles and the operations of God the Glorious Himself. ### Chapter nine: On the demonstration of the substance of the soul, and that it can exist or stand without the body according to the logical path.

<margin>A</margin>
One of the logical demonstrations in the affirmation of this inquiry is that we should first set out certain premises. Among these is the fact that a human being forms **universal intentions**, in which many things share, such as "man" in the absolute sense and "animal" in the absolute sense. 

<margin>B</margin>
And indeed, among these universal intentions, there are some formed with a particular composition. Others are formed without composition, but simply. As long as the "final division" or "final part" is not formed, it is impossible for the "first division" or "first part" to be formed. Furthermore, we do not form each of these universal intentions except as a single form, or a **species** stripped of the particular traits of individuals perceived by the senses. This is because the particular or singular examples of any universal concept are not limited in their potential, nor can they be fully numbered; one individual is no more representative of the concept than another. 

Another premise is that whenever a form <note>an essence or quality</note> inhabits a body—or, in short, anything **divisible**—it is then clothed by that body completely throughout all its parts. Thus, whenever a form is fully taken up by something divisible, the form itself becomes divisible. Therefore, every form "clothed" by a body is divisible.

Therefore, there is no necessity for an organ for it; or rather, it does not need an organ for its apprehension. For this reason, it is something that apprehends through itself.

### Clarifications on the ninth chapter.

<margin>A</margin> *AND WHILE the first division is not formed, etc. That is, as long as the intellect does not form simple conceptions, it is not possible for the first division to be formed, that is, for a particular composition to be made by the intellect—such as "this man is a man," or "this man is a rational animal"—because such a particular composition is made from simple **intentions** <term>intentions: here referring to the mental concepts or "aims" of the mind toward a specific object</term>. Wherefore, if the intellect does not form simple thoughts or intentions, it cannot form composite ones. Furthermore, we do not form, etc. That is, our intellect does not form any of those simple intentions except with a single **intelligible species** <term>intelligible species: the mental "form" or essence of a thing as it exists in the mind, stripped of its physical matter</term>, which species is indeed stripped of sensed particular individuations <note>original: "individuationibus"; the specific traits that make one thing different from another, such as height, color, or location</note>. For example, when the intellect forms the universal intention of "man [as] animal," it does not form any of these except with the intelligible species of man stripped of the sensed particular individuations that exist in the individuals contained under "man" and under "animal." Hence, one who understands through the intelligible species of "man" understands "man" absolutely, and does not understand this or that man, nor the individuating conditions existing in this or that 
<margin>B</margin> particular man. For singulars and particular individuals contained under the species of man—although those that exist in actuality have a limited number—nevertheless, those that exist in **potentiality** <term>potentiality: things that could possibly exist but do not yet exist in reality</term> do not have a determined number, nor can they be counted; and the intellect cannot comprehend them, nor are any of them more worthy to be apprehended by the intellect than others and numbered by the intellect and not others. Wherefore the intellect, in forming the simple universal intention of "man," does not form it nor apprehend it except as a single intelligible species, stripped and abstracted from individuals and from the individuating conditions of the particulars contained under the species of man. For it is not necessary that the intellect, in understanding the universal intention of "man," should understand it or form it through all the intelligible species of every individual man, because those individuals are infinite in number in potentiality; nor even through the species of certain individuals, because there is no greater reason for some than for others; wherefore it does not form the universal intention of man except through a single intelligible species, and not many. And what we have said regarding the universal intention of "man" is understood more clearly regarding "humanity" and "animality" in the universal. For each of these intentions is not understood except through a single universal form and species.*

**AND IF THERE** are not some things more worthy than others, *the Arabs <note>original: "Arabes"; referring to Islamic philosophers like Avicenna and his commentators whose work shaped this Latin tradition</note> explain: that is, that there are no individuals more worthy than others in this regard—namely, for forming a universal **intention** <term>intention: a mental concept or the "aim" of the mind toward an object</term>—than any other individuals. Therefore, only one is formed, and by species alone.*

**AND FROM** these [premises] it follows that whenever a form clothes a body, etc. *That is, from these premises, it follows that whenever a form "clothes" a body—meaning the form inheres in a body and is extended along with the extension of the body—it then completely clothes its parts; that is, it is extended to the full extension of its parts.*

**AND FROM** these, *that is, from the premises, it follows that every universal form, etc. For example, "humanity" or "animal nature," when considered simply according to its essence, then it is not possible that if division is considered within it, its parts would be similar to the whole according to its common intention, etc. The text is clear. And the multiplication of individuals within species does not necessitate a division in the abstract reality. For although there are many individual humans with whom the concept "human" communicates, nevertheless, "human" in common, and the essence of "human" in the universal, is one. For "human" in common is one thing and is not divided, just as "unity" in common is one; and although it may exist in this or that thing, nevertheless the division belongs to the **supposita** <term>supposita: the individual, concrete subjects or "things that stand under" a general category</term> which are contained under it, not to the unity in common according to its essence. Thus let it be said of the universal, or of the universal form, that its communication to its individuals is not an essential division of itself.*

**AND FROM** these, *that is, from those premises, it follows that in the aforementioned universal form, when division is considered, it is not possible for its parts to be stripped of all the intentions that are in that universal form or species. For example, in the universal species "human," there is the intention of animality and rationality, because a human is a rational animal. It is impossible that the parts of the universal species of human—namely, individual humans in general—be stripped of the intention of animality and rationality, and so on for others. For if we said that were possible, and said that those parts are separated from the completeness of the universal form—such that those parts are separated and stripped of every intention existing in that universal form, and that the universal form does not **befall** <term>befall: original "accidit"; in medieval philosophy, an "accident" is a property that happens to a thing but is not part of its essential definition (like hair color vs. being human)</term> its parts except through the gathering of those very parts, and that those parts would be things stripped and empty of that form, which only happens to them upon composition and the gathering of the parts themselves—then those parts of the universal form would have the manner of receiving parts, like **matter** <term>matter: the physical "stuff" that receives a form to become a specific thing</term>, and like the integral parts of some quantitative composite. For it is clear that matter, and similarly integral parts—such as the head, hands, and feet—are stripped of the "form of man" before the matter is united to the substantial form of man, and before the hands, feet, and other parts are organized, gathered, and joined; and the form of man does not come to the matter nor to the integral parts, except after the composition, or gathering—*

<summary>This page argues that universal concepts (like "humanity") are indivisible and unified, even though they apply to many different individuals. It contrasts how a physical body is made of separate parts (hands, feet) with how a mental concept remains a complete, single essence.</summary>

# AVICENNA

aggregation. If, therefore, the parts of a universal form were stripped of that universal form—which only comes to them through composition and aggregation—then such parts would have the nature of matter, of integral parts <term>integral parts: the physical components that make up a whole, like bricks in a wall</term>, and of receiving parts. In this way, the parts of "human" in the universal sense, which are the individuals themselves, would have the nature of integral parts. Thus, this human being in himself, and **Plato**, and **Cicero** <note>original: "Plato, & Cicero"; standard examples in Medieval logic for individual people</note> in themselves would not truly be "human." The same would have to be said for other individuals. Consequently, "human" as a universal would not be truly predicated <term>predication: the act of affirming a quality or category of a subject, e.g., saying "Socrates is human"</term> of any individual by themselves or specifically, but would only be predicated of all individuals aggregated together at once, and not separately—which is false. Therefore, in a universal form, division does not occur into parts that are stripped of that form in all its essential meanings.

---

<margin>II</margin>**AND FROM** these [premises], etc. That is, from the aforementioned premises comes the conclusion of the two previous points: that in a universal form, when it is possible for division to be considered, then the parts of that universal are not empty of perfection <term>perfection: in this context, the "completeness" or "fullness" of a definition</term>. Nor are those parts, in themselves, equal to that universal form in a complete equality, such that any one of those parts would possess every perfection held by the universal form that is divided. Therefore, when division is considered in a universal form, those parts are not entirely empty of the perfection found in that universal form, nor are they equal to it—meaning they do not have every perfection that the universal form has. Instead, those parts relate to that universal form like the parts of its definition or description.

Therefore, when "human" in the universal is divided according to consideration, its parts are the parts of its definition, which are the **genus** and the **difference** <note>In Aristotelian logic, a definition is made of a general category (genus) and a specific trait that distinguishes it (difference)</note>—namely, "animal" and "rational." It is clear that the genus—for example, the term "animal"—is not a part that is empty of the perfection of "human" in the universal, because "animal" is included in the universal concept of "human." Yet, the term "animal" does not contain every perfection that "human" contains, because "human" contains the perfection of the "difference" <note>the trait of being rational</note> beyond the perfection of being an "animal." Similarly, the term "rational"—which is the difference and a part of "human" in the universal—is not emptied or stripped of the perfection of "human"; rather, it is included in it. It is not equal to the whole, but is a part of "human" in the universal, just like a part of a definition. It appears, then, that the term "animal" [and "rational"] are what is found when division is considered in them.

Having established these premises, let us say that without doubt the **intelligible form** or **intelligible species** <term>intelligible species: the mental image or concept of an object held in the intellect</term>, and similarly all knowledge, requires a subject. This subject exists from the essence of the human being; it is substantial in itself and serves as the foundation for knowledge. Such a subject is not "empty," but must be either a corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note> substance or an incorporeal <note>non-physical or spiritual</note> substance. And it is not possible for it to be corporeal, because then the universal intelligible species would be divisible...

<summary>Avicenna argues that universal concepts (like "humanity") cannot be physically divided into parts. Instead, they are logically divided into genus and difference, which form a complete definition that applies to every individual.</summary>

# ON THE SOUL

...universals. But in a universal form, or in an **intelligible species** <term>intelligible species: the mental representation or abstract concept of a thing, as opposed to a physical image</term>, no other division can be considered than the one we spoke of first. That is to say, as mentioned above, its parts—when considered in one way, namely simultaneously and joined together—are similar to the whole; yet in another way, they are separate from it. In this second way, those parts possess some of the perfection of that universal whole and some they do not, just like the parts of a definition, as has been said.

In short, each of those parts of that universal form, or universal intelligible species, is itself a certain **universal intention** <term>intention: a mental concept or "meaning" that the mind directs toward an object</term>. For the parts of a definition are the **genus** and the **difference**, or things similar to a genus and a difference <note>In traditional logic, a definition is made of a "genus" (a broad category like 'animal') and a "difference" (the specific trait that sets it apart, like 'rational')</note>. It is clear, moreover, that both the genus and the difference are universal intentions.

If something is composed from a universal form that holds its meaning, such a universal form used in that composition is nothing other than the genus and the difference. Therefore, the parts of a universal form are nothing but the genus and the difference, and each of them is itself a universal form. Because of this, the same must be said of each of those parts as was said of the first: that it has no parts other than those we have mentioned—namely, those of genus and difference.

Finally, because this process cannot go on forever, one must eventually arrive at an **ultimate universal form** which cannot be divided into a genus and a difference. Therefore, since that ultimate universal form has no parts within itself or within its own essence, it cannot <margin>5</margin> inhabit <note>original: "inhærere," a technical term meaning to exist within something as a quality exists in a subject</note> a body or be spread out across the physical extension of a body. If it were, it would have quantitative parts upon which it is based, which is false; for it has been stated that the form exists as a unity without any such parts.

Furthermore, a universal form composed of a higher genus and a difference—which are themselves universal forms—cannot inhabit a body either, because such a form has no parts other than that genus and difference. For example, "human" in the universal sense is composed of the genus and its own specific difference. It is impossible to understand "human" insofar as it is a **rational animal**, or insofar as it is a being possessing life and reason, unless one understands "animal" and "rational," and unless the intelligible species of "life" and the intelligible species of "rationality" are understood. It is impossible for <margin>6</margin> universal forms containing a genus and a difference to be grasped except through the simultaneous grasping of that genus and difference.

Therefore, since a universal form has no parts other than those we have described, it cannot inhabit a physical body. Consequently, the claim of anyone who says that a universal species is based in a body is a false claim. The substance in which a universal intelligible species is based, or into which it arrives, is therefore a **spiritual substance**, not a corporeal one. The soul, then—to which these universal intelligible species come—is an incorporeal substance. And this is what we intended to demonstrate.

...the golden mountain; afterwards, by understanding that a golden mountain is not found [in reality], then a human destroys the species of the golden mountain. And because he understands and knows that a golden mountain is not found, and understands the true mountain as it is found in existence, it is clear that by understanding the true mountain as it is found in existence, and by understanding that a golden mountain is not found, then the intellect receives the **intelligible species** <term>intelligible species: the mental concept or abstract form of an object, rather than a physical image</term> of the true mountain. Thus, it "suffers" <note>In scholastic philosophy, "suffering" (passio) refers to the passive reception of an impression or being acted upon by an external cause</note> from the intelligible species of the true mountain. However, insofar as it understands that the golden mountain—which the human imagines—does not exist, it removes from itself the intelligible species of the golden mountain and its intellection. In this way, the intellect acts.

**AND IT IS NOT** empty of the fact that it be that, etc. That is, such an operation—namely, receiving a species (which is a kind of "suffering") and removing an intelligible species from itself (which is a kind of "acting")—is not empty of the fact that it either occurs with an operation proper to the body, or an operation proper to the **rational power** <term>rational power: the faculty of the soul responsible for abstract thought and reasoning</term>, or an operation common to both of them (namely, the body and the rational power). And it is now clear that such an operation cannot be attributed to the body alone with its own properties. Otherwise, it is explained as "to the body alone, or with its own properties," meaning to the body as a body. For if so, every body would act and suffer, which is impossible; for it is impossible that a body should receive through itself an intelligible form or species, and remove another species from itself, because in that way it would both act and suffer.

<margin>C</margin>
**AND I SAY** that neither, and with commonality. That is, I say that such an operation cannot occur with commonality—namely, of the body and the rational power—in such a way that the body assists the rational power. For the body cannot assist the rational power so that it acts as the subject for the form or intelligible species, and for something through itself, while the power itself strips away or removes from itself the form or intelligible species through itself. For then the body along with the power would become two subjects for this arriving form or species, whereby there would then be two subjects through themselves under the same [form], which is false. Likewise, because nothing is attributed to a corporeal subject except "suffering," as will be said below, therefore the body cannot assist the power to act and remove a species from itself.

<margin>D</margin>
**AND TO THE SUBJECT** it is not attributed. That is, nothing is attributed to a corporeal subject except "suffering." And each of these two are operations—that is, receiving a species and removing a species are operations, one of which is an active operation and the other passive. To a corporeal subject, nothing is attributed except pure passive operation. Therefore, the body does not assist the rational power so that it may be the subject of the species and remove the species from itself; for in that way the body would be the subject of those intelligible species, and thus it would act and suffer, which is false. Therefore, this operation—namely, receiving an intelligible species and removing an intelligible species from itself—is a proper operation proportioned to the rational power.

<margin>E</margin>
**EVERY** thing, however, etc. That is, every thing which, in an operation proceeding through itself from its own essence, does not need another thing to assist it, nor even needs in its own subsistence through itself another thing to assist it:

...*helps: for the presupposition of existing by itself precedes the presupposition of the procession of operations by itself.* <note>In scholastic logic, for something to act independently (procession of operations), it must first be able to exist independently (presupposition of standing).</note> Therefore, if the aforementioned operation is proper to the **rational power**, and proceeds by itself from the rational power, it follows that—just as the rational power causes the aforementioned operations (namely, receiving a species and removing an **intelligible species** <term>intelligible species: the abstract essence or concept of a thing, distinct from its physical appearance</term> from itself, etc.) without the help of the body, as has been proven—and such operations proceed by themselves from the rational power without the help of the body, so also such a rational power can subsist by itself without the body. <margin>F</margin> *RATHER, custom runs in most of them, etc.* <note>original: "IMMO consuetudo currit in plurimo ipsorum"</note> Note that this is verified in well-balanced, well-disposed bodies, in which, although the bodily powers are weak in old age, the intellective power flourishes more than before. In truly unbalanced bodies, however, in which "superfluities" <note>An excess of bodily fluids or "humors" thought to cause illness or mental cloudiness</note> abound in old age, the intellect fails, as seen in those of old age who are not naturally disposed. And in children, because of the poor disposition of the brain, it is necessary for one who understands and acquires knowledge through the discourse of reason to look upon **phantasms** <term>phantasms: mental images derived from the senses, which the mind uses as raw material for abstract thought</term>; and therefore, where the organ of the imagination and the **cogitative power** <term>cogitative power: a faculty in medieval psychology that links sensory data with the intellect; it was believed to be located in the physical brain</term> is poorly disposed, then the soul joined to the body cannot reason or move through natural material things. This is because in such a discourse, as was said above, the intellective soul uses the cogitative power, which is an organic power <note>meaning a power that requires a physical organ to function</note>. In well-balanced elderly people, however, although such an organic cogitative power is somewhat weakened, because the superfluities are not many and the intellective soul is well-disposed for understanding, even a tiny amount of help from the cogitative power is enough for it to reason. And if it is said that from these words it follows that the soul united to the body needs the organic cogitative power, the answer is: it is conceded that the soul needs it in the process of reasoning and in acquiring knowledge from things perceived by the senses. Nevertheless, in the certification of the truth of any thing and in abstraction, the intellective soul refuses the operation of the sense, as was said above, and then it operates by itself, not needing a bodily organ.

Therefore, the emanation itself exists by itself: and whatever has an intelligible form within itself by itself is a substance, not a body, nor in a body, but existing by itself. ...or this source from which the emanation flows, to which the soul is joined, is an intellectual substance—not physical, nor residing within a body, but existing independently. It adheres to, or accompanies, or assists the rational soul, much as light interacts with the sense of sight. Indeed, light—through the simplicity of its own essence—bestows upon sight only the power of apprehension itself, not the specific form being seen. In the same way, this [intellectual] substance, through its simple essence, grants the rational faculty the power to apprehend, and it also causes the intelligible forms <note>the abstract concepts or "blueprints" of things understood by the mind</note> to enter into it, as we have previously explained.

**E** Since the shaping of the rational soul toward these higher forms acts like an accidental instrument through its connection with this substance, the body's preoccupations—arising from its own perceptions, its sorrows, its joys, and its desires—hinder the soul's power from maintaining that connection. Therefore, the soul is not united with this substance except by setting aside all these powers <margin>the powers, namely the sensory ones</margin> and gaining mastery over them, or only when these powers are rejected and controlled. 

Nothing, therefore, prevents the soul from maintaining a persistent union or continuity with that substance except the body itself. Once the soul is separated from the body, its connection to that which perfects it **F** and to that upon which it depends is no longer obstructed. And whatever is connected to its perfecting source and the thing on which it depends is secured against decay—especially if it is not destroyed when the body is cut away or removed. 

**G** Therefore, after death, the soul remains continuously immortal, depending upon this noble substance called the **Universal Intelligence** <term>Universal Intelligence: in medieval philosophy, a higher, divine mind that radiates knowledge to human souls, often identified with the "Active Intellect"</term>. Among the learned teachers of the various faiths, **H** this is referred to as "Divine Wisdom" <note>original: *scientia divina*</note>. 

As for the other powers, such as the animal and vegetative <note>the 'animal' power handles movement and sensation, while the 'vegetative' handles growth and nutrition</note> faculties, they are of such a nature that none of them can perform its specific function without the body. Consequently, they cannot be separated from the body at all; instead, they perish when the body dies. For anything that exists independently but has no function is in **I** vain, and in nature, nothing is created in vain. 

However, through its connection with these lower powers <margin>of them, namely the powers: specifically the animal or vegetative powers</margin>, the rational soul has already acquired their benefits or perfections **K**, and its growth is rooted in them. Had this not been the case, the soul would not have employed these animal powers, nor would it have directed them in its activities. Therefore, the rational soul is separated [from the body] with the extraction—or rather, the fulfillment—of these powers after death. We have now, therefore, set forth the discourse...
