<meta>The previous page discussed Avicenna’s views on the soul’s immortality and its relationship to divine beings. This page, numbered 35, provides commentary on the tenth chapter of a treatise on the soul, contrasting Avicenna’s views with those of the philosopher Averroes and exploring the limits of empirical observation in forming universal truths.</meta>

# ON THE SOUL

### Declarations on the tenth chapter.

<margin>A</margin> From this chapter it appears that Avicenna posits an intellectual substance separate from the body, which inheres in or assists each human soul in the same way that light assists the sense of sight. And such an intellectual substance is the "universal intelligence" <note>often referred in medieval philosophy as the Active Intellect, a celestial force that enables humans to think</note>, which is the principle and cause of understanding, just as light is the cause of vision. And just as one light—for example, the sun—is the cause of many distinct acts of vision, so this intellectual substance and universal intelligence is the principle and cause of many distinct acts of understanding among different men. And if anyone asks the difference between Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd, a 12th-century Andalusian philosopher</note> and Avicenna in this matter, let it be said that according to Avicenna, the principle of understanding in man is the "intellectual soul." This soul is a substance that is not "drawn forth from the potential of matter" <note>meaning it is not merely a product of physical biology</note>, but is the substantial form of the human being. Through the mediation of mental images and the presence or assistance of the aforementioned universal intelligence, this soul is the cause of understanding. Averroes, however, posits that the soul—the substantial form of man—is indeed drawn forth from the potentiality of matter and is destroyed when the man dies. He believes humans possess a "cogitative power" more perfect than the "estimative power" <note>the instinctive ability to perceive intent, like a sheep fearing a wolf</note> found in animals, but that this cogitative power understands only particular, individual things.

<margin>A</margin> **EXPERIENCE** does not cause a necessary judgment, etc.
Note that experiment <note>original: 'experimentum'; in this context, it refers to both a controlled trial and general sensory experience</note> is of two kinds. One kind is approved by everyone, such that nothing is found to contradict what has been experienced—for example, the fact that scammony <term>scammony: a resin extracted from the root of *Convolvulus scammonia*, used since antiquity as a powerful laxative to purge yellow bile</term> purges bile. Such an experiment approved by all causes a "necessary judgment" and certain knowledge. This is what Aristotle meant when he said that art and science are generated from experiment. The other kind is an experiment not approved by everyone. It is possible for something to be experienced by us while something we have not seen or experienced remains different. For example, we have seen and experienced that the animals in our land move their lower jaw when eating; and yet in Egypt, near the Nile, it has been seen and experienced to be otherwise: namely, that the crocodile, when chewing, moves only its upper jaw. Therefore, our experience—that all the animals we have seen move the lower jaw—does not produce a certain and necessary judgment, nor does it produce "science" <note>referring to *scientia*, or certain, universal knowledge</note> that *every* animal moves the lower jaw. Alternatively, it is said that experience does not cause a necessary judgment—that is, a universal judgment or universal science that is true in all cases. When Aristotle said that art and science are generated from experiment, it is understood that they are generated from an experience that is true in *most* cases, but not necessarily in all cases of that category. Therefore, universal science is not generated by mere experiment. Universal science is, instead, the knowledge of things like "the whole is greater than its part" <note>an analytical truth that is true by definition, rather than observation</note>.

<meta>The previous page introduced Avicenna’s concept of the "intellectual soul" as a substance separate from the body, acting as the cause of understanding through the assistance of a "universal intelligence" or "Active Intellect." ->AVICENNA<-

...which is true in all cases. Therefore, such knowledge is not generated from sensory experience, and so forth. <margin>B</margin> **WHEREFORE** our apprehension, or our understanding, that the whole is greater than its part, does not occur because we have sensed every individual part, and so forth.

For the declaration of this text, it must be understood that by "whole" here, the author does not mean "this specific whole" or "that particular object of the senses"; and similarly, by "part" he does not mean "this or that specific sensed part." Rather, by "whole," he understands a being that is greater in an absolute and universal sense, common to any quantity—whether it be discrete <note>original: "quantitate discreta"; refers to items that can be counted, like numbers or people</note> or continuous <note>original: "continua"; refers to things that are measured, like a line or a surface</note>. And by "part," he understands a being that is lesser in an absolute and universal sense, common to both the continuous and the discrete.

With these things established, it must be said that our understanding—that the whole is greater than its part—is not because we have sensed every single part, nor because every "whole" is naturally of this disposition. That is, it is not because we have sensed and experienced through the senses that every whole is greater than its part and every part is smaller than the whole. For it is not impossible (that is, it is possible) for a [particular] whole and part to be different from this rule. For instance, it is possible that a "whole" perceived by the senses is actually smaller than a "part" perceived by the senses, because a sensed whole is a particular object and not a universal, and a sensed part is particular, not universal (since the universal itself cannot be sensed, as is evident).

It is possible for some particular "whole" that is sensed—which is a whole only in relation to what is smaller than it—to not be larger than some other sensed "part" (that is, something that is considered a "part" of something else). For the same thing can be "greater" or "lesser" depending on what it is compared to <note>For example, a cat is a "whole" compared to its tail, but that cat is "smaller" than the "part" of a mountain (like a boulder)</note>. Therefore, some particular whole perceived by the senses, which is "greater" in respect to one thing, is "smaller" in respect to another thing. Thus, our understanding that the whole is greater than the part does not come from sensing these individual things. As has been said, it follows that such an understanding is caused not by the senses, but by divine emanation <note>The "pouring out" of knowledge or light from a higher, divine intellect into the human mind</note>. This understanding, "the whole is greater etc.," simply means that that which is greater is greater than that which is lesser.

<margin>C</margin> **AND SIMILARLY**, it is impossible for two contraries to exist in the same thing at the same time, and whatever things are similar to a third thing are similar to each other: all these truths are understood by divine emanation. And the same discourse applies to our certification, or our knowledge, through demonstration, and so forth.

That is, just as we said regarding the knowledge that the whole is greater than its part—that it is obtained from divine emanation—so it is for the knowledge of the premises used in a demonstration <note>A logical proof</note>. For when such premises are true, they are known and understood by divine emanation. If every premise had to be understood and known through a prior demonstration, then there would either be an infinite process <note>a "regress," where you need a proof for the proof forever</note>, or it follows that one must eventually arrive at certain premises that are not known by the senses (since they are universal truths) nor by demonstration. Therefore, the understanding of these primary premises is obtained from divine emanation, as has been said.

Hence, they seem to forget that knowledge; yet, if the impediments are removed and they wish to investigate that science again, they easily recall and understand what they previously knew. 

Because the soul is entirely removed from these impediments after its separation from the body, it can know many things simultaneously. Therefore, after death, the soul understands what it understood in this life and possesses the sciences it acquired here. *...these things follow intellection and happiness, and what the nature of the soul is, which things do not follow from that, and in what manner souls separated from the body understand those things which they previously understood while they were in this life. And because it was stated above according to the mind of <term>Avicenna<note>original: "Auicennæ"; Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician and philosopher whose work "On the Soul" deeply influenced Western medieval thought.</note></term>, that the aforementioned **universal intelligence** is the most noble substance above all other intelligences immediately after the glorious God, and that it moves the ultimate <term>stellar sphere<note>original: "orbem stellatum"; the outermost shell of the universe containing the fixed stars.</note></term>, and by its power—infused into it by God—all things superior and inferior are moved; and that other intelligences do not act, nor understand, except by its power. Indeed, this universal intelligence, by the will and power of God, flows into the lower intelligences—namely, the intelligences that assist the lower spheres of heaven, such as the sphere of the sun and the moon—providing the power to move the aforementioned spheres and all the knowledge possible to them. For Avicenna said that every single celestial body is animate, and besides a soul, there assists each celestial body an intelligence directing and governing the motion of that celestial body which it assists; and through that medium, it flows into these lower regions the appropriate powers and influences. And because the intelligence moving the <term>sphere of the moon<note>original: "orbem lunae"; in the medieval cosmos, the moon was the closest celestial body to Earth, marking the boundary between the unchanging heavens and the changing world of the four elements.</note></term> is nearer to us, it understands by the power of the superior intelligences (especially by the power of God and the universal intelligence), and in this lower world it flows into mixed bodies <term>substantial forms<note>original: "formas snbstantiales" [sic]; the essential nature that makes a thing what it is (e.g., the "human-ness" of a human).</note></term> and a celestial <term>complexion<note>original: "complexionem"; the specific balance of physical qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) that makes a body fit to receive a specific soul.</note></term>, as well as the powers, qualities, and properties suitable to each mixture and its form. And according to the disposition of matter, it flows substantial forms in such a way that, into matter having the most noble complexion—namely, the complexion proportioned for a human form—it flows and creates a human soul by the power of the glorious God and the aforementioned universal intelligence. Therefore, the intelligence moving the sphere of the moon, because it is more proximate to this lower world and because it imprints more upon these lower things by producing forms, etc., as was said, is called by Avicenna and his followers the **efficient or operating intelligence** <note>original: "intelligentia efficiens seu operans"; often known in English as the "Agent Intellect."</note>, because it operates and effects changes in these lower things and carries out the generation and corruption of mixtures according to the will of God and the universal intelligence. From the aforesaid, therefore, it is clear how, according to Avicenna, the universal intelligence is the most noble over all other intelligences and that it is closest to God, by whose power it flows and distributes knowledge to the other lower intelligences and the power of influencing this lower world. And so that this opinion may be confirmed by reasons, it must be known according to Avicenna and other <term>Arabic philosophers<note>original: "philosophos Arabicos"; referring to the Islamic Golden Age thinkers whose Latin translations revolutionized 12th and 13th-century European science.</note></term> that among those things counted as first principles known through themselves is this: that **from the one, insofar as it is one, only one proceeds** <note>original: "ab uno, inquantum unum, non prouenit nisi unum"; a central Neoplatonic axiom used to explain how a single, simple God could create a complex, diverse universe.</note>. Moreover, it most greatly suits the glorious God to be one, insofar as He is one, since God is the most simple and pure of all. Therefore, from God there proceeds only one thing; this one thing, however, which proceeds from God and has a dependency upon Him, is nothing other than the universal intelligence mentioned above...*

...written, which is a more pure abstract substance beneath God, possessing less dependency than other lower intelligences. While those lower beings depend for their existence, knowledge, and action not only on God but also on the higher intelligences above them, the **universal intelligence** depends solely upon the glorious God. For this reason, it is more simple, pure, and noble than all other intelligences.

This opinion harmonizes with the words of Scripture in the first chapter of Genesis: *And the spirit of the Lord was moved over the waters* <note>original: "Et spiritus domini ferebatur super aquas"; Genesis 1:2.</note>. From this, it is inferred that this spirit was created before the earth and the water. Therefore, according to Holy Scripture, the first thing God created was the spirit—that is, a spiritual, intellectual substance separate from any body, just like the aforementioned **universal intelligence**. The <term>Arab philosophers<note>original: "philosophi Arabes"; likely referring to thinkers like Al-Farabi and Avicenna who synthesized Aristotelianism with Neoplatonism.</note></term>, in accordance with their faith, say this was created immediately by God.

According to other philosophers who maintain the <term>eternity of the world<note>A controversial philosophical view (often associated with Aristotle) that the universe has no beginning in time, contrasting with the creationist view.</note></term>, it is said that such an intelligence depends more directly on the glorious God than the other intelligences do.

According to <term>Avicenna<note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), whose works formed the backbone of medieval psychological and cosmological study.</note></term> and other faithful Arabs, a pure and simple spirit first proceeds and is created by the glorious God; this is the **universal intelligence**, from which many other things are caused and proceed. For this universal intelligence understands that it was created by God, and that by God’s power it flows into the lower intelligences. It acts through secondary causes—the sun and the moon—and through the intelligence that moves the <term>sphere of the moon<note>original: "orbem lunæ"; in medieval cosmology, the moon was the closest celestial body to Earth, and its 'intelligence' (the Agent Intellect) mediated between the divine and human realms.</note></term>, which is known as the <term>agent<note>original: "operans seu efficiens"; often referred to in philosophy as the "Agent Intellect," the force that makes potential knowledge actual in the human mind.</note></term> or efficient intelligence.

Therefore, because it depends on God and because other lower things depend on it, many things are caused by this intelligence. From what has been said, it is clear how the universal intelligence, according to Avicenna and other Arabs, is the most noble of all intelligences, closest to God in knowledge, understanding, and other perfections. It also explains how ultimate <term>blessedness<note>original: "beatitudo, et felicitas ultima"; the state of supreme spiritual joy and fulfillment.</note></term> and happiness result from the union of the human soul with this universal intelligence, as previously mentioned.

# AVICENNA’S BOOK ON THE RETURN, TRANSLATED FROM ARABIC INTO LATIN BY ANDREA OF BELLUNO.

### *The first chapter concerning the definition of "Almahad"—that is, the state or place to which a person or their soul returns after death.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'A' featuring a classical or floral design within a square frame.</image-desc>

**A**lmahad <note>original: *almahad*; from the Arabic *al-ma'ād*, meaning "the place of return" or "resurrection."</note> is indeed derived in the Arabic language from the Arabic word *alhaud* <note>original: *alhaud*; likely a transliteration of *al-awd*, meaning "the return."</note>, meaning "return." Its true nature, essence, or definition is the place or state in which a thing once existed, from which it was separated, and to which it later returns. Subsequently, this name *mahad* has been applied to the state or place that a person reaches after death. Indeed, manifest judgments and many opinions agree that from the state one reaches after death, there was a separation before this first life began. For many peoples believe that spirits or souls exist before bodies, and that they existed in a world that is secondary to this world <note>The text suggests a Neoplatonic view where the spiritual realm is the primary reality, and the physical world is a secondary "place" the soul visits.</note>. Their return to that world, for those who are perfect or who have done good works, is to the highest good, which is Paradise and the heavenly place. For the wicked or those who have done evil, the return is to a place of sorrow, which is Hell and punishment. Most of these people believe that a man's father and mother also come from that world, which is why there is a continuous likeness and offspring returning to it. In the first books, as well as the books of the ancient Israelite and Christian prophets, this "return" (*mahad*) is testified and confirmed. Furthermore, in the book of Muhammad <note>The Quran.</note>, God said: "Come, O beautiful soul, return to your Creator, so that you may receive the reward for your merits." <note>original: "Veni o anima formosa, redi ad tuum Creatorẽ..."; a Latin rendering of Quran 89:27-28, usually translated as "O reassured soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing [to Him]."</note> He did not say "return" except to a "where," a place, or a state from which it came. Thus, we have now explained what *mahad* is.

**I**T SHOULD BE NOTED that *mahad* is a common name for every kind of return of a person after death, whether that return is according to the body alone—as the <term>vain-speaking Arabs<note>original: *Arabes uanaloquentes*; likely referring to the *Mutakallimun* or traditionalist theologians who argued for a purely physical resurrection, a view the philosopher Avicenna found intellectually lacking.</note></term> have said—or whether it is according to both body and soul together, or according to the soul alone, which returns after separation from the body to its simple being which it possessed before its union with the body. In this aforementioned return, the soul receives its reward or punishment.

<summary>This page introduces Avicenna's treatise on the afterlife, defining "Almahad" (The Return) as the soul's journey back to its pre-corporeal state. It reconciles Islamic, Jewish, and Christian views on the soul's pre-existence and its eventual return to a state of reward (Paradise) or punishment (Hell).</summary>

### Chapter Two: On the diversity of opinions concerning the *mahad*.

The world holds opinions regarding the *mahad* <note>The "Place of Return" or Resurrection.</note> according to two sects. In one is a smaller number of people who are lacking in intellect and who deny the *mahad* itself. In the other, however, is a great crowd of people who possess clear knowledge and intellect and who affirm the aforementioned *mahad*. Among these latter thinkers, a difference of opinion arises: for some attribute the *mahad* to bodies alone; some to souls only; and some to both souls and bodies together.

Those who say the *mahad* pertains only to bodies were among the number of "vain-talking" Arabs <note>original: *Arabum vaniloquentium*; likely referring to the *Mutakallimun* or Islamic dialectical theologians, whom philosophers like Avicenna often criticized for using rhetorical arguments rather than strict logic.</note>, who said that the body alone is the living being, and that a human is human by virtue of the "life" and "humanity" generated within him. They argue that both of these are accidents <note>In medieval philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change or disappear without the thing itself ceasing to exist (like the color of a shirt), as opposed to an "essence."</note> of the person, and that death is the deprivation of these properties or something contrary to them. They believe that in the "second world" <note>the afterlife</note>, life and humanity will be created anew in that body after its corruption and disintegration, and thus that person will be made the same living being again.

Furthermore, the aforementioned Arabs diversify after this point and branch out into different views. For some of them say that humans after that—that is, after the first death—will be divided into two different groups: the virtuous good and the vicious. The virtuous will be affected by a reward and eternal bliss, while the vicious will be tortured by eternal punishment. Others say that humans at that hour, or in the other world, will be divided into three groups. For then the people who were of good belief and were virtuous will be blessed forever.

<margin>A</margin>

Regarding those who believed well but lived badly, it is said that they are subject to the judgment of God; He punishes them or shows them mercy if He wishes, and no perpetual burden is imposed upon them. Others say of these people that they will not be tortured at all, nor will anything be imposed on them forever. Those, however, who were heretics <note>original: *heretici*; those who held "wrong" or "bad" beliefs.</note> will be tortured with perpetual punishment. 

Concerning those who will be punished—namely, the good believers who lived badly or the bad believers like heretics—some say that the punishment of things will not be eternal, but that for the blessed, the bliss will be eternal. Others say that neither bliss nor punishment will be eternal. 

Those who say the *mahad* pertains to the soul and body together all posit that life is caused by the presence of the soul in the body, and death by the separation of the soul from the body. They posit that in the next age, the soul returns to the same body in which it previously existed, and they affirm that the soul is something spiritual...

**AND CERTAIN** ones will that thing—namely, blessedness and punishment—to be in the soul itself, along with its perfection in its own substance and its liberation, etc. *And these are the most illustrious wise men. Note that the most illustrious wise men who posited this were Plato, Socrates, and their like; for they said that blessedness and happiness exist when the soul has acquired speculative and practical sciences, and that the soul, beyond this, possesses moral habits such that the soul is free from material impressions—namely, from sensible things—in such a way that the soul is not dominated by the senses. But when the soul has a contrary disposition—for example, if it is deprived of scientific and practical habits and moral habits, and sensible things make an impression upon the soul, and the senses dominate reason—whence the soul becomes vicious, then it is unhappy. And according to these philosophers, unhappiness exists in this world just as in the other; but in the other world it will be more intense. *It should be noted that the opinion of the "al-tanasukh"* <note>original: *altenasach*, from the Arabic *tanāsukh*, meaning transmigration or metempsychosis</note> *is so named because "nasakh" in Arabic is the same as the permutation of a thing from one disposition to another, or from one being to another; therefore, the opinion which holds that souls are permuted from body to body is called "al-tanasukh".*

**UNTIL SUCH A SOUL IS PERFECTED** and disposed so that it may be liberated from matter, etc. *It must be known, according to the opinion of these men, that a vicious soul is not disposed to be liberated from the body and from matter, and, having been separated from the body, to return to its creator and to its principle. For according to them, the soul is not united to a body except so that, by the mediation of the organic senses, it may acquire cognition, knowledge, and moral and virtuous habits. Therefore, a virtuous and learned soul, once separated from the body, since it is perfect, does not need to be permuted into another body, but returns and goes to its principle and is united with it, and then it possesses happiness completely. But a vicious soul does not cease being permuted from body to body until it is perfected—namely, by abandoning vicious habits and acquiring virtuous habits; for a soul which was vicious in one body can be made virtuous in another body, and through such a permutation from one body to another body, it can be perfected and disposed so that it is fit to be separated from matter and return to its creator, to be united with him, and to acquire perfect happiness.*

<margin>H</margin>

### Chapter Three: Regarding the refutation of false opinions concerning the Return.

The sect of those who asserted that the <term>Return (mahad)</term> <note>original: *mahad*, from the Arabic *al-ma'ād*, referring to the "place of return" or the afterlife</note> belongs to the body alone were moved to hold that position by those things affirmed in any law or faith regarding the resurrection of the dead. <margin>A</margin> And those following this sect were of the opinion that whatever is considered according to the essence of man is the body; afterward, they arrived at this conclusion out of their excessive hatred toward the wise <note>likely referring to the philosophers or *falasifa*</note> and the excessive inclination of their minds toward those things which differ from the opinion of the wise, to the point that they denied that a soul or spirit exists at all. I say that such truth as described above cannot be manifested to the common people. **Addition by a most learned man.**
To this argument, one can respond according to the various opinions of the doctors <note>The "doctors" refers to established academic authorities or theologians.</note>. And first, according to the mind of **Plato**, who holds that man is solely an intellectual soul and the body is merely the soul's instrument. In this opinion, the same man returns in number <note>The phrase "in number" refers to numerical identity—being the exact same individual, not just a similar one.</note>, because the soul "informs" <note>In philosophy, "to inform" means to give shape, life, or essence to matter.</note> different bodies and different matters at different times; and since the soul is the same in number, the same man returns in number. According to the way of **Averroes**, the soul alone belongs to the <term>quiddity</term> <note>From "quidditas," meaning the "what-ness" or the essential nature of a thing.</note> of the composite; however, the material parts of a man flow and ebb, as he himself holds in the first book of *On Generation*, commentary 38.
</margin>

is not a man by virtue of his matter, but by virtue of his **form** <note>Following Aristotelian logic, "matter" is the physical stuff (like clay), and "form" is the organizing principle or soul (like the shape of a vase) that makes a thing what it is.</note> existing in his matter. And the operations of a man do not proceed from him except because of the presence of the form in the matter. When the form is removed from its matter and has returned—or if its matter has been changed into earth, or into another thing—then that man is already destroyed. Afterward, when a new human form is produced in that same matter, then another man arrives or results from it; he is **not that man who was there before**. For in this second case, that which is found from among the things that were in the first is his matter, and not his form. And this second man is not the one who was there before, nor is he the one who was to be praised or blamed; nor does he deserve a reward, or happiness, or punishment by virtue of his matter, but by virtue of his form. And it is by this—that he is the **same in number**—that he is a man, and not by the fact that he is earth. Therefore, it is manifest that the man who is blessed or damned would not be the same man who acted well or acted poorly. Rather, he would be another man sharing with him the matter which he previously had. Therefore, that **resurrection of bodies** or that aforementioned "return" of bodies will not be that which causes happiness to reach those who lived well, and punishment to reach those who lived poorly. Instead, one distinct from him who worked well would be made happy, and one distinct from him who worked poorly would be punished. Therefore, those discourses most remote from what is appropriate regarding the <term>mahad</term> <note>From the Arabic *al-ma'ad*, meaning "the place of return" or the afterlife.</note> are those which posit that the *mahad* itself pertains only to the body. However, those who posited that spirits or souls remain—and that true reward or true punishment is distributed to those same remaining souls, and that the body is not renewed upon them except as an **accident** <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a non-essential quality (like hair color) that can change without changing the core substance of a thing.</note> is renewed upon a substance existing through itself—they have judged falsely. And their opinion will appear unstable or incorrect if [it is presented]...

<summary>Avicenna argues that human identity is defined by "form" (the soul) rather than "matter" (the body). He concludes that a physical resurrection of the same matter without the same continuous form would result in a different person, rendering divine reward and punishment unjust.</summary>

### CONCERNING THE RETURN

<margin>
By this path, it would be said that the same man returns according to the intellectual soul, which constitutes the human quiddity <term>quiddity: the "whatness" or essential nature of a thing</term>, even though the material parts and the matter itself are constantly changing (whatever may be the case regarding the human cogitative faculty). But among the holy doctors <note>original: "sacros doctores." Likely referring to Christian theologians who attempted to reconcile Avicenna with church doctrine.</note>, they would say that the "radical matter" contracted from the origins of birth is preserved by God through His omnipotence, and thus the same individual returns in number <term>in number: numerical identity, meaning the exact same individual rather than just a similar one</term> in the resurrection.
</margin>

...these presuppositions or premises having been granted, and it having been known: first, that given that opinion, the matter existing in created things would not be sufficient for the individuals of the soul existing separately from the body at the time of resurrection or the union of the soul with the body. Or it was known second, that [the divine judgment is one and unchangeable in its predestined course <margin>a. Alternative reading: divine operation is one and not changeable.</margin>]. Or it was known third, that the soul's existence in its body is contrary to the true happiness of a human being; and that bodily pleasures are different from true pleasures; and that while the soul exists in the body, it suffers pain. Or it was known fourth, that many things which were revealed concerning faith in this place, or in this life—when they are understood exactly as they are publicized—are empty and false.

Now, the knowledge of the first point is made manifest through the explanation of divine operation; and we have already verified this in both divine and natural science. The knowledge of the second point is made manifest when it is declared that the first being <note>The "First Being" refers to God.</note>, existing through itself, is stripped of all types of alterations and changes; and that its operation, proceeding from its judgment and its will, conforms to its eternal and predestined judgment, and its determined eternal will. This has already been certified in divine science. For the knowledge of the third point, I will create its own specific chapter. 

As for the knowledge of the fourth point, the wise man perceives it from within himself without need for instruction. Indeed, it is not appropriate that this be revealed to the ignorant, lest they look upon the true laws with an ambiguous eye, or with an ambiguous mind that despises them, since the true laws must be firmly believed without any contempt or ambiguity. For those to whom the grasp of wisdom has been granted—and who do not hastily deny those things which were most fittingly revealed through appearances and sensible things, nor blame those things which are not manifest, in which the true intention is hidden and intrinsic, perceived only by the wise—they will finally clearly know those things pertaining to faith. This is especially true when faith has been revealed according to this form or condition: namely, that the true intention in those things which are affirmed and publicized is hidden. 

Indeed, this condition is one of the greatest conditions of faith, or of the true law, which is revealed—whether according to the true form, or according to a likeness or metaphor—in which a wise man does not doubt as he might doubt in the faith or law of the Magians <note>original: "Almagius." Referring to the followers of Zoroastrianism.</note> and the Sabians <note>original: "Althenię." Referring to a religious group often identified in Islamic philosophy as star-worshipers or Hellenized pagans.</note>.

<meta>This page continues Avicenna’s investigation into the "Return" (the afterlife). # ->AVICENNA<-

<meta>catchword: nourishment.</meta>

...because such a faith, or the law of the **Magians** <note>original: "Almagius," referring to the Zoroastrians</note>, was revealed according to a mode and form such that the things published within it appear true externally and to the senses among the ignorant. But the internal and hidden meaning, as far as the rational intellect is concerned, is false. And this form and condition of revealing faith and law is the primary characteristic of a corrupt and false faith, which does not proceed nor emanate from divine grace.

For in the aforementioned faith or law of the **Magians**, it is said that good proceeds from light, and evil from darkness. And they claim that light and darkness are the only two principles of all things. These things are indeed stated externally, and to the senses they seem true, but internally among the wise they are false. 

From these premises, therefore, the falsehood of the aforementioned opinion appears. It will be made even more manifest when the falsehood of the opinion of **transmigration** <term>Altenafach: a Latinization of the Arabic *al-tanasukh*, referring to the transmigration of souls or reincarnation</term> is declared, and when the impossibility of the return or reunion of the separated soul to bodies is affirmed. We shall declare that in its proper place. 

Truly, we will not leave this discussion without some clear explanation, contradicting those who have posited that the **Return** <term>mahad: from the Arabic *ma'ad*, meaning "the place of return," used here for the resurrection</term> applies to the body and soul together. They claim that the soul, in the resurrection, will be reunited to the same matter and the same body with which it was previously united. 

Let us say, therefore, that it is impossible unless the soul returns either to the matter from which it was separated, or to some other matter. Now, it has already been stated in the accounts of the opinions of those who speak on this topic that they intend for the return of the soul to be made to that same matter from which it was separated. If this is so, it must be either the matter that was present at the moment of death, or the total sum of matter with which the soul was joined during the entire duration of its first life. 

If it were only that matter which was present at the hour of death, then it would be necessary for a person to rise wounded, perhaps with a severed nose or ear, or missing a limb, just as they were in battle at the hour of their death, according to that physical state. And this is considered an error even among those who hold this opinion. 

Or, if they claim that all the parts should rise which a person possessed during the entire time of their life, then it follows from that opinion that one and the same body would rise with those same members—namely, the hand, head, liver, and heart—and with the same parts of those members. But this is false and impossible, since the firm truth is that the members are continually being dissolved and restored. The parts of the members are continually being broken down and exchanged through **nourishment** <note>original: "nutricatione," following the catchword "tione"</note>...

<summary>Avicenna critiques the Zoroastrian dualism of light and dark and argues against the physical resurrection of the body, pointing out the logical absurdities of returning to a body that is constantly changing its material makeup.</summary>

### ON THE RETURN

...tion. And some of these are nourished from the excess nourishment of another, and thus it is impossible that the same body should rise again with the same members and with all the matter that it possessed throughout the entire time of its life. Otherwise, a man would rise with his members in an excessive quantity, as large as a mountain <note>Avicenna argues that if every bit of matter a person ever consumed throughout their life were restored at once, the resulting body would be gargantuan.</note>. 

And it follows necessarily from that opinion that a man nourished on human flesh—in those regions where it is said that men eat men—after he has grown and reached perfect increase from the nourishment of human flesh, would be unable to rise. For the substance of his parts, which was once the substance of another, will either rise in that other person, or he himself will rise and the parts of the other who was eaten will be missing. Therefore, the one who was eaten will not rise. 

And if they say that the parts in the one rising will be the <margin>L</margin> **primary or substantial parts**, by which it is verified that his life consists, this argument is not valid. Even in this statement, they do not escape the inconsistency. For it is already established among them—and they deem it right and fitting—that for the life of a man, certain of his parts are "substantial" and "radical" <note>original: "radicales," meaning the fundamental roots or essence of the physical body</note> to his life, and certain of them are merely "auxiliary" to life and not substantial. 

And if they say that the resurrection occurs from that specific earth [or] from the earth of another equally and indifferently: then <margin>M</margin> <margin>Another version: and</margin> they take away and remove the judgment of justice which they themselves place in the resurrection of the body's members—unless they posit that the parts appropriated for resurrection have a "property of intention." Yet such an intention was removed by them, and this is that intention: that those very parts, in the time or disposition of the prior life, were the matter of the substantial parts of life. 

But <margin>N</margin> this discourse, which without reason appropriates some similar parts of the body to the resurrection and does not appropriate others, is an untrue discourse. It posits that the "privation of intention" <term>privation of intention: a technical term referring to the lack of a specific formative purpose or capacity in matter</term> mentioned above is the cause for why something should possess and receive that intention, while another thing—namely, that which does not have the privation of intention—should not possess it, nor ought it <margin>O</margin> to receive that intention. 

And indeed, the disposition of the privation of a thing [having been made, and of a thing possible to exist in being, which nevertheless does not exist] <margin>Another version: existing, or the privation of a future thing not existing.</margin> is in a single matter that receives that very privation, because there is no greater reason for one matter than for another. And when you have considered and scrutinized this, it will appear...

<meta>This page continues Avicenna’s investigation into the material paradoxes of physical resurrection. He is specifically refuting the idea that a body can be reconstituted if its constituent matter has been recycled through the natural world—consumed as food and integrated into the bodies of others.</meta>

### AVICENNA

...to you, that most of those things which are upon the face of the earth are bodies of the dead, stripped of their souls and turned into earth, over which the plow has passed. And in these, seeds have been sown. From these seeds, food is produced and manufactured, and thus nourishment occurs, either by the consumption of the corpses of other bodies, or by the consumption of matter which was previously under the form of other bodies. 

How, therefore, is it possible that matter—which at two different times served as the subject for the forms of two different men—should rise at the same time in a single hour, without a division of that matter? Since matter itself, by its very nature, is not divisible <note>Avicenna argues that a specific quantity of matter cannot be split to satisfy the "substantial" requirements of two different people simultaneously; if it is divided, neither person is "whole."</note>? 

But if someone should say that the soul will be reunited to a body composed of whatever earth, air, water, or fire happens to be available, and that it is not a condition—nor is it necessary—that there be in that aforementioned resurrected body those same elements, or those same parts of elements, which existed in the first life: then such a statement is the same as the doctrine of manifest **Altenasach** <note>original: *Altenasach*; a Latinization of the Arabic *al-tanāsukh*, which refers to the transmigration of souls or reincarnation. Avicenna is accusing his opponents of accidentally supporting reincarnation by suggesting the soul can inhabit "new" matter.</note>. 

<margin>Q</margin> And indeed, the first statement is also really the doctrine of **Altenasach**, even if in appearance and manner of speaking it seems to differ and behave otherwise. 

<margin>R</margin> For the truth is that there is no difference between two types of matter, or between two similar elements, or between two similar parts of elements, in one of which there was a human form of which it is now deprived, and in the other of which there was never a human form. 

But [the matter] now puts on a human form and receives it—namely, at the hour of informing <note>The "hour of informing" refers to the moment the soul (the "form") enters and organizes the physical matter into a living body.</note> and the reunion of the soul in the second life, or in the other world. And if the spirit or soul returns, or is reunited with one of those two matters, the opinion of **Altenasach** follows. Similarly, **Altenasach** becomes true if the soul is united to the other matter. 

Since the second human body is not the same human body that existed before, and the return or union of the spirit or soul to a body other than the first body is true **Altenasach**—that is, it is to posit that a transformation of the soul from body to body truly occurs, just as the proponents of **Altenasach** maintained. 

<margin>S</margin> If they wish, and if it pleases them, that by the name **Altenasach** we should understand the migration of the soul to a body that does not share even one numerically identical part of matter with the first body (as they themselves affirm in their own speech), nevertheless, the underlying intent in these views is the same and not at all different.

<margin>
**1.** Regarding the things produced by God in the human body, namely **impassibility** <note>original: *impassibilitate*; the theological concept that the resurrected body cannot suffer, die, or be changed by external forces</note>. For the body of the blessed can be affected by no alteration or tearing apart of its parts. **2.** There will be **clarity** <note>original: *claritas*; a divine radiance</note>: for the body will be made luminous and bright by such clarity, just as the body of Christ appeared to the disciples when they said, "It is good for us to be here," for the face of Christ then shone with the clarity which is the second gift of beatitude. **3.** The third gift is **subtlety** <note>original: *subtilitas*; the ability of the glorified body to pass through other matter</note>, that is, the penetration of the blessed body through any other body, just as the blessed Christ entered through closed doors saying, "Peace be unto you." **4.** The gift with which the body of the rising blessed person is adorned is **agility** <note>original: *agilitas*</note>, because according to their will, they will be able to transport themselves from place to place in the shortest circuit of time. 

Truly, there would be a difficulty as to whether a blessed person, affected by this gift of agility, moves from place to place in an instant—and especially in the Empyrean heaven <note>the highest, most spiritual part of heaven in medieval cosmology</note>, where there is no external resistance—nor can there be a descent to the internal resistance of the heavy and light elements. This is because in the blessed body there would be no internal weariness, and again, the resistance of heavy and light elements happens in the sphere of active and passive things; but in the Empyrean heaven, there is neither ascent nor descent. Or, if it is said that this motion will be successive <note>occurring in a sequence of time rather than all at once</note> because of the opposition of the starting point and the destination—for one cannot be at the starting point, the middle, and the destination at the same time—otherwise there would be no succession, and consequently no motion, as is clear from its definition. For motion is the "act of a being in potency insofar as it is in potency" <note>A classic Aristotelian definition of motion</note>. Or one might imagine it according to the opinion of the **Subtle Doctor** <note>original: *doctoris subtilis*; a standard reference to the Franciscan theologian John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308)</note>. Since the body of the blessed possesses this gift of agility, and since this agility is a finite power, it will act with a finite action; consequently, it cannot be in the middle and the destination at the same time. I believe this opinion should be followed more closely by our theologians.

<margin>The belief of faith is greater than all natural reason, because God can neither deceive nor be deceived.</margin>

<margin>We have two laws revealed by God: one of the Jews, the other of the Christians. <margin>The Christian law, truly, [is] from the blessed Christ, who is God and man.</margin>

<margin>Therefore, there is greater belief in faith than there is in natural demonstrations, because God himself cannot make a law revealed by him be false; but indeed, the glorious God, since he is above nature, can overturn and annihilate nature.</margin>

<margin>Therefore, it must be learnedly asserted that the truths handed down in faith are more certain than natural truths: although natural truths are more evident to us, because they proceed according to our mode of understanding, which depends on the senses and mental images <note>original: *phantasmatibus*; the internal images the mind uses to process sensory data</note>.</margin>

[The text discusses] the unity of [God] himself, and concerning his judgment and his justice, and concerning his stripping away <note>original: *denudatione*; the philosophical process of removing human limitations from our concept of God</note> of conditions that imply defect or diminishment; and concerning the nature of angels, and the narration of divine causes in a general or coarse way <note>original: *groffo modo*</note>, not in a particular or subtle speculative way, but describing them in a manner that the common people may appropriately perceive and understand. This is done by figuring or describing them with the best and most appropriate imagery, so that the people may imagine and grasp them, rather than describing them according to pure rational intent. Let spiritual substances also be described in the aforementioned "shadowy" manner <note>original: *vmbrose*; meaning figuratively or indirectly</note>, which none perceive except the intellect of the wise. Furthermore, Muhammad <note>original: *Maumethus*</note> said that the people should be attracted, and fear and horror should be struck into them by announcing reward and punishment, or bliss and torment. Let the bliss of those who have deserved well be described not with a divine and sublime description—which is what they truly possess—but rather with a description intelligible to the people and more suitable to them. That is to say, that bliss is delight, and tranquility, or joy; and let torment and punishment be described as being the opposite of this. Let bodily delight be divided into things seen, heard, smelled, touched, and tasted, and into intercourse <note>original: *coitum*</note>, in which there is the delight of things felt by touch. And he asserts that in paradise itself there are palaces, and houses, and tents in which are spread cloths made of silk. And he says that the width of each paradise is according to the width of heaven and earth, and those things which run in their course. The division of spiritual delight or bliss, however, is because there is a deprivation of sadness and fear, and a continuation of gladness, and joy, and mirth; and the greatest delight and bliss of all these is to be visited by Him who created the two worlds—or it is to gaze upon Him who created the heaven

# ON THE RETURN
<note>original header: *DE ALMAHAD*; from the Arabic *al-Ma‘ād*, a term used in Islamic philosophy to describe the resurrection or the "return" of the soul.</note>

...and the earth, and the veil covering God himself, is removed from him, so that he may be perceived by the blessed. And although some deny these things, they are nevertheless true, and must be held firmly in the law according to the judgment of many wise men who agree on these aforementioned matters, which have been frequently revealed.

For the unrefined people <note>original: *populus rudis*; the common folk or those without philosophical training</note>, when they are exhorted to goodness and to the justice that pertains to humanity, are then exhorted to that which is different from their own sensual nature. They are asked to act in a way that is contrary to the movements of the powers of the sensitive soul <note>the part of the soul responsible for physical senses and emotions</note>, which often dominate the rational soul—as if the rational soul does not exist at all, or has no being at all, or as if the rational soul were entirely deprived of its own operations and powers. In such a state, the unrefined people do not obey, nor do they comply with those things to which they are exhorted according to the law, justice, and goodness.

Furthermore, it is impossible for there to be one man whom all nations and peoples fear, and in whom they hope, and whom they obey, unless a punishment for evil deeds and a reward or prize for good deeds is made manifest to them. Therefore, it was necessary to affirm and manifest that which God has prepared in the other world for those who act well and those who act poorly. And it was necessary to describe it in a description through which the nations might understand it and be able to imagine it.

Therefore, for those who act well, Muhammad said that the things we have listed <note>referring to sensory delights of paradise</note> should be described; but for those who act poorly, the opposite of those things should be described—namely, that there will be fire and afflicting cold. And there will be harassing demons casting the bodies of the wicked into the fire and into the cold. And there will be iron <margin>x</margin> chains, and constraints, and bonds; and there the wicked will eat things that are unclean and dung-like, and they will drink poisons. Their heads will be struck, and their skin will be renewed after their skin has been eaten away by fire, so that their torment may never end.

For if true blessedness and true torments—both of which, as they exist in truth, are far removed from the understanding and intellect of the common people—were not made manifest through clear and well-known examples, then the nations would not hope for the good to come, nor fear the evil to come. And if they did not believe in the resurrection of their bodies, then those people would not believe in these two things: namely, future blessedness and punishment. Therefore, it was necessary among the wise men of the divine laws to affirm and manifest the *mahad* <note>the "Return" or Resurrection</note> and the resurrection of bodies.

# AVICENNA

...resurrection, and the accounting—or retribution—of good and evil works, and to affirm blessedness and future punishment according to this manner. This is the manner which Muhammad <note>original: *Maumethus*</note>, the founder of our law, described more perfectly than all others, so much so that it is impossible to add anything at all to the aforementioned way. 

However, what the Christians affirm concerning the resurrection of bodies—that they must remain in another life without food, clothing, and sexual intercourse—is a weaker and less rational discourse, toward which people are less inclined regarding the matter of the <term>mahad</term> <note>From the Arabic *al-Ma‘ād*, meaning "the place of return" or "the resurrection."</note>. This is because if the reason for the resurrection is that man is a body, or that he is a body sharing with the soul in good and evil actions, and it is therefore necessary that a resurrection occurs, then this reasoning must lead to a specific conclusion: it necessitates that the body must be rewarded and punished with a physical reward or corporal punishment that is understandable to the common people or the nations. 

If the blessedness and torment were to be spiritual only, as the Christians say, what then would be the intention, or what would be the intended purpose of the resurrection of bodies? Furthermore, one must ask what kind of blessedness and spiritual reward that would be, and what kind of torment or spiritual punishment it would be, and how it could be described or made manifest to peoples and nations so that they might hope for a reward and fear a future punishment. 

Certainly, there is no assignable way in which these things can be described. Indeed, according to the Christians who posit that reward or punishment is only spiritual and not physical, nothing of the aforesaid can be made manifest or described, except that men in the other life will be like angels. And if it were described to these peoples that reward and punishment in the other life will be spiritual—while adding a description different from that predicted by those Christians who claim rewards are only spiritual—then the people will be seduced away from the knowledge of blessedness and punishment, and they will wander in error regarding it. Concerning the spiritual <term>mahad</term> and the spiritual blessedness and punishment of the other life, they will understand something entirely different from what has been published and revealed by the Christians themselves. 

Truly, that which the unrefined Christian people imagine regarding what has been said—namely, that after the resurrection men will be in paradise like angels—although these unrefined Christians do not dare to express their own imagination concerning this, nor...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the resurrection (mahad). # CONCERNING THE RESURRECTION

...to make known: it is that if humans in the next life are to be like the angels, then they would not be rewarded in any way that involves pleasure and tranquility. This is because if they were like angels—neither eating, nor drinking, nor engaging in sexual intercourse—then the unrefined people <note>original: *populi rudes*; referring to those without philosophical training or spiritual "intellect."</note> imagine that even if humans were to pray incessantly day and night and become like angels in the next life, they would still not achieve true happiness or a reward. 

Indeed, the reason why the unrefined imagine within themselves that if humans are like angels in the afterlife they are not truly rewarded—even though they do not dare, out of shame, to express such an idea that opposes the words of the Law—is because true happiness and spiritual pleasure are not perceived or understood at all by unrefined men. Such true happiness is not affirmed to exist or be found according to the common people. Although some of them might recognize and perceive this "true happiness" in words alone, they do not do so through the intellect or true knowledge. Therefore, because the unrefined do not perceive true happiness, they imagine that if humans in the next life are like angels, they will not be rewarded. These points, then, are sufficient to show the detestation held for those who claim the <term>mahad</term> <note>The "Return" or Resurrection.</note> belongs to the body alone, or to the body and soul together.

### *Explanations regarding the third chapter, concerning the rejection of false opinions about the resurrection.*

<margin>A</margin> AND THOSE FOLLOWING this sect have opined, etc. That is, they have held the opinion that the essence of man is the body. Out of the hatred they held toward the wise—driven by envy and the difference in their moral characters—and due to their ignorance, etc., they did not perceive the things said by the wise. They reached the point where they denied the existence of the soul and deviated from the wise, imagining things in their own way based only on what can be sensed. They failed to perceive spiritual things, which are not grasped by the senses but by the intellect alone. 

Consequently, they fell into many errors. We see this in modern times among the ignorant Jews who, by denying Rabbi Moses <note>Referring to the philosopher Maimonides (Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon).</note> and all the wise theologians and failing to understand their doctrine, have devised another erroneous sect based on the senses that is far removed from theological truth. It is the same with many Christians who, not perceiving the things said regarding the Trinity and similar matters, deny what has been stated by theologians and philosophers, insulting them and asserting that the wise are heretics, and so on.

<meta>This page continues the critique of the literalist view of the resurrection. While the previous page discussed why the unrefined (non-philosophers) cannot imagine happiness without physical bodies, this page addresses how Avicenna interprets scripture metaphorically to argue for a more rational, intellectual understanding of the soul's return, contrasting this with the doctrines of the three major Abrahamic faiths.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>AVICENNA</header>

...that this <insert>the Return</insert> should be attributed to bodies alone. This is because the Jewish, Christian, and Muslim faiths assert the resurrection of the dead, and consequently that bodies rise and return. From this claim, which every faith holds, they argue and affirm that the <term>mahad</term> <note>From the Arabic *ma'ād*, meaning "the place of return" or the Resurrection.</note> applies to bodies alone. 

But Avicenna, as will be shown extensively below, declares that many statements and revelations in the Old Testament, the New Testament, and in the book of the <term>Alcoran</term> <note>The Quran.</note> are spoken metaphorically and in parables, so that the common people might better grasp them. These are not true in the literal sense of the words, but according to a hidden sense and intention which the wise understand and perceive. Because the statements of faith are interpreted in various ways and are not true in their literal sense, the foundation they have assumed from the dictates of faith is not valid.

In this resurrection, as Avicenna will demonstrate below, although the matter is the same, it is not the exact same body that is reunited with the same soul it was previously joined to, but another similar body. 

Therefore, according to this position, the true reward and true punishment are distributed to the souls because they remain the same; however, the bodies do not remain the same, nor are the same bodies, as was said, reunited with the same souls in the resurrection, but other similar bodies. For since matter is finite, and at the time of resurrection the souls will be infinite in number—as new souls are continually created and united to specific <term>disposed matter</term> <note>Matter that has been prepared or organized by nature to receive a human soul.</note> from the beginning of the world until the end—it follows that there are more souls in number than there are parts of matter disposed to receive the intellectual soul. This is especially proven by presupposing that the same matter may have been shaped by different souls at different times, and that all the elements and mixtures existing in the world require a certain quantity of matter to complete the universe. Therefore, if we take the quantity of matter necessary for the elements and mixtures, and the specific quantity of matter designated for the intellectual soul, it will be clear that due to the multiplication of souls, the finite matter assigned to the intellectual soul will not be sufficient at the time of resurrection. It would be impossible for every soul to then take back its own part of matter with which it was previously united, because there will be more souls than there are parts of available matter.

The second thing presupposed is that divine judgment is a single thing, unchangeable from its predestined course, or unchangeable from that which has been determined by God himself. With this presupposed, it follows that if God from eternity predestined a finite, determined amount of matter for souls, nothing can be added to it or supplied; otherwise, the divine judgment would be changed from what was determined from eternity, which is impossible.

Therefore, although the resurrection has been revealed in faith, it is to be understood not as it is publicly described, but in a "sane" or rational manner.

Thus, finite matter, which has parts finite in number, will not suffice for the aforementioned changes of souls that are not finite in number. Although the souls may be finite, nevertheless the matter will not suffice for infinite changes, as has been said. And if the souls are posited as infinite, then matter also will not suffice. # AVICENNA #

...me in good or evil works, they would not be punished, but other members [would be].

<margin>M</margin>
**NOW THEY** themselves take away and remove the judgment of justice, which they themselves place in the resurrection of the body's members. Note that Christians posit and affirm that the body and its members must be reunited with the soul, so that the soul, together with the body and its members, may receive reward or punishment. For if the body and its members, together with the soul, were the cause of sin, it is fitting according to the judgment of equal justice that the member and the body should be punished and suffer just as much as the soul. If, therefore, the supporting members <note>original: "membra coadiuuantia"; referring to non-essential tissues like fat or flesh that support the vital organs.</note> that assist in life were the cause of sin, and such members rise from that [original] earth or from another matter indifferently, then the very members that were the cause of sin will not rise. Thus, those same members that participated in a good or evil deed will neither be punished nor rewarded, but rather other members different from them. In this way, the judgment of justice—which the aforementioned thinkers affirm to be the cause for the resurrection of the body and its members—would be undermined.

**UNLESS THEY** posit that the parts designated for resurrection have the property of "intention," etc. This means that those who posit that the principal parts of the body's life <note>original: "partes principales"; the vital organs essential to identity, as opposed to the "supporting" flesh.</note> rise, and not the supporting parts (as was said above), claim that some parts of the body are designated for resurrection and others are not. They posit that the parts of the body designated for resurrection are those that possess the property and trace of "intention" <note>In scholastic philosophy, "intentio" (intention) here refers to a formal designation or a specific "meaning" that matter holds, identifying it as belonging to a particular individual.</note>—which intention was indeed removed from those parts at the time of death. For such is the intention of the aforementioned principal parts of human life: that these same parts, in the time of the first life (that is, before death), were the matter and the substantial parts of that prior life. After death, however, as is evident, such parts and their matter do not have that "intention." That is to say, after death, this "intention"—namely, being the substantial parts of life—is no longer truly predicated <note>original: "praedicatur"; a logical term meaning "to be stated as a true quality of a subject."</note> of those parts and their matter, as it was previously predicated during the first life. For then it was true to say that those parts of the body were the substantial parts of that man’s life, and that the matter of those parts existed under the form of the members which were the principal and substantial parts of life; but after death, such a statement is no longer true. Therefore, after death, that predication and that aforementioned intention are removed from those parts and their matter. However, because the aforementioned parts and their matter once possessed that true intention and predication (namely, that they were the substantial parts of life, etc.), there now remains in those parts and their matter after death a certain property and a certain inclination to be the principal parts of the human body once again, just as before, and for their matter to receive the form of the aforementioned parts again. Because of such an inclination, property, and trace, the aforementioned principal parts are the parts designated for resurrection, as has been said, while the supporting parts are not.

### ON THE RETURN ###
<note>original: "DE ALMAHAD"; from the Arabic *al-ma’ad*, referring to Avicenna’s treatise on the soul’s "return" or resurrection.</note>

**N** But this discourse and this position is without reason—namely, to assign to certain parts (specifically the <term>substantial parts<note>The essential components of a body that define its identity, such as the vital organs, as opposed to transient matter like fat.</note>) the quality of being fit for resurrection, as has been said, while other parts (the supporting parts) are not assigned or fitting for resurrection.

**IT IS THE DISCOURSE** that posits privation, etc. This means the discourse which posits that some parts are assigned to the resurrection because of a <term>trace<note>original: "vestigium"; a philosophical term for a mark or remnant left by a form in matter.</note> and a property of "intention" <note>original: "intentio"; here meaning a specific formal designation or "purpose" that identifies matter as belonging to a specific individual.</note> removed from them, as was said above. Furthermore, it posits that some parts of the body are not assigned to the resurrection, affirming that the "privation of the aforementioned intention" is the cause, etc. This means it is the discourse which affirms that the privation of the "intention" (or the aforementioned designation)—or the removal of that designation from those substantial parts and from the matter itself—is the cause. Specifically, it argues that because those parts were substantial parts of life in the first life and are not so now, this very "privation" is the reason why those parts (or their matter) will once again possess that same designation. In the resurrection, the matter of those substantial parts, because of the aforementioned "trace," will again exist under the form of the substantial parts or members of life, just as before.

**AND NOT ANYTHING OTHER** than it—that is, the other parts that support life, in which the "privation of intention" is not present in the same way as in the substantial parts, will not have that designation. This is because the supporting parts were not the substantial parts of life. Therefore, "anything other than it" (meaning the supporting parts, which are distinct from the substantial parts) will not possess that designation which the substantial parts will have. At the hour of resurrection, the supporting parts and their matter do not possess that property and inclination which the substantial parts possess. Therefore, the matter of the supporting parts will not receive the form of the substantial members, because it does not have the "privation of the aforementioned intention" which the matter of the substantial parts possesses. Thus, the aforementioned discourse (which is not true) posits that the "privation of intention" is the cause why something (the substantial parts or their matter) will newly possess the aforementioned designation, while anything else (the supporting parts and their matter) will not have that designation or description mentioned above.

**O** And indeed, the disposition of the privation of a thing already made, etc. This means that the disposition of the privation of a thing already made and the disposition of the privation of a thing yet to come—or the privation itself of the completed thing and the privation of the future thing—exist in matter, which is one and the same. Therefore, if you posit that the aforementioned principal parts and their matter are assigned to the resurrection because they possess the "privation of the aforementioned intention," and for this reason they possess the privation of a future thing (namely, that they will newly receive the forms of those substantial parts in the resurrection), then the matter which was under the form of those aforementioned parts must be one with the matter...

It argues against the idea that supporting tissues are excluded from this process based on their lack of a specific "intentional" designation.</summary>

# AVICENNA #

...matter which in the resurrection receives the forms of the aforementioned parts, it follows
<margin>¶</margin> that, just as the matter of the <term>substantial parts<note>The essential organs or components necessary for the body's existence, as opposed to secondary tissues.</note></term> after death—by the fact that it holds within itself the **privation** <note>original: "privatio"; an Aristotelian concept meaning the lack of a form that a thing is naturally supposed to have, like the way a blind man has the "privation" of sight.</note> of the thing once made (for instance, the privation of the principal members)—also holds the privation of the future thing. This is because it is fit to receive the forms of the principal members during the resurrection. Thus, the same must be said regarding the matter of the **supporting members**. By the fact that this matter possesses the privation of the thing once made—namely, the
<margin>¶</margin> supporting members, because it was once shaped by their forms—it follows that it also possesses the privation of the future thing: namely, those same supporting members which will return in the resurrection. Therefore, just as you say that the matter of the substantial parts is "assigned" to the resurrection because it possesses the privation of the thing once made (the lack of the form of those parts which it once possessed), and through this, that same matter possesses the privation of the future thing (the lack of the form of the substantial parts that will rise anew); and because of this, the matter of the aforementioned parts is said to be "assigned" to the resurrection—by that same reasoning, it should be said of the matter of the members and parts of the body that **assist in life**, that it also is assigned to the resurrection. Because it possesses the privation of the thing once made (the privation of the form of the supporting members), it must also possess the privation of the future thing: namely, the privation of the future form of the supporting members in the resurrection. Thus, it is assigned to the resurrection of the supporting members and parts. Therefore, just as you posit that the matter of the principal parts—because it once held the forms of the principal members and was shaped by them, and now is not, but possesses the privation of the **intention** and **predication** <note>"Intention" here refers to the specific identity or "designation" of the matter, while "predication" refers to whether it can still be truly called a "member" of a specific person.</note> which we spoke of above—and because of this, that same matter possesses the property and inclination toward resurrection, and is reunited in the future resurrection with the forms of the principal parts; in the same way, it must be said that the matter of the supporting parts—because it was shaped by their forms and now is not, but possesses the privation of the intention and predication it previously held (because in the first life it was true that such matter was shaped by the form of the supporting members, and now it is not so shaped)—since therefore that matter possesses the privation of the intention we just mentioned, it follows that it has the same property and inclination toward resurrection and toward receiving the form of the supporting members. And so, by the same logic you use to posit that the same matter of the principal parts will rise, the same matter of the supporting parts will rise and receive the form of the aforementioned parts. And note that this argument proceeds against **Christian theologians** who posit that the matter of the <term>radical members<note>The foundational parts of the body that remain constant through growth and change, a concept often used by Scholastic thinkers to explain how identity is preserved in the resurrected body.</note></term> is more fitting for the resurrection of the dead than other matter, as is clear from *Saint Thomas* in *Against the Gentiles* <note>original: "Contra gentiles"; referring to Thomas Aquinas’s *Summa contra Gentiles*, specifically Book 4, where he discusses the resurrection.</note> Book 4, in the chapter where he responds to objections against the resurrection. And the intention of *Avicenna* in these arguments is that the resurrection will not occur naturally, but **supernaturally**. For any matter...
