# ON THE RETURN #
<note>original: "DE ALMAHADVA"; a Latinized title for Avicenna’s work *Al-Ma'ad*, which deals with the afterlife or "the place of return."</note>

...is separated, it is of one and the same nature; therefore, speaking naturally, there is no more reason for one [part of matter] to be restored than another. In the resurrection, then, the fact that *this* specific matter is reunited to *that* specific form, rather than some other matter, will not happen according to the laws of nature, but according to divine power and the divine will. **Avicenna** <note>The Latin name for Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician and philosopher whose work deeply influenced Western medieval thought.</note> confirms this view in his philosophy, where he asserts that the resurrection of the dead cannot be demonstrated through natural logic. However, because such a resurrection is possible through divine power and has been revealed by the prophets through God, it is to be believed as a truth proven in every Law <note>original: "lege"; here meaning a religious system or divine law, such as Islam, Christianity, or Judaism.</note>.

**ANOTHER READING** <note>original: "ALIA LITERA"; indicates a variation found in a different manuscript copy of the text.</note> says: *the disposition of an existing privation or of a non-existing future privation is in one and the same matter*, etc. To explain this passage, it must be understood that a "disposition of existing **privation**" <note>original: "privatio"; an Aristotelian term for the absence of a quality or "form" that a thing should naturally have, like a seed "lacking" the form of a tree.</note> is said to be in matter when that matter previously possessed a certain form but does not possess it now; in this case, the matter is "deprived" of that form, and the privation is actually present in the matter. However, a "disposition of future privation" occurs when matter has not yet been shaped by a form but will be in the future, and will later be deprived of it. Before the matter is shaped by that form, we say there is a "future privation" in the matter, rather than one currently existing. 

With these points established, it is clear that both the actual privation of a form and its future privation are things outside the essential nature of matter. Each of these privations exists in "one matter"—that is, matter of the same nature. Therefore, there is no greater reason for one piece of matter to be "appropriated" for resurrection than another. Thus, any argument claiming that some parts of matter are similar while others are specifically designated for resurrection (and that "privation" is the cause of this) is not a true argument.

<margin>P</margin> **AND YET when you consider**, etc. In this section, Avicenna makes another argument against those who claim that souls are reunited with the exact same body and the exact same matter, and the text is clear.

<margin>Q</margin> **AND THE FIRST DISCOURSE**, that is, the argument which affirms that in the resurrection, souls are reunited to the same composite body made of the same matter and the same elementary parts.

<margin>R</margin> **FOR THE TRUTH IS that there is no difference**, etc. Here Avicenna proves that even if we assume the soul is reunited at the time of resurrection to a body composed of the same matter and the same elements, it still results in <term>Altenasach<note>A Latinization of the Arabic term *Tanāsukh*, meaning the transmigration of souls or reincarnation. Avicenna argues that the traditional view of physical resurrection accidentally implies this heretical concept.</note></term>. For let us suppose there are two portions of matter: the first was never shaped by an **intellectual soul** <note>The highest part of the soul in medieval philosophy, responsible for reason and understanding.</note>, while the second was. If that first matter were to receive an intellectual soul for the first time during the resurrection, it would be called <term>Altenasach</term>, because a form is being moved from one matter to another.

# AVICENNA #

...and from one body to another, thus, *Altenasach* <note>original: "Altenasach"; the Latinized version of the Arabic *al-tanasukh*, meaning the transmigration of souls or metempsychosis.</note> would be true, if at the time of the resurrection the soul were reunited with a "second matter"—that is, with the matter that was previously formed by that same soul. For although such a soul is united to a body composed of the same matter it previously shaped, it would nonetheless not be united to the *same* body; because even if the matter remains the same, the "corporeity" <note>The quality or state of being a physical body.</note> would not be the same as that which existed in the first life.

**HOWEVER**, the intention in these arguments is one and the same: this is made clear because, although they may seem to differ in their wording, whether it is proposed that the soul reunites with a body that shares the identical matter of the first life, or whether it reunites with a body that does not share it, in whatever way it is stated, the underlying meaning is effectively the same. This is because the "corporeity" is numerically distinct from that which existed before, and consequently, the body is a different one; thus, by necessity, *Altenasach* <note>In this context, the author is exploring the technicality that if the resurrected body is "newly" formed, it might be framed as the soul entering a new body, similar to reincarnation.</note> would be true at the time of resurrection. In responding to this argument, it is said that just as from the beginning of a man's life until his old age the total matter is not the same, nor is the corporeity the same, and yet he is said to be the same man—so it is in the resurrection.

**THOSE WHO SPEAK** <note>original: "LOQVENTES"; likely referring to the *Mutakallimun*, the practitioners of Scholastic theology in Islam.</note> more weakly, etc. In this section, the Translator <note>original: "T"; likely referring to the translator or commentator.</note> draws a comparison between Christians and Muslims regarding their position on the *Mahad* <note>original: "Mahad"; Arabic *al-ma'ad*, meaning "the Return" or the afterlife.</note>. He says that the Christians have spoken more weakly and more sparingly concerning the Return and those things which pertain to the divine law. **Muhammad** <note>original: "Maumethus".</note>, however, taught and delivered the divine laws in a better way and more completely than was even possible to be delivered or revealed; and for this reason, Muhammad is called the "Seal of the Laws" and the "Last of the Prophets." And in this place, if Avicenna did not fear the length of the discourse, he would have demonstrated the perfection of the Islamic law and its nobility over other preceding laws that were divinely revealed. As he himself says, Avicenna wishes to take from the whole sum of the Islamic law only the worthy and fitting opinion concerning the *Mahad*, which Muhammad set down in the book of the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcoran".</note>. For Muhammad said in that same place, where he speaks of the Return: that the better and more worthy purpose of the divine laws is the practical part, which concerns the actions of man, etc. For the <term>speculative part</term> <note>Theoretical or contemplative knowledge, such as philosophy or theology.</note> is ordered toward the <term>practical part</term> <note>Ethics and the actual performance of good deeds.</note> and toward the good and moral actions of men. For once knowledge of God and the soul is gained through speculative science, man recognizes God as the first cause and the supreme good, with whom the virtuous soul ought to be united and achieve supreme happiness. And a soul does not become virtuous and perfect except through the mediation of good works, and through the mediation of divine love, which inclines the soul itself to be conformed to the Supreme Principle and the Glorious God as much as is possible in this state. And just as God performs only what is good and virtuous, so the soul wishing to imitate its first principle must perform only what is virtuous. And because love and will are not directed toward the unknown, therefore speculative knowledge concerning God and these lower things causes delight, love, and inclination in the soul...

-># CONCERNING THE RETURN<-

...were not predestined by God, they are necessary for which reason, etc. And some of those who posited **Altenasach** <note>original: "Altenafach," a variant of *Altenasach*, referring to the transmigration of souls or reincarnation.</note> said that souls are diminished in their perfection, and that because of this diminution, they seek out perfection by means of bodily instruments. Therefore, the aforementioned souls, recognizing at the hour of separation from the body that they are diminished in perfection, desire to be reunited with a body to acquire that perfection. For if they were not reunited, they would remain diminished in perfection after their exit from the body, and they would exist in the world in vain and without use; but in nature, nothing is found to be in vain, for which reason, etc.

For if they did not change from body to body, then during the time when souls are found between two bodies—that is, in the middle time between the separation of the souls from the first body and the change to the second body—the souls would exist in vain. But in nature, nothing is found [to be in vain]...

-># AVICENNA<-

...in vain, for which reason, etc. This man Ebencora <note>original: "Ebencora," the Latinized name for Thabit ibn Qurra (c. 826–901), a Sabian scholar and philosopher.</note>, however, forbids this and says it is impossible and unfitting that souls should exist in vain for a finite or limited time; yet he posits it to be necessary that the soul remains in vain for an infinite time—and this is even more strange: 
<margin>I</margin> namely, what he says: that after their separation from the physical body, souls put on a "subtle body" <term>subtle body: an ethereal or quasi-material envelope (pneuma) often theorized in Late Antiquity as a vehicle for the soul after death.</term> which is not like these earthly bodies. He claims that souls are not liberated from matter suddenly or immediately; rather, they are freed only after a period of time, for which reason these souls are not existing "in vain." 

But it must be asked of this Ebencora: what is his intention, or what does he mean by the "subtlety" of this subtle body? Does he mean that it is a body that is transparent, or rare and light? In whatever way such a body is structured, it is undoubtedly a "natural body" subjected to the soul, or supporting the soul. Therefore, this entity would be an animal that is neither a "rational animal" <note>original: "animal rationale," the standard definition of a human being in Aristotelian logic.</note> nor an irrational one—but this is false. 

This, therefore, is the summary <margin>K</margin> of the points with which the proponents of **Altenasach** <note>original: "Altenasach," from the Arabic *al-tanasukh*, referring to the transmigration of souls or metempsychosis.</note> argue in general. 

Those who say that **Altenasach** occurs—that is, that souls are exchanged into every species of animal—have demonstrated this to be true for this reason: if the soul was able to prepare for itself a dwelling-place such as the human body, it can also prepare for itself a dwelling-place lower than that, or a dwelling-place less worthy than the human body is. 

And if that occurred <margin>L</margin> through divine power, or through divine predestination, or through celestial governance: then human bodies and the bodies of non-human animals are both included in that governance, and in that power or predestination. Thus, it is not forbidden or impossible for the soul to dwell in non-human bodies. 

According to the <margin>M</margin> first division of their argument, it is fitting that when the habits of a non-rational animal are present in a soul, and such a soul does not possess human nobility or virtues, it can then make or prepare for itself a non-human body. As we have said, it can then make or prepare a body similar to itself in its habits: so that if the soul was prone to anger, it can prepare for itself the body of a lion; if it was lustful, or a slave to appetite, it can prepare for itself the body of a lecherous creature like a sow or a pig, and of those which are similar to it in character, and it can dwell in them. 

According to the second <margin>N</margin> division, it is said to be fitting that a wicked and vice-ridden soul deserves to be chastised and punished by being imprisoned in bodies that are tortured, sorrowful, full of fear, and prone to flight <note>referring to prey animals that live in a constant state of terror.</note>. Some of those who hold the view of **Altenasach**...

->## CONCERNING THE RETURN<-
<note>original: "DE ALMAHAD," from the Arabic *al-Ma'ad*, meaning "the place of return" or the afterlife/resurrection.</note>

...and they believe and confess the Islamic law <note>original: "legem Maumethanam," literally the Law of Muhammad.</note>. They have said that in the book of the Quran <note>original: "Alcoran"</note> of Muhammad, it is written that those beasts which walk upon the earth, and the birds which fly with their wings, are communities <note>original: "turba," often used in medieval Latin to translate the Arabic *ummah* (community/nation) in the Quranic verse 6:38.</note> similar to us humans. This, they claim, is a certain and true opinion, because irrational animals are like us. However, they are not like us in **act** <term>act: the state of being fully realized or functional</term>; rather, they are like us in **potential** <term>potential: the capacity to become something or develop a certain quality</term>, and we likewise are like them in potential. 

Therefore, according to the sayings of Muhammad in the book of the Quran, some affirm that the opinion of **Altenafach** <note>original: "Altenafach," a variation of *Altenasach* (al-tanasukh), referring to the transmigration of souls.</note> is true. Yet others, while agreeing with the general concept of *Altenafach*, differ from those who allow transmigration to occur in bodies other than human ones. They argue that it is not possible for the human soul to be exchanged into the species of any other animal. For if the soul is the **form** <term>form: the defining principle that makes a thing what it is</term> and the perfection of the human body, it is within its very nature that a human being differs from other species by that soul. These species do not share in that differentiating form in their totality, nor in their perfection. 

It follows, then, that the soul cannot be transferred into bodies of a species other than human. Aristotle also stated this in his book *On the Soul* <note>original: "Aristo. in libro de anima." Referring to Aristotle's critique of Pythagorean transmigration in De Anima, Book I.</note>. For he says that anyone who claims a human soul enters a body other than a human one is essentially asserting that it is possible for the form or shape of the letter 'a' to enter into the matter of the letter 'b', even while that matter remains under the form of the letter 'b'. 

This conclusion is true. The path or reasoning for this conclusion is that a man is not a human being because of his physical shape alone, nor by his natural power alone; rather, his humanity is not completed or perfected except through his soul. This soul is the principle of the "ultimate essential difference" that constitutes the species. It is impossible for another species to share in this soul and then later differ only by things that are not "substantial differences" but merely **accidents** <term>accidents: non-essential qualities, such as color or size, that do not change what a thing fundamentally is</term>. Therefore, a human being does not share his soul with any other species of animal. 

Now that we have recalled the demonstrations and reasons of the men who propose the theory of *Altenafach*, and the diversity of opinion among them, we encounter a logical fallacy in their speech: namely, where they presuppose that souls **pre-exist** before bodies. Furthermore, there is a point of doubt in their arguments to prove that aforementioned presupposition, where it is said: "That which happens with the arrival of the **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific physical mixture of the four elements/humors in a body</term> is a material form." These sayings are certainly not self-evident first principles, nor are they things that are absolutely well-known.

### AVICENNA

And if these opinions were famous, perhaps they are not famous except among certain distinguished wise men. Furthermore, it is not necessary that the existence of the soul after its separation from the body be the same as its existence before the body itself—namely, before it was united to the body. For it is possible that before the aforementioned union, no cause occurred which prevented its entry into bodies, or no cause preventing its union with bodies; and yet, that such an impediment might occur later, during the time the soul exists within the body. Therefore, when the aforementioned premises are invalidated, the arguments based on their admission or their presupposition are not proven true. 

But let us declare, by a demonstrative proof, that it is not possible at all for the soul to return into bodies after the death of a human being. Let us say, then, that there are several possibilities: either the existence of the soul in the body occurs by way of association or the soul's proximity to the body after the body already exists (as if it were something external to it); or it occurs by way of the soul’s arrival within the body at the moment the body itself comes into being, such that the **temperament** <term>temperament: (Latin: *complexio*) the specific proportional mixture of elements or qualities that makes a body fit to receive a specific soul</term> of the body necessitates the soul's arrival or its **emanation** <term>emanation: the philosophical concept of a "flowing forth" from a higher, universal cause or intellect</term> from a universal efficient cause. Or, perhaps, it happens by chance and by fortune. 

I say, therefore, that it is not possible for the soul to exist before bodies. This is because human souls are one in species and one in essence. If they existed separately from corporal matter, then either there was a multitude of them, or all souls were just one single soul. If there were a multitude among them, and yet they are one in **intention** <term>intention: (Latin: *intentio*) the essential concept or "meaning" of a thing that defines its species</term>, then their multiplication was not according to their essence, but through multiplied matter—matter which multiplies when it multiplies those essences, or which is itself multiplied by the multiplication of essences caused through it. 

Therefore, those souls would have had different matters. Such matters would either be their spiritual or intentional matters—and then the same question regarding the multitude or multiplication of those spiritual matters would arise as before—or those matters were corporal and quantitative, receiving multiplication through the division of quantity.

# AVICENNA

Therefore, when the bodily **temperament** <term>temperament: (Latin: *complexio*) the specific mixture of physical qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that makes a body fit to sustain life</term> begins: then the soul begins to exist along with it, depending upon it in the way previously described. It follows that what is said regarding **reincarnation** <note>original: *Altenasach*, a Latinization of the Arabic *al-tanasukh*, referring to the transmigration of souls</note> cannot be true: because an animal is a single unit by virtue of having a single soul. If, therefore, it were said that the position of reincarnation were true, it would be necessary for two souls to exist in one body: namely, the soul arriving or beginning to be with the start of the body, and the "reincarnated" soul which existed before the body and moves from body to body. Each of these souls would be a "perfect" soul, and identical in kind to the other. Yet a soul only exists in a body because of the necessity of performing life-functions through that body. In any given body, there is never any operation except that of a single soul; for an animal is not constructed such that its essence consists of two different things with two separate sets of life-functions. 

<margin>R</margin>
Indeed, what is universally known confirms that the "outer" part of a human and of other animals is a single thing, and the "inner" part of a human, by which knowledge occurs, is one and the same. They are not two different things: for the outer part of a human and his inner part constitute one single human, not two humans. For this reason, it is apparent that two souls do not exist simultaneously in a body. This is because a second soul—which would be distinct from the one 

<margin>S</margin>
by which perception or conception occurs, and which performs the functions of the body—would have no connection to the body. For "connection" or "dependence" means that through the soul, conceptions are made and functions are carried out that pass through and depend upon the body; thus, a second soul would have no reason to exist within the body. It is manifest, therefore, that the soul of every body arrives or begins to exist only with the arrival of its temperament, and that the soul of the body did not exist before it. Nor is the soul currently "giving form" to a body after having separated from bodies that existed previously. 

Nor is this contradicted by the concept of **reincarnation** <note>original: *intentio de Altenasach*</note> spoken of by excellent philosophers such as Plato, Pythagoras, and the followers of Pythagoras. For that which these philosophers affirmed concerning reincarnation is like a certain likeness or metaphor, similar to the language of divine law. For their intention was to condemn bad habits or evil morals which remain in souls after their separation from bodies. When those souls have been wicked and vicious, they are punished or

# ON THE RETURN
<note>original: *DE ALMAHAD*, derived from the Arabic *al-ma'ād*, referring to the "Place of Return" or the Resurrection/Afterlife.</note>

The existence of souls in bodies is not a matter of physical mixing, nor of mere proximity, nor is the soul's essence stamped directly into matter. Rather, it exists through a **trace** <note>original: *vestigium*</note> impressed upon the soul by bodily powers, and through the soul's need to operate within the body—or rather, through those operations of the soul that can only be carried out while in a body. These two conditions—this dependency and this bodily impression—hinder the soul from reaching its own proper perfection and from the [desire which it holds in its own substance.]

<margin>Another reading: "...from the operation which is in its substance, and from knowledge joined with delight, which is proper to it."</margin>

For when one of these states, or one of these two aforementioned conditions, exists—specifically, when a trace from bodily powers is impressed upon the soul and remains after its separation from the body—then the disposition of such a soul remains as if it were still in the body. And since a "bad trace" or a "bad impression" in the soul is either the appetite for the lust of wanton beasts, or the wrathful appetite of a lion, that trace remains fixed in the soul. It dominates the soul as if it were still inside the bodies of those lustful, gluttonous, or predatory animals. This was the true meaning of those ancient philosophers when they said that the souls of wicked and vicious people are transformed after death into the bodies of animals that possess those same bad habits, such as lions or lustful beasts.

And I say that most of the sayings used as a foundation by those I have encountered and heard from the sect of **Reincarnation** <term>reincarnation: (Latin: *Altenasach*, from Arabic *al-tanasukh*) the belief that the soul moves into a new physical body after death</term> are taken from the writings and authorities of **Plato**, **Bengemar** <note>likely a Latinized reference to a philosopher such as Abu Bakr al-Razi or a similar medieval authority</note>, and others. One should not put faith in the doctrine of reincarnation because of such erroneous arguments, nor because of the misunderstood words of Plato and others.

Therefore, since it has been rejected that the **Return** <note>original: *Mahad*</note> should be attributed to bodies alone, and rejected that it should belong to the body and soul together [by natural necessity], and likewise rejected that the Return happens through the way of Reincarnation, it follows that the Return pertains to the soul alone, as we shall later confirm. However, everything we have said about the Return—namely, that it pertains to the soul alone—is stated according to the discourse of **reason** or pure intellect. But according to the discourse that is joined with matters of **faith**, and according to the true and mandatory divine revelations of the laws, one must affirm that the Return is attributed to the body and soul together, and believe that it will come to pass. And we have already verified, and...

### ON THE RETURN
<note>original: *De Almahad*, a Latinization of the Arabic *Al-Ma'ad*, referring to Avicenna's treatise on the afterlife and the destination of the soul.</note>

*...is permanent and stable; whereby, at the hour of the separation of the aforementioned soul—or the aforementioned material form—from the body, the aforementioned soul (which began to exist with the body) is not destroyed. It then follows from such a statement that the matter composing the aforementioned material forms and souls would be something other and distinct from that primary matter* <term>primary matter: in Aristotelian philosophy, the most basic, formless "stuff" that underlies all physical things</term> *by comparison to which the aforementioned forms and souls are called "material forms." Thus there would be two kinds of matter, and matter would not be one, as the philosophers say. It would follow that the matter composing the substance of souls would be founded upon another matter: namely, upon primary matter.*

<margin>E</margin> *AND CONCERNING this there would be the same question—that is, regarding the very matter from which the substance of the aforementioned material forms is composed—the same question that was raised above. For it must be asked whether such composing matter, which is a part of the aforementioned souls, is changed at the hour of the soul's separation from the body, or is not changed. It cannot be said that it is not changed, because just as a material form is changed according to its substance, its substantial parts are also changed. Therefore, the matter composing material forms is changed; and then it is asked whether such matter is simple, according to its substance, or composite. If it is simple, then in such a change it is destroyed and nothing of it remains; if it is composite—made of matter and form, as was said before regarding material form—then it is asked whether this matter (which is a part of the aforementioned matter) is changed entirely during the aforementioned separation because it is simple, or whether it is composed of yet another matter and form. And then the question is asked again concerning that last matter, and so on into infinity. Therefore, the aforementioned response—namely, that the aforementioned souls and material forms are changed according to their substance at the hour of separation from the body, and that they are composed of matter and form—is false. If, however, it is said that in the separation of the aforementioned souls, the souls are not changed according to their substance, but only according to their accidents,* <term>accident: a non-essential quality (like color or position) that can change without changing what the thing fundamentally is</term> *and that their essences are firm and stable* IN TWO *dispositions—that is, before their separation from the body and after separation—then it follows that the joining of souls with the body or with matter would be a mere accident to them. Thus, they would not be inherent in their own substance; indeed, they would not need matter. Yet it was said that they are inherent in matter because in their being they depend upon the complexion,* <term>complexion: the specific physical balance of elements or humors that makes a body fit for life</term> *nor do they begin to exist unless the matter is properly disposed and balanced. Therefore, it seems that the aforementioned souls depend upon the complexion and are inherent in matter with their substance; and this is false. Consequently, it is false to say that souls begin to exist with the body.*

<margin>F</margin> *FURTHERMORE, if the substance of these souls, etc. In this part, he assigns another reason and presupposes that the substance of the soul is not inherent in matter, because it was proven above that the soul is not a material form. It was also said above by the adversary that in the separation of the soul from the body, the substance of the soul is not changed, but only the accident is changed, because...*

<meta>This page continues the logical refutation of transmigration, moving from the physical nature of matter to the metaphysical relationship between the soul and the body. # AVICENNA

...only the union and the proximity of the soul previously established with the body is changed. This proximity was accidental <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a property that does not belong to the essence of a thing; it can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist</note>, and the soul in its own substance does not need matter, nor does it inhere in matter. If, therefore, the substance of the soul does not inhere in matter, it follows that it cannot clothe itself in matter; otherwise, it would then be extended according to the extension of that matter, and would be a material form inseparable from matter. This would contradict those who posit that souls did not exist before bodies, but rather come into being and begin to exist simultaneously with the body. Thus it is clear how the argument proceeds, and the literal meaning is plain.

**AND ALTHOUGH souls are separate, etc.** This is part of the preceding argument. For the explanation of this part, it must be understood how souls, insofar as they are forms, cannot be separated from the body according to their being <term>being: *esse*, the actual existence or essence of the thing</term>, although they are separate from the "sum" mentioned above—namely, from dimension, quantity, and division, etc. For human souls, insofar as they are the forms of the body, are the principle of operations within the body; and yet they are neither inside the human body, nor outside the human body. This whole concept is made clear through the example of the sun. For the sun, as is evident, is the principle of generation and corruption <note>the cycle of birth/creation and death/decay</note> in this lower world <note>original: *mundus inferior*, referring to the sublunary realm, or the Earthly sphere below the heavens</note> by means of the influence of its power and its heat. Yet the sun is not an intrinsic form of this lower world, nor is it extended to the extension of the lower world, nor does it inhere in the earth like the substantial form of mixed things <note>referring to physical compounds like minerals or plants</note> or like other material forms. Therefore, the sun is not "inside" the world, nor "inside" the earth. However, the sun is also not "outside" this lower world or outside the earth in a functional sense, because if it were, then generation and corruption would occur without the sun. Because the sun impresses itself upon this lower world, it is not "outside" the world, nor is it separated from the world according to its being; yet it is not "inside" the world in a physical sense, as has been said.

In the same way, it must be said of the intellective soul <term>intellective soul: *anima intellectiua*, the highest part of the human soul capable of reason</term> that it is neither inside the body, nor outside the human body. That it is not inside the human body is demonstrated because the soul is not extended to the extension of the body, nor is it a quantitative material form inhering in matter; therefore, the soul itself is not "inside" the human body. Nor is it "outside," because the soul itself—insofar as it is the form of the body and while it informs the body—is the principle of the body’s operations. And although the soul is separate from the conditions and dimensions of the body (because it is not an extended quantity), nevertheless the soul is not separated from the body according to its being, because it is the cause of the being and life of the human body. For if the soul, insofar as it is the form and while it informs the body, could be separated from the body according to its being, then the human body could live without the soul, which is false; therefore it is not "outside" the human body. And just as this has been said regarding the intellective soul, so can it be verified regarding Glorious God: that God himself is not in the world, nor is He outside the world. It is first verified that He is not in the world because He is not a quantity, nor a material quality; therefore God is not "in" the world in the same way it was said that the soul is not "in" the body. God is also not "outside" the world, because He is the First Mover <term>First Mover: *primum mouens*, the Aristotelian concept of the primary cause of all motion in the universe</term> and the first cause in the entire universe.

G

It refutes the idea that the soul is a material substance subject to physical extension.</summary>

...which cannot be separated according to its being from the whole universe, and therefore it is not outside the world. Just as it has been said of the soul—that it is neither within the human body nor outside of it, and it is understood how the soul operates in the body and is the principle of life for the human body—so too it is understood that God is not in the world, and that He is not outside the world; and it is understood how God is the cause of all things that happen in the entire universe. From this, the truth of Avicenna’s statement in the introduction to his compendium on the soul is clear, where he says that it is written in the Quran <note>original: *Alcoran*</note> that "he who knows his own soul, also knows his own creator," <note>original: *qui cognoscit animā suam, cognoscit etiam creatorem suum*</note> namely the glorious God. Such a saying is proven true because he who understands how his soul is neither in the body nor outside his body, similarly understands that God is neither in the world nor outside the world, and thus he knows God his creator. Such a verification and exposition of the aforementioned authority, taken by Avicenna from the book of the Quran, is approved among the Muslim <note>original: *Maumethanos*</note> theologians and philosophers, and among them, the aforementioned explanation is held as something worthy and a secret.

Returning to the main point: from what has been said, it appears that although souls are separate from the aforementioned "sum" of bodily conditions—meaning they are not extended, nor do they have quantity, etc.—nevertheless, while they inform the body <term>inform: to provide the "form" or organizing principle that makes a body a living human</term>, they are not separated from their bodies according to their being <term>being: *esse*, the actual existence of the soul as a functioning part of a living person</term>, nor can they be separated. And if some have thought otherwise, they have held a false opinion. Aristotle, in his book of *Metaphysics*, declared their error and said that if souls were at any hour separated from matter—that is, according to their being while they are informing—then they would not be forms dependent on the bodily complexion <term>complexion: the specific physical balance of qualities (like heat and moisture) in a body</term>, nor would they be pure simple forms existing in matter, which is false. For this reason, souls are said to be pure simple forms existing in matter and depending on complexional matter: because they are not extended and have no quantity, they are called pure simple forms, not mixed with matter nor with quantified matter, and they are not extended. They are, however, existing in matter because they inform the matter, and they depend on the complexional matter because they are not perfected except through a passing operation, such as thought and similar things; for it is necessary for the one who understands to look at phantasms <note>original: *fantasmata*, the mental images derived from the senses which the intellect uses to form concepts</note>, etc. Therefore, because souls are not forms separated from matter according to their being, even though they are separate from the aforementioned "sum" (namely from quantity, etc.), it follows that souls are not among the number of those things that begin to exist with the body. Wherefore it follows that they existed before bodies; therefore the argument of Altenas <note>Likely referring to a specific philosopher or a school of thought mentioned in the broader debate, possibly a corruption of an Arabic name</note> is true. *And the literal meaning is plain.*

# THE CANON OF AVICENNA
### A 3

... death, and after separation from the body, the soul remains with a wicked and vicious habit of luxury and gluttony, as if it were still in the vicious human body in which it previously existed, or as if it were in the body of a pig. Such a vicious soul is said metaphorically to be transformed after death into the body of a pig, because in that soul separated from the body there remain evil, vicious habits similar to the gluttonous and vicious habits found in a pig. Similarly, the soul of a wrathful or proud man is said to be transformed after death into the body of a lion, because in the aforementioned soul there remain habits similar to those in a lion. 

The philosophers spoke of this metaphorically so that the common people might better and more easily perceive and grasp the truth; such people, believing their souls might be transformed into the body of a pig, a lion, or the like, abhor the idea of such a change occurring, and thus they abstain from similar vices and evil morals. Therefore, those who propose **Altenasach** <note>original: *Altenasach*; a Latinized Arabic term for the transmigration of souls or reincarnation</note>, basing themselves on the aforementioned sayings of the philosophers, have misunderstood the authorities and the sayings of the philosophers—namely Plato and others.

### Chapter Four: On the Permanence of the Selfhood of Man.

<margin>A</margin>
**W**hen a man begins to consider the thing because of which he is called "man," or because of which it is said that he is his very self, he speaks or responds to himself and imagines that this "self" is his belly and his body. Afterward, when he thinks, or observes, or examines closely, he realizes that his hands, his feet, his ribs, and the rest of his visible members—even if they were not part of his body—would not cause the destruction of the **essence** <note>original: *intentio*; here meaning the core concept of identity or the "meaning" of the person</note> that is attributed to him or which is predicated of him.

<margin>B</margin>
And from this, he knows that these parts of his body do not enter into this essence <note>original: *intentionem*</note>, until he arrives at the principal organs, such as the brain, the heart, and the liver, and those things that follow their course.

<margin>C</margin>
For upon the removal of many of these, this essence is not immediately destroyed within him, but perhaps after a short or long time; and the heart and brain remain. Sometimes, indeed, the brain allows a part to be separated from it, and yet that essence remains firm and permanent in that man. In the heart, however, this is not possible in actual existence, but it is possible in the imagination. For sometimes a man knows that his **selfhood** <note>original: *alaniæ*; a Latinization of the Arabic *anniyya*, meaning "I-ness," "ipseity," or the subjective sense of "I"</note> of which he speaks exists, and it is possible that he does not know then whether he has a heart, or what kind it is, or what it is, or where the heart itself is. <margin>I</margin> Furthermore, those things that happen to the body itself—such as desire, anger, habits, and physical "good" or "bad" states—do not reach the soul except in a secondary manner. <margin>K</margin> Since it is clear that this individual "self"—which is distinct from the body—is the soul itself, it follows that the good and bad things happening to the body are external to the soul. The soul does not share in them except through the path described above.

### Clarifications on Chapter Four.

A MAN *when he begins to consider etc.* <note>The opening words of Avicenna's fourth chapter</note>. *In this chapter, Avicenna <note>the 11th-century Persian philosopher Ibn Sina</note> investigates the permanent thing by which a human is substantially called a "human." Because a human consists of both bodily members and a soul, Avicenna proves that this permanent thing—by which a human is substantially called a human, and which he calls <term>Selfhood</term> <note>original: *Alanie*, from the Arabic *al-aniyya*, the "I-ness" or essence of the self</note>—is not any of the members, nor the body itself. He then concludes that this Selfhood is the intellectual soul, because it is through the soul that the human body is placed into its specific category, and it is to the soul that human actions are attributed as their first principle. He argues that true reward and true punishment are appropriate to the soul; and consequently, he affirms that the <term>Return</term> <note>original: *Mahad*; the Islamic concept of the resurrection or place of return</note> applies to the soul remaining after its separation from the body, and not to the body. That none of the members is the aforementioned Selfhood is clear through the discourse laid out by Avicenna: for any of the members, except the heart, can be separated either entirely or in part from the human, and yet the human remains realistically a human. Consequently, that thing by which a human is essentially, substantially, actually, or realistically called a human must remain. Therefore, no member can be called the aforementioned Selfhood. Nor is the heart the Selfhood, because of the reason Avicenna brings forward: namely, that it is impossible for the same thing to be both known and unknown at the same time <note>Avicenna's "Floating Man" argument suggests you know your "self" even if you are unaware of your physical heart</note>. Furthermore, everyone affirms that the body and its members are not realistically the same from childhood to old age because of continuous dissolving and restoration <note>referring to metabolism and physical growth</note>; yet it is said that the essence of this or that man is the same from the beginning of life until the end. Since no part of the body is permanent in the way the intellectual soul is, the real essence of the man—the thing through which a man is realistically or substantially a human—is the intellectual soul itself, which depends on the body for its outward operations until death. I say "real essence" because while the definition of "human" is called the essence of human, that is merely a mental concept composed of genus and difference, and is dependent on the work of the intellect.*

# ON THE RETURN
<note>original: *De Almahad*, referring to Avicenna’s work on the afterlife or the "Return" of the soul.</note>

...either moves, and that the human fundamentally understands, or moves: and the human is essentially the **Selfhood** <note>original: *Alania*, referring to the "I-ness" or core identity</note> of the human, or the essence; that is, the thing through which this body is a human. This essence and selfhood is the **intellectual soul**, which places the human body into the category of "human" and which is the source of all operations. It is the soul which remains continuously the same, whereas the body and its members do not materially remain the same from the beginning to the end of life because of the constant **dissolution** <term>resolutio; the breakdown of bodily matter</term> and **restoration** <term>restauratio; the replenishment of the body through nutrition</term>. The soul, therefore, is that to which actions are attributed as their primary source. 

And although according to **Aristotle**—who said that to say the soul "understands" is as if one said the soul "weaves" or "spins"—this is understood to refer to the soul by itself alone and to the kind of understanding that originates from the senses. For the soul by itself, without dependence on the body, cannot have that specific kind of sensory understanding; thus, the soul does not understand purely on its own, but as a soul depending on the body in a certain way, as was discussed in the preceding chapter. 

Such a dependent soul is the human being in a fundamental sense. However, it was stated above that the understanding of **universals** <note>general concepts rather than specific objects</note> and of abstract substances is proper to the soul's own substance. When the soul wishes to move from a state of potentiality to the actual act of such understanding, it does not require the body. But the understanding which has its origin in the senses is attributed to the soul insofar as it depends on the body. 

The soul is not united to the body except so that, through the mediation of the senses, it may be perfected and acquire the understanding of the most noble substances. Once this understanding is acquired, the soul is then perfected and no longer requires the body for this purpose. It is clear, therefore, when he says that the "human" understands or moves, etc., that such 
<margin>20</margin>
actions are attributed to a person in an absolute sense—that is, to a human fundamentally, or to the soul insofar as it depends on the body. 

And just as the actions attributed to the human in an absolute sense (not to the body as mere matter, nor to its limbs) are attributed to the soul as the primary source, so it must be said that both the **good** and the **reward** which a human hopes for in this world and the next for their good deeds, and the **evil** or **punishment** they fear for bad deeds, are nothing but the good and evil that truly happen to the soul itself. For just as good or bad actions are attributed to the human essentially—that is, to their soul—so too must reward and punishment be attributed to the soul in truth. Such reward or punishment will be nothing other than the good or evil proper to the soul itself. 

For this reason, **Avicenna** in this section 
<margin>*</margin>
said: **AND NOT feared, nor hoped**, etc. For **EVIL** and **good** happening to things that are external to the soul do not happen to the soul in truth, but through a **shared connection** [communication], etc. 

From these words, Avicenna hints that there is a certain good and evil that is proper to the soul, and another kind that is not proper but arrives through this "communication." As it is said in the second book of *On the Soul*, there are some experiences that begin in the soul and overflow into the body, and some that begin in the body and overflow into the soul. Therefore, physical pleasure and physical punishment do not reach the soul except through this shared connection.

And he thinks that there is no happiness or punishment other than corporal happiness and punishment. Common people imagine this together, nor is it possible to remove such an imagination from them **AT ONCE** and suddenly. Therefore, it was necessary for those who published the laws <note>Referring to prophets or divinely inspired lawgivers</note> that, when speaking of the reward or punishment of the other life, they said and affirmed that the happiness of the other life would involve sensual pleasure and the punishment would involve sensual pain.

<margin>P</margin> <margin>a</margin> **IF THEREFORE** *rewarded and punished in the other life etc. That is, if in the other life we will not be bodily as we are now, and nothing will be rewarded or punished except <margin>b</margin> a part of man—namely the soul—then it is as if one were to say that for the good and evil actions which a man performs in this life (that is, the body together with the soul), only a man’s foot or only a man’s hand will be punished or rewarded. This is considered absurd, because one must ask how a just and equal remuneration or punishment could follow from the delight, reward, or pain of only a foot or only a hand for good and evil works committed not just by the hand or foot, but by the whole body and similarly by the soul. It is clear that if only the foot or hand were rewarded or punished, it would not be according to right justice. Similarly, if in the other life we will not be bodily, nor will we be rewarded or punished except according to the soul, then the reward and punishment would not be fitting according to right justice. ### Chapter five: concerning the affirmations, or demonstrations,
### that the soul is excused <note>here meaning "set apart" or "exempt"</note> from the body in its existence, or that
### the soul can exist without the body.

<margin>A</margin>
We have already provided a declaration of the substance of the soul in several of our books, and especially in our exposition upon Aristotle’s book *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle’s *De Anima*</note>. What must be taken from that exposition and summarized in this book is that we should argue by demonstration that the human soul, called the "rational soul," is not imprinted in matter, nor is its existence dependent on the body; and this indeed we shall demonstrate in several ways.

<margin>B</margin>
One of these ways is this: It is not possible for any body to have an entirely infinite power; nor is it possible for an infinite power to be found or to exist within a body. Since every body is divisible into parts, or susceptible to being divided into parts, the power existing within it will of necessity be susceptible to division into parts. Therefore, the power of any one of those parts <margin>Another reading: existing as a part of the whole.</margin> will either be a finite portion [taken from the sum] of the infinite power—which is capable of all things—and then, if the aforementioned power of any of those parts is finite, it follows that the whole aggregate must be finite. And this contradicts the idea of an infinite power, because the whole would then only be capable of finite things, or would be of finite power. But this is false and contrary to what was stated. Therefore, etc. Or, every part, or some specific part, would have to be capable of everything the whole is capable of, and this is indeed impossible, for the power of the whole is more intense and stronger than the power of a part, and more resistant. Therefore, it is manifest from this

<margin>C</margin>
that it is not possible for an infinite power to exist in a finite body. Furthermore, the soul is of infinite power, for the **intelligible forms** <note>original: "species intelligibiles," the abstract concepts or universal ideas that the mind grasps</note> which it can apprehend are infinite. This is because certain intelligibles are physical things, others are mathematical, and others are divine **metaphysical intentions**; and the power of the soul, which is capable of grasping any of these—which are infinite—is a single power. Whence it is manifest that it is impossible for the soul to be corporeal, nor is it possible for it to be in a body in such a way that it is a power within a body.

<margin>D</margin>
Nor is it even possible for it to be in an indivisible thing among those which

And the contrary of this statement is not valid or verified—namely, the claim that sensory things do not have a **position** <note>original: "situm"; a specific physical location or arrangement in space.</note> 
<margin>Another reading: correspond or be proportional to those sensory things.</margin> so that <insert>there might be a proportion or conformity between the ideas themselves and those sensory things</insert> which are understood from them. For every sensory object has two modes of being: one of them is the being by which it is sensed or perceived by the senses, and this is entirely different from its being as understood by the intellect. Such a "sensory being" is a being that has a physical position. However, the second mode of being of a sensory thing is the being by which it is understood or perceived by the intellect, and such a being has no physical position. Therefore, the truth is that the <term>intelligible species <note>The mental representation or "form" of an object stripped of its physical matter.</note></term> of sensory things correspond to, or conform with, their existence when it is stripped of physical position.

<margin>M</margin> Among the things that verify and make manifest that the soul subsists or exists by itself and not in matter, is that its intellectual operation <note>The act of thinking or reasoning.</note> inevitably proceeds from its essence alone. In this operation, it does not require anything other than its own essence to serve as an instrument or organ. Alternatively, one might ask if its intellectual operation occurs with an instrument, organ, or body in which it exists. If that operation proceeds from its essence, then the soul possesses an essence and is **simple** <note>In philosophy, "simple" means not made of parts and therefore indivisible/immortal.</note> by itself. For if it did not have a simple or pure essence, it would not have an operation proceeding from a simple or solitary essence, since **operation follows essence.** <note>A classic philosophical principle: how a thing acts (operation) depends on what it is (essence).</note> Therefore, if the essence is independent by itself, it is possible—or must be granted—that its operation is independent by itself, not according to physical being. And if the operation is independent according to its being, then the essence even more so, or more worthily, exists as independent according to its being. It is not possible for an essence to be not independent by itself while its operation is independent by itself and according to its being.

<margin>N</margin> But if someone, contradicting this, argues that "Nature" <note>Referring to the "natural soul" or the force that governs biological growth and movement.</note> is a material form, and yet it moves the matter in which it resides, and its operation—which is to move or "motion"—is found to be separate, because moving (or motion) belongs to it alone and flows from it alone; 
<margin>Another reading: matter indeed is only moved.</margin> <insert>while matter is only that which is moved</insert>: It is answered that the operation of Nature is motion, which is inseparable. For the essence of motion exists in matter, and "moving" is motion in itself, even if they are distinguished respectively or relatively. And the essence of motion, which is a relative state of being, does not have existence or sub[sistence...]

<vocab>materia (matter), esse intelligibile (intelligible being), sensatum (sensory thing), anima (soul), essentia (essence), intellectus (intellect), motio (motion), forma materialis (material form)</vocab>

<summary>Avicenna argues that the soul exists independently of the body because the act of thinking (intellection) does not require a physical organ. He distinguishes between an object's physical existence and its conceptual existence, concluding that the soul's "simple" essence allows it to operate without matter.</summary>

If it were, matter would be part of its definition, just as a part is included in the whole definition of a thing. If that were so, it would be possible for one part of a definition to precede another, or for a part of the definition to precede something that is not part of the definition. Truly, it is impossible for something that is not part of the definition to precede that which is a part.

From this, it is manifest that it is entirely impossible for anything whose essence precedes its operation to possess an essence that is not "separate" <note>In medieval philosophy, "separate" means independent of physical matter.</note> and an operation that is not "separate." The **human soul** is certainly not exempt from this: either it operates in its understanding of intellectual concepts through a physical instrument, organ, or matter, or it operates through its own essence alone. But let us propose that it does this neither by means of an organ, nor by means of matter.

Therefore, it is concluded that the essence of man is a separate substance existing through itself.

# ON THE RETURN #
<note>original: "DE ALMAHAD"; referring to the Arabic term *al-Ma'ad*, meaning the "place of return" or the afterlife.</note>
1

<margin>A</margin> [The author] proves that the soul remains after death, and that the body is something external to the soul, which he promised to prove above in the preceding chapter. And Avicenna strives to demonstrate the aforementioned conclusion with many reasons, through which it will be clear that the soul remains after death and does not require a body. From this, it can be easily perceived that <term>mahad <note>The "return" or resurrection of the soul.</note></term> pertains to the soul alone, as was affirmed above and will be better declared below. This chapter is divided into several parts, just as he brings forward several reasons; the parts will be clear in their respective places. Note that Saint Thomas [Aquinas], in *Against the Gentiles*, Book 2, Chapter 51, proves that intellectual substances are forms subsisting through themselves and are not material, as if their being does not depend on matter—see that source.

<margin>B</margin> **IT IS NOT** possible, etc. This is the first reason of Avicenna, in which he presupposes two things. First, that it is not possible for any body to have an altogether infinite power. Second, that it is not possible for an infinite power to exist in a body, and so on. And although these two seem to mean the same thing, they are nevertheless different: because for a body to have an infinite power is to have it through itself essentially, or as its own property or accident. But for an infinite power to *be in* a body implies something being in the body as if external to the body, whether that be a substance or something else; the text is clear.

<margin>C</margin> **FURTHERMORE** the soul is of infinite power: this is the reasoning confirming the presupposition. And Saint Thomas, in *Against the Gentiles*, Book 2, Chapter 49—where he proves that an intellectual substance is not a body—says that in no finite body can there be infinite power (as noted above in Book 1, where he argues that God is not a body). However, the power of the intellect is in a certain way infinite in its understanding; for it understands the species of numbers unto infinity and by increasing them, and similarly it knows the species of infinite shapes and proportions. It also knows the <term>universal <note>original: "universale"; a general concept, like "humanity," that applies to an unlimited number of individuals.</note></term>, which is infinite in its power according to its scope, for it contains individuals which are infinite in potential. Therefore, the intellect is not a body, etc. **NOR** is it possible even for the soul itself to be...

<margin>d</margin> **IN AN INDIVISIBLE THING** concerning those things that accompany the body, such as in a point: in this part Avicenna proves that the soul cannot exist in an indivisible thing among those that communicate with or follow the body, such as a point or a line and similar things. For these are said to "follow" the body because they are in the body as things that bound the body itself or its dimensions, and yet they are not a part of the body. For a point, although it terminates a line, is nevertheless not a part of the line; and we say that in a line there are infinite points. Avicenna therefore proves here that the soul is not in a point, because the soul is not received in the body except by means of a <term>complexion <note>original: "complexio"; in medieval thought, this refers to the specific "temperament" or balance of physical qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that makes a body fit to receive a soul.</note></term>. For matter, as was said above, does not receive the soul unless the matter is organized and "complexioned" for the human form. But because a "complexion" cannot be received in a point, therefore the intellectual soul can neither be received nor exist in a point. **ACCORDING TO** this path, that is, by means of a
<margin>e</margin> complexion.

It also argues that the soul requires a specifically balanced physical "complexion" to inhabit a body, a quality that mathematical points and lines lack.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical demonstration that the soul is not a physical body nor dependent on a body's physical "complexion" (the balance of elements). It focuses on the distinction between properties that belong to a body essentially and those that are only attributed to its points or indivisible parts by association.</meta>

<page-num>31</page-num>
->**AVICENNA**<-
<meta>catchword: proves</meta>

<margin>E</margin> **ON THE CONTRARY, it does not happen, etc.** That is, on the contrary, no <term>complexion <note>The specific mixture or balance of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) that makes up a physical body.</note></term> happens to the point or the indivisible itself, except according to a relationship and abstractive attribution of the intellect—that is, unless by accident, and in respect to something else. For example, in respect to the body or a part of the body in which the soul exists; for if the complexion is in the aforementioned body and its part, and the point is the extremity of that body, it follows that the complexion is in the point by accident, and in respect to another thing. The intellect does not attribute complexion to the point and the indivisible except through relation and respect to the body or its part of which the point is the extremity. No complexion is attributed to it (that is, the indivisible) according to the nature of things existing in a stable state—that is, according to the way something is attributed to another through itself, not in respect to something else. In this way, complexion happens to and is attributed to a body composed of elements, because complexion belongs to it through itself and according to its being, not through an abstractive attribution and respect toward something else created by the intellect.

<margin>F</margin> **AND IT IS so that it may be the extremity.** In this part, Avicenna declares how the indivisible is not attributed [with complexion] except according to a relation and respect to something else, and not according to the nature of existing things—that is, not through itself. For Avicenna says, "And it is so that it may be," etc., meaning it is possible for a complexion to be attributed to an indivisible thing in relation to another by assuming that the aforementioned point or indivisible is the extremity of a part of an element. This element is indeed simple and is a component part of that body in which the soul resides; for an integral part is called "simple" in respect to its whole, and is also called its "element" in a broad sense. And just as that part (namely of the aforementioned element) is the extremity of the body in truth and through itself, so it must be said that whatever is founded in the aforementioned part is an extremity <gloss>by accident</gloss>, because it inheres in the aforementioned part and body. Therefore, such a thing inhering in a body is quantitative by the quantity of the body. For <term>whiteness <note>original: "Albedo"; often used in medieval philosophy as a standard example of an "accident" or property that cannot exist without a physical host.</note></term> inhering in a body and in the extreme part of a body is quantitative through the quantity of the body in which it resides; such whiteness is also an extremity of the body by accident, because it inheres in the part of the body which is, in truth, the extremity of the body. Similarly, an indivisible thing like a point is an accident inhering in the extreme part of the body, and it is an extremity <gloss>by accident</gloss> because it is quantitative and an extremity by reason of the part of the body in which it resides, which is in truth the extreme part of the body. And just as being the extremity of a body is not attributed to a point through itself and according to the nature of things existing in being, but is attributed by accident according to relation and abstractive respect, as has been said; likewise, no complexion happens to or is attributed to a point and an indivisible thing (namely a point), except by accident and in respect to the part of the body in which the point resides. This is what we wished to say in this argument.

<margin>G</margin> **FURTHERMORE**, the point has a position. This is another reason through which he proves...

<meta>This page continues the logical demonstration from page 72 regarding the nature of the soul. Having previously argued that the soul is not a physical body, the text now focuses on proving that the soul cannot be located in an "indivisible point" because the soul and its thoughts (intelligible species) lack physical position.</meta>

# ON THE RETURN
<note>Latin: *De Almahad*, referring to Avicenna's *Al-Ma'ad* ("The Return" or "The Afterlife"), a treatise on the soul.</note>

k

[Avicenna] proves that infinite power, and the soul which is an infinite power, is not located in an indivisible thing, such as in a point. For a point has a position; however, the soul has no position, neither through itself <note>Latin: *per se*</note> nor by accident. Therefore, the soul is not in an indivisible thing nor in a point. AND THE DEMONSTRATION of this—that is, the proof that the soul does not have a position—is this: since an <term>intelligible intention <note>A mental concept or the meaning of a thing as grasped by the mind.</note></term> and an <term>intelligible species <note>The "mental image" or form of an object that exists in the intellect, stripped of its physical matter.</note></term> do not have a position, because the species itself abstracts from position and place. This is because it is a universal intelligible species, which abstracts from "here and now" <note>Latin: *hic et nunc*</note> and from all particularity. Furthermore, such an intelligible species is received in the soul, and everything that is received is received only according to the mode of the recipient. Therefore, if such an intelligible species abstracts from matter, and from quantity, and from position—otherwise it would not be a universal intelligible species—it follows that the soul receiving such a species must also be abstracted from matter, quantity, and position. 

It is proven, moreover, that the intelligible species does not have a position; for if it had a position, then it would either have a position that could be pointed to with a finger (namely, that it is situated in this or that place manifest to the senses), or it would have a position through the comparison of parts to one another (for example, a square position, or a triangular one, or a position that is higher or lower, and so on for others). And a point indeed has a position according to the primary intention, because it can be shown to be in this or that place where there is a part of a body or of quantity, of which the point is the boundary or extremity. But a point does not have a position according to the secondary intention, because it does not have a triangular position, which is a position resulting from the arrangement of parts in relation to one another. 

If intelligible species had a position just as a point has a position in the primary sense, then the species themselves would be the very boundaries of things existing through themselves in spaces or dimensions, or they would be so by accident, because they would adhere to something that bounds a space or dimension. If, therefore, intelligible species had a position like a point, it follows that they would have the nature of a point; and thus, just as a point serves as a boundary in dimensions, so also the intelligible species would be boundaries. And thus "any intelligible species considered toward that, etc.," <note>original: *considerata ad id &c.*</note> that is, any intelligible species caused by a thing which adheres to matter, would be the extremity of that thing with respect to the thing of which it is the species, and this is false; therefore, etc. 

Or according to another reading: if the intelligible forms or souls—that is, if souls had a position like a point—then the souls themselves would be the souls of those things which exist through themselves, or which are an extremity by accident. And thus souls would not be the souls and forms of bodies, but would be the souls of indivisible things, and of points, and of extremities, because the souls would have a position just like a point. And it would agree with its own disposition, and thus every intelligible form and soul, with respect to some thing founded in matter in which we say the soul exists, would be an extremity of that thing, and would be the form of that indivisible extremity, and not the form of the body. But this is false; therefore, it must be entirely denied that the soul has a position, or that intelligible species have a position like a point.

->Avicenna,<-

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the soul’s immateriality. Having established that the soul is not a physical body, the text now explores why "intelligible species"—the abstract concepts held in the mind—cannot have physical dimensions or a specific location, unlike sensory images which are tied to the physical organs of the body.</meta>

<page-num>25</page-num>
# AVICENNA 1

Avicenna. **IF TRULY** <term>intelligible species <note>The abstract mental "forms" or concepts of things (like the concept of "Humanity") that exist in the intellect.</note></term> were to have a physical position according to a <term>second intention <note>A logical term referring to how the mind classifies its own concepts—for example, recognizing that "Man" is a "Species."</note></term>. In this section, he proves that intelligible species do not have a physical position, etc., because if they did, they would possess magnitude and quantity. Thus, the universal intelligible species of "man" would have a specific size. However, such a species of man is a single essence in which all individual humans agree. It follows that if such a species and such a single essence had a physical quantity in the intellect, then all individual human beings would have to share that same single quantity. For the quantity in a "man" as perceived by the intellect as a universal must correspond to or be proportional to the quantity "outside" <note>Latin: *ad extra*; referring to the physical world outside the mind.</note> the mind. Therefore, just as there is a common quantity in the essence of man perceived by the intellect, it would be necessary for there to be a single quantity in the physical world in which all men agree, which is false.

<margin>I</margin> **AND THIS** indeed is the demonstration. To clarify this, it must be understood that above, after Avicenna demonstrated that the soul is not in the body, he adds that it is not possible for it to be located in a single point. He declared this through several arguments, as seen previously. In this part, he says that the preceding demonstration not only affirms that an intelligible species—or, according to another reading, an "intellectual form"—cannot exist in a point, but rather that it is impossible for it to exist in a body at all, or in anything that has a position through itself <note>Latin: *per se*</note>, which are characteristic of things with physical quantity. Wherefore, from the above, it is manifest that the soul (in which the universal intelligible species, abstracted from position and quantity, is received) is separated from matter. It is not among those things that can be demonstrated by the senses to be "here" or "there," nor is the soul or the intelligible species a boundary or extremity of a physical thing, such as a point is. Nor is it among those things that exist in a place at all. From these premises, it is clear that the soul is not in a body, nor in a position, nor in a place, nor in a point, nor in any indivisible physical thing. Therefore, the soul is separated from matter, and it does not require a body for its own existence.

<margin>K</margin> **SENSORY FORMS** or <term>sensory species <note>The mental images of specific physical objects, such as the sight of a specific red apple, as opposed to the abstract concept of "redness."</note></term>. In this part, he silently responds to an objection and establishes the difference between an intelligible species and a sensory species. Although an intelligible species has neither position nor quantity, a sensory species *does* have quantity and position. This is because sensory species are not universal like intelligible species. It is necessary that just as the things sensed are "quanta" <note>Physical entities with size/magnitude.</note> and have quantity and position, so too must the sensory species—impressed by those sensed things upon the organ of sight (for instance, in the <term>glacial humidity <note>Latin: *glacialis humiditas*; a historical term for the crystalline lens of the eye, which medieval scholars believed was the primary organ of vision.</note></term> of the eye)—have a quantity and position conforming to the quantity of the external objects. For example, when some red body impresses its species into the glacial humidity of the eye, that which is then seen in the eye or in the lens is the species of the red body, possessing a quantity and position conforming to the quantity and position of the red body outside. This is proven: for if the aforementioned red body is three feet <note>Latin: *tripedale*; literally "three-foot," a measurement of length.</note> long, and the eye sees and discerns it to be three fe...

### AVICENNA

You say that intelligible things have a position in the intellect: for just as sensory species <note>original: *species sensibiles*; the mental images or "likenesses" of physical objects perceived by the senses.</note> have a position and a size corresponding to the position and size of the sensed objects outside the mind, and just as the sensed object outside the mind has a position and size, so too do sensory species have a corresponding position and size, and so forth. In the same way, it might be said that if intelligible species existing in the soul have a position, it must be that the intelligible species of things separate from matter <note>original: *rerum separatarum a materia*; referring to entities like God or abstract concepts that do not have physical bodies.</note> understood by the soul have a position in the soul. By consequence, things separate from matter outside the soul would have a position conforming to the position of their intelligible species existing in the intellect. For it is necessary that the intelligible species in the intellect be conformed to the things understood outside the mind which impress their own proper and fitting intelligible species. 

However, things separate from matter do not have a position, and they possess only one kind of being, which is "intelligible being" <note>original: *esse intelligibile*; the state of existing as an object of thought or an abstract reality, rather than a physical thing.</note>. For their being is intelligible being only, because their existence makes an impression only in the intellect as a species, and not in the senses as material sensed things do—which impress species in both the sense and the intellect, but in different ways. Therefore, material things have two kinds of being, as will be declared below, but things separate from matter have only one kind of being, which is intelligible being. And for that reason, their being corresponds and is conformed to their species existing in the intellect. If, therefore, their aforementioned intelligible species had a position in the intellect, it would follow that things separate from matter would have a position outside the mind, which is clearly false. Therefore, intelligible species do not have a position, and by consequence, they cannot be received except in a substance separate from position and size. The intellectual soul <note>original: *anima intellectiva*.</note>, therefore, in which the intelligible species are received, has neither position nor size, etc.

If, therefore, the intelligible species of sensed things in the intellect do not have a position, it follows that sensed things outside the mind would not have a position; otherwise, there would be no conformity between the intelligible species of sensed things existing in the intellect and the sensed things causing the aforementioned intelligible species in the intellect.
