<meta>catchword: Avicenna</meta>

For such a soul is material and sensory, because it has no being except in a physical, sensed thing, and it has no operations except sensory ones; such a soul is also mixed with imperfection <note>original: "malitia," which in this philosophical context refers to metaphysical "badness" or a lack of goodness rather than moral evil</note> and with privation <note>privation: the absence of a quality that should naturally be present</note>, for it is deprived and diminished of many perfections. Such is the soul of brute animals: it is "thick" because it is material, and it is a turbid, watery substance. Therefore, the comparison between the intelligences <term>intelligences: pure spiritual beings that govern the celestial spheres</term> and human souls separated from the body is this: that the capacities attributed to the sensory soul of brute animals are also attributed to the human soul while it is still within the body. It is therefore **MANIFEST**, etc. The word **TRUE** is explained differently: as their essence or root, etc. For the intention of <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina, d. 1037) was a Persian polymath whose works on soul and afterlife deeply influenced Western medieval thought.</note> in this part is that the human soul, once separated from the body, possesses this perfection: that it is stripped of all alteration <note>alteration: the process of physical change or becoming, which cannot happen to an eternal soul</note> and that it knows all beings. Because of this, it is made similar to the intelligences, as has been said; nevertheless, the principle and root of the human soul is the spiritual substance of our Creator. This is because the Universal Intelligence, as has been said according to <term>Avicenna</term>, is the principle from which the human form emanates, which is the intellectual soul. Such a Universal Intelligence is a spiritual essence, and it is the instrument and secondary cause through which God works, creates, and pours souls into the bodies of men. This Intelligence is therefore called a spiritual substance, and it is said to belong to "our Creator" because it is an instrument serving our Creator. But the principle and root of physical substance is a sensed thing mixed with imperfection and privation, and it is a turbid, thick thing.

It is explained otherwise and better: that there is a difference between the essence of the human soul and the physical essence because the essence and root of the human rational soul is the spiritual essence and substance of our Creator—that is, emanating and created by our God, the Glorious Creator, by means of the Universal Intelligence, as was said. But the physical substance or essence is a sensed substance mixed with imperfection, with potentiality, and with privation, because it possesses within itself a diminution and the privation of many perfections, and it exists only in a state of potentiality regarding many operations and perfections. And the comparison of these four "intentions" <note>intentions: here meaning specific attributes or characteristics</note> is what is attributed to the human soul, which are the aforementioned intentions: one of which is that the substance of the soul is "apprehensive" <note>apprehensive: having the power to perceive or understand</note> and more noble than other sensory apprehensive powers. Second, that the knowledge of the human soul itself is more noble than the knowledge of other powers. The third intention is that the things which are apprehended are more noble and fitting, etc. The fourth intention is that the perfections of the rational soul itself are more noble than the perfections of the sensory powers. It is manifest, moreover, that these four aforementioned intentions, which belong and are attributed to the intellectual soul, are more noble and worthy than the final intentions mentioned which are attributed to physical substance. And the aforementioned intentions are worthier than the perfections attributed to the sensory soul; wherefore the pleasures of the intellectual power are worthier than the pleasures which—

at the end of life and after death. **HAPPINESS** <note>original: "FOELICITAS"</note> therefore of the other world is found at the point of separation—that is, it is perceived by the soul at the separation and liberation of the soul from the body, and at the liberation of the soul from natural impressions—that is, from the impressions of the senses, which are otherwise called natural impressions in comparison to those things which proceed from reason and from the will. **AND AT** the complete stripping of the essence—that is, at the complete despoiling of the essence—namely, when the essence of the soul is completely stripped of bodily impressions and from the impressions of the senses. And then, at such a separation of the soul from the body and the aforementioned complete stripping of the soul's essence, the soul itself beholds and understands the divine essence, etc., and contemplates the sublime essences and the arrival of the soul’s own perfections; and it also contemplates the excellent delight which is made its own in that hour—that is, in the other life, when the soul is separated from the body and stripped, etc. **TORMENT** <note>original: "CRVCIATVS"</note> truly, etc. After he has shown the happiness and delight which belongs to the perfect, virtuous soul in the other life, in this part he shows the punishment and torment of the wicked soul in the other life. **AND SINCE** the rational soul is not in the body like a form in matter, etc. In this part, Avicenna responds to someone drawing this conclusion from the things said before—namely, that the body itself is that which hinders the soul from grasping the aforementioned delight and the aforementioned pain and torment. Therefore, although it was said above that the happiness of the other world is grasped at the separation of the soul from the body and the soul’s liberation from natural impressions, etc.; nevertheless, because the rational soul in the body is not like a form in matter—that is, it is not in the body as other material forms are, which are in the body and which are drawn out from the potentiality of matter <term>potentiality of matter: the Aristotelian idea that matter has the "potential" to become something when given a "form" or identity.</term>, and depend in their being upon matter itself, and are immersed in matter. But the rational soul in the body is not drawn out from the potentiality of matter, nor is it immersed in matter, nor dependent in its being upon matter itself or the body, because, as Avicenna proved above: the essence of the intellectual soul can exist without matter. Because, therefore, the rational soul in the body is not like a material form in matter depending on it for its being, but is in the body as an informing form <note>informing form: a soul that gives life and structure to the body rather than being a mere product of it.</note> existing as a principle of natural animal and intellectual operation in itself. Therefore, the substance of the body is not what hinders the rational soul from grasping that happiness which is understood in the other life; rather, the things that mediate and prohibit the soul from that happiness are the impressions. It is explained in another and better way: that Avicenna in this part responds to a silent objection, namely: someone might say that just as the happiness and delight of the other world cannot be grasped and known by the soul while existing in the body except in part and according to some degree, and not totally because the body hinders and darkens it; just as the soul of even the most virtuous person, while it is in the body, cannot totally grasp that happiness

->## ON THE RETURN <note>original: "DE ALMAHAD," from the Arabic *Al-Ma'ād*, referring to the afterlife or the "place of return."</note><-

*not because of the obstacle of bad character, and because of vicious habits, because it is presupposed that such a soul is virtuous; rather, it is because of the obstacle of the body. Therefore, just as the soul cannot completely grasp that happiness in this life because of the obstacle of the body, so too in the other life after separation from the body, the soul will not be able to obtain that happiness and aforementioned delight—specifically because the soul within the body is darkened by the body and by the matter which it informs.* <note>The OCR reads "infirmat" (weakens), but in this philosophical context, it is likely "informat" (gives form to), meaning the soul gives life and shape to the physical matter of the body.</note> *To this, Avicenna responds: although the rational soul in this life is in the body, it is nonetheless not "immersed" in the body as if its existence depended upon it, like a form exists in matter.* <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, a "form in matter" (like the shape of a statue in bronze) cannot exist without the material. Avicenna argues the human soul is different; it uses the body but is a distinct substance.</note> *That is, it is not like a material form drawn out from the potential of matter, which exists in matter by giving it shape and being immersed in it, and upon which it depends for its existence. Therefore, because the soul in the body is not like a form in matter drawn from the potential of matter and immersed in it, but the rational soul itself is in the body as a form giving it shape—acting as the principle of natural, vital, and intellectual operation—it does not depend on the body for its existence, because it can exist by itself without the body, as Avicenna proved above. Thus, the substance of the body in which the soul resides in this life is not what hinders the soul from the knowledge of the divine essence, nor from the grasping of happiness and the aforementioned delight when it shall be in the other life and separated from the body. Rather, the "mediator" and the thing that prevents the soul, once separated from the body, from achieving its happiness is not the body's physical substance, as was said, but the qualities or "vicious habits"* <term>vicious habits: "habitus uitiosi," referring to deeply ingrained bad character traits or moral dispositions</term> *impressed upon and confirmed in the soul by the body and the senses; these are what prevent the soul, once separated from the body, from achieving its happiness. For it is manifest among all philosophers that good, virtuous habits and bad, vicious habits acquired in this world are founded in the soul as their proper subject, and not in the body. And therefore, even if the soul is separated from the body, these vicious habits—acquired from the senses dominating over reason—remain in the soul even after it is separated from the body. And just as such vicious habits hindered and obscured the soul while it existed in the body—so much so that such a soul was very little inclined or disposed toward the knowledge of theoretical and divine things—so after death, in the other life, those vicious habits impressed and remaining in the soul prohibit it from the knowledge of the divine essence and prohibit it from its happiness. The Arabs* <note>Referring to Islamic philosophers and theologians like Al-Farabi or the Mutakallimun.</note> *say that just as images are easily impressed upon a mirror that is polished and clean, so the knowledge of things is impressed upon a virtuous, clean soul. And just as images are not impressed upon a mirror that is dull and unpolished, so the knowledge of divine things is not impressed upon a dull, vicious soul.* WHEN

->AVICENNA<-

*...to pass from body to body. For the most famous philosophers, such as Plato and others speaking metaphorically, affirmed that such a change occurs, as was said above. For a lustful man is likened to a pig, a greedy man to a wolf, and a proud man to a lion, and so on. Therefore, when the vice of lust or pride has been impressed and becomes a habit in the soul, then that habituated vice of lust remains in the soul when it is separated from the body—the soul in which that vice previously existed—just as if that soul were still in the body as before. Because, therefore, the aforementioned vice of lust remains in the soul as if it were in the body, and the animal possessing a soul habituated to such a vice of lust and gluttony is likened to a pig. For this reason, the aforementioned philosophers said that the soul of a lustful person after death is transformed into the body of a pig, because such a soul still retains and preserves the vicious habits of lust and gluttony, just as if it were in the body of a pig; and the soul separated from the body of a proud man, who is likened to a lion, retains the habits of pride as if it were still in the body of a lion. And as has been said concerning the vice of lust and pride, so it may be said of other habituated vices, which remain in the soul after death and prevent the soul from its perfection and ultimate happiness. And thus it is clear how the sayings of the philosophers who proposed that* Altenasach <note>original: "Altenasach," a Latinization of the Arabic *al-tanāsukh*, meaning the transmigration of souls or reincarnation.</note> *occurs are to be understood and explained. It is also clear from the sayings of Avicenna and other philosophers who propose* Altenasach, *as was said above, that just as evil, vicious habits remain in the soul separated from the body as if that soul were still in the body, similarly it must be said that practical virtuous habits remain in the soul in the other life, as if the soul habituated to virtues were still in the body; and just as virtuous habits remain in a virtuous soul separated from the body, so it must be concluded that speculative habits and knowledge remain in the aforementioned soul, as if such a learned soul were still in that state in which it was before. By this, the saying of Saint Jerome is confirmed, namely: let us learn on earth, so that knowledge may remain in the heavens.*

<margin>A</margin>
**TEMPERATE** in heat etc. <note>original: "TEMPERATVM in calore &c."</note> meaning it is neither hot nor cold in any absolute sense, but rather perceptibly so. **AND IT IS** one in intention, because just as each of the contrary extremes has one intention in itself, and each of them is one in intention distinct from the other, similarly the middle and temperate point between two contrary extremes has its own intention, and is one in intention. However, how virtue is a middle point between extremes, and how all vicious extremes are removed from a virtuous person, those who contemplate moral science declare most excellently; therefore, let one look there. <note>This refers to the Aristotelian "Golden Mean," the ethical theory that virtue is the desirable middle ground between two extremes of excess and deficiency.</note>

<margin>B</margin>
**FROM THE OBSTACLE** drawing away. Namely, from perfection and from happiness. **PRAYERS** or divine adorations, i.e., the prayers or adorations which men perform for the glorious God, and contemplations concerning God himself. **FROM THIS** harm, i.e., from the habituated corporeal sensory qualities in the soul, which harm and prevent the soul from its proper end and from its happiness.

# CONCERNING THE RETURN

<margin>C</margin> **AND INDEED THE SOULS** *separated from the body have ranks, etc. After Avicenna <note>The Latinized name for Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most significant thinkers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> demonstrated that rational souls remain after death, and that happiness or torment is appropriate for them, he consequently declares here that souls separated from the body have different ranks and degrees of reward or punishment in the other life, according to the variety of the soul's merits or demerits; and the meaning of the text is clear.*

<margin>D</margin> **AND SUCH** *souls are in* berzach <note>original: "berzach," from the Arabic *Barzakh*, referring to a barrier or liminal state between death and resurrection.</note>, *that is, in purgatory, which is between the souls themselves—meaning that purgatory is a middle state for the aforementioned harmful souls. This is because before these souls ascend to their happiness and before they are stripped and freed from the bodily qualities and bad habits impressed upon the soul by the body—habits which prevent the souls from attaining and reaching absolute and immeasurable happiness at the highest level—it is necessary for such souls to remain in the aforementioned* berzach. *By means of this state, they are purged and their vicious bad habits are removed. Because while these souls were in the body, they did not recognize the happiness we mentioned, nor did they recognize themselves as being vicious and habituated to bad habits, due to their occupation with worldly things and activities. Therefore, after death, such souls are no longer occupied with worldly activities as they were in the body, and they begin to recognize the happiness we spoke of, and they realize they are deprived of such happiness because of the bad qualities impressed upon the soul by the senses and because of vicious habits. Hence, such souls are hurt and intensely tormented by this realization. And since such bad habits impressed upon these souls are not substantial or essential to the souls themselves, and are not so fixed that they cannot be removed, these souls are eventually freed and purged from those vicious qualities and habits after a period of time. Consequently, the souls are then no longer tormented by the knowledge of their vices and imperfections. Thus, at last, the souls freed from such vicious habits reach true happiness in the end; for once they are stripped and purged of those vicious habits that hindered true happiness, they finally attain the highest good and true bliss. The Arabs say that just as gold is purified by fire, so the human soul in this life is purged through the infirmities and calamities that happen to the body, and it comes to the knowledge of its vices and to repentance for them. Similarly, separated souls are purged of their vices and sins in purgatory.*

<margin>E</margin> **SOME**, *however, are diminished souls, etc. In this section, Avicenna proposes another rank and another degree of souls separated from the body. This is the third rank or degree, in which are the souls that are "diminished" in the speculative sciences <term>theoretical or philosophical knowledge</term>, but were virtuous, living according to moral acts and being harmless—that is, not performing evil. And to these souls, while they were in this life*

...when they were immersed in the pleasures of sensible things and, being ill-habituated, they desire similar pleasures in the other life, and they are tortured by the deprivation of the sensory pleasures which they desire. Therefore, Avicenna says here that the souls of the fourth rank, and the souls of infants and fools, since they are harmless, are not ill-habituated by vicious acts or by the impressions of pleasurable senses and natural qualities contrary to the soul's substance; and therefore such souls in the other life do not desire the pleasures of the senses, nor are they saddened by the deprivation of them. Note that "natural qualities"—that is, sensible qualities and the impressions of pleasurable senses—are contrary to the substance of the soul, because they darken the soul itself and impede it from the speculation and contemplation of divine things, and from happiness.

<margin>K</margin> **AND CERTAINLY THE FIRST ORDER** <note>original: "ET ORDO quidem primus"</note> of souls, etc. Through these words, Avicenna establishes the difference between the fourth rank and the fifth rank, because it has been said that these two ranks of souls—namely, the fourth rank and the fifth rank—are such that no soul of these ranks attains absolute happiness or absolute punishment. Therefore, in this part, Avicenna posits a certain difference between them: that the "first order"—meaning the first of the two ranks mentioned above, namely the fourth rank—is capable of having some impression, or some vestige or part of happiness, according to the measure of knowledge concerning the First Principle <note>original: "primo principio," referring to God as the source of all existence.</note> which the souls of this rank received from some teacher. For if such souls were taught by someone’s instruction and had some knowledge of the First Principle—that is, of God—then they possess in the other life some small or minimal happiness according to the measure of the knowledge they had of God.

It is explained in another way: **AND CERTAINLY THE FIRST ORDER.** That is, souls of the first rank, of whom it was said that they are souls perfected in habits and speculative sciences <note>The "speculative sciences" include theology, metaphysics, and mathematics—subjects that require pure contemplation.</note> and in moral acts, and they are harmless, and such souls have absolute happiness. And although souls of this kind have absolute happiness from the fact that they are perfect in speculative sciences and in divine knowledge, nevertheless, because one soul of this rank can have greater knowledge of God than another, and can have greater perfection in speculative sciences than another; and because by means of the speculative sciences and the knowledge of God held and acquired in this world, souls are disposed to receive union with the First Intelligence <note>original: "intelligentia prima," in Avicenna's system, this is the first being that proceeds from God.</note>, according to Avicenna, while they are separated from the body, and are consequently disposed to receive the knowledge of God and true happiness; therefore, according as one soul is more knowledgeable <note>original: "scientificus," meaning one who has mastered the systematic sciences.</note> and more disposed, and according to the measure of knowledge which the soul had of God in this world, it will have in the other life a vestige and impression of happiness. For if it had much knowledge of the First Principle, it will have much happiness. And if it had little knowledge, it will have little happiness.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "ranks" of souls in the afterlife. Having previously discussed the fourth rank (innocent but unlearned souls), the text now moves to those who are "noxiae" (harmful or vicious) and addresses the philosophical debate regarding whether the soul survives death at all.</meta>

# **AVICENNA**

**AS FOR SOULS** that are diminished in their habits of contemplation <note>Latin: *habitus speculatiuis*. In medieval philosophy, "speculation" refers to the intellectual ability to see or contemplate divine and universal truths.</note> but are harmful. In this section, Avicenna explains the punishment that will be experienced by souls who lacked knowledge of the speculative sciences—specifically, the souls of the ignorant who were harmful and lived viciously. He argues that such souls either possessed some knowledge that a state of absolute perfection and happiness exists, or they were entirely empty of such knowledge. In the first case, because these souls recognize they are now deprived of that perfection and happiness, they are tormented by eternal punishment. If, however, they were entirely empty of that knowledge but were still vicious, then their torture and punishment will be shaped by the vicious qualities and habits they acquired in this world. They long for the sinful sensory pleasures they enjoyed in this life, and because they are deprived of those pleasures in the next, they are filled with sorrow and torment.

<margin>M</margin>
**THAT** which is attributed to the opinion of Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias (fl. 200 AD), a famous commentator on Aristotle who argued that the human soul was a "form" of the body and therefore perished when the body died.</note>. Here Avicenna responds to a silent objection: someone might argue that, according to the opinion of Alexander, souls are destroyed and do not remain after death, and therefore there is no need to investigate the punishment or torture of souls in the afterlife. Avicenna responds that Alexander’s opinion on this matter is not true, nor is it the actual view of Aristotle <note>The author is defending Aristotle's reputation by claiming he believed in the immortality of the soul, contrary to Alexander's interpretation.</note>. The text of this is clear.

<margin>N</margin>
**CERTAIN WISE MEN HAVE SAID** that good souls. After Avicenna explained the various ranks of souls separated from the body and the degrees of reward and punishment (or degrees of happiness and pain), and after he affirmed that Alexander’s opinion is false, he consequently introduces the opinion of certain wise men. They said that souls separated from the body acquire an increase in their delight and their "goods" through encountering or associating with perfected and virtuous souls. Thus, a soul in the other life, by associating and meeting with perfected souls—and by knowing and contemplating that it is in the same place as those perfected souls—is delighted by gazing upon them, and its own happiness and pleasure increase. For pleasure is caused by the contemplation of a delightful thing; therefore, when these souls associate with perfected souls, they contemplate not only their own joy, but also the joy and perfection of the others. Because of this association, their delight is magnified.

The vicious souls, however, behave in the opposite manner. Just as the consideration of a delightful thing causes pleasure, the consideration of sad things, tortures, and punishments causes sadness and painful suffering. Because vicious souls are associated with other vicious souls, they contemplate not only their own individual punishment and torture, but also the punishments and tortures of all the other vicious souls. Therefore, while virtuous souls delight vehemently in their union and association with the perfected, the vicious souls follow the contrary path—punishment and sorrow that is infinite for them. And each soul is joined and associated with that which is similar to it—that is, with the soul...

It also refutes the idea that the soul dies with the body and describes how social association in the afterlife magnifies either the joy of the virtuous or the misery of the wicked.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how souls interact after death, specifically focusing on the "intellectual association" between souls of similar character and responding to the theory of transmigration (reincarnation).</meta>

# CONCERNING THE RETURN

<margin>M</margin>
...to souls like themselves in quality and habit, which conjunction and association or encounter is purely intellectual. Therefore, when a perfect and virtuous soul is joined and associated via the intellect with souls that are pure and perfect—that is, when a good and perfect soul understands other perfect souls and their delight—it also feels delight. Likewise, when a vicious soul is joined and associated via the intellect with vicious souls, then by understanding their punishment and imperfection, as well as its own imperfections and vices, it is greatly saddened and tormented.

<margin>O</margin>
**AND EACH AND EVERY** rational soul. Here Avicenna <note>Avicenna (c. 980–1037) was a Persian polymath and one of the most influential philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age. This text is a Latin translation of his work on the afterlife.</note> declares that souls separated from the body, whether they are perfect and virtuous or vicious, are joined with other souls in an intellectual conjunction, as has been said. This is because every soul understands its own essence and understands that which is similar to its own essence. This knowledge continually increases more and more, because the soul is continually purified from the impressions of sensory things <note>In this philosophy, the physical senses are seen as a "veil" or distraction that prevents the soul from achieving pure, direct intellectual knowledge.</note> which hinder perfect cognition. Since this is the case, it follows that virtuous souls, by knowing their own essence and the essence of other virtuous souls, achieve an increase in their delights. Similarly, vicious souls, by knowing their own essence and the essence of other vicious souls, achieve intense sorrow. 

But regarding the claim that "each rational soul understands its own essence," etc., Avicenna explains by saying: "Do you not see, or must it not be granted, that these aforementioned souls understand the intellectual principle—that is, the First Intelligence <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, the "First Intelligence" is the first being to emanate from God; it is the highest created intellect.</note>, which is their cause and their own beginning?" It is as if he says: "Yes." For even though vicious souls are deprived of the divine vision, as has been said, they nevertheless understand that God and the First Intelligence are their source. If, therefore, vicious souls understand the First Intelligence—and if it is not granted that vicious souls *lack* such understanding—then it certainly cannot be denied in the case of a perfect soul. If, then, a perfect and virtuous soul understands the First Intelligence and God, it will be much more able to understand its own essence and to understand that which is similar to its own essence.

<margin>P</margin>
**AND CERTAIN** other wise men have said that the way of *Altenasach* <term>Altenasach: a Latinization of the Arabic *al-tanasukh*, referring to the transmigration or reincarnation of souls.</term> etc. This is another opinion of the wise, who said that although the path of *Altenasach* concerning the "Return" <note>original: *Mahad*. From the Arabic *al-Ma'ad*, meaning the place of return or the afterlife.</note>—the state of the soul separated from the body—is impossible and false if understood literally (as was demonstrated above, and you may refer back to that section), nevertheless, there are aspects of this position on *Altenasach* that are possible and not forbidden. But before we bring forward the reasoning for the aforementioned opinion, let us state the difference between the opinion of <term>Altenasach</term><note>The Latinized version of the Arabic word *al-tanāsukh*, meaning the transmigration of souls or reincarnation.</note>, as the word sounds, and this current opinion. The opinion of <term>Altenasach</term> posits that souls after death are truly transformed from body to body in a physical sense. And as soon as any man dies, in that same instant, the soul separated from the body of that man is transformed into another new body; it becomes the <term>substantial form</term><note>In medieval philosophy, the "substantial form" is the essential nature or "blueprint" that makes a thing what it is and gives it life.</note> of the newly generated body and is the source of all actions in that body, just as it was in the previous body. And such a soul, after separation from that body, is similarly transformed into another new body, giving existence and life to it, and so on successively into other bodies. This opinion, speaking in such absolute terms, is impossible, as was declared above in chapter 3. 

But the opinion of the wise men, which Avicenna <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina, c. 980–1037) was a towering figure in Islamic philosophy whose works on the soul deeply influenced Western medieval thought.</note> discusses here, holds that the "Path of Altenasach"—when understood in the way described above—is impossible and false. However, if one understands <term>Altenasach</term> as this specific school of thought defines it, then these wise men concede that it does occur. As stated before, <term>Altenasach</term> is an Arabic word and implies a change or passage from one thing to another. Because the soul, according to the aforementioned erroneous opinion, passes from body to body successively, providing substantial being and life to each of those bodies, that opinion is named the path or opinion of <term>Altenasach</term>. 

Similarly, because this opinion of which Avicenna speaks here holds that a soul separated from the body remains connected afterward, it is united with another soul that is currently animating another body—specifically a body with a <term>complexion</term><note>The "complexion" refers to the specific physical temperament or balance of qualities (like heat and moisture) that defines an individual's constitution.</note> similar to the first body from which the soul was separated. 

*For example: Socrates now dies, and his separated soul is united with the soul of Plato, who possesses a body with a complexion just like Socrates' body had. Thus, it continues successively with the soul and body of another man who has a similar complexion to that of Socrates and Plato. However, this opinion does not claim that the soul of Socrates—though it is united with the soul of Plato or another by impressing good or evil upon it—is the "substantial form" of Plato or the other person; it does not give life or existence to that man to whom it is united.* 

*It is clear, therefore, from this opinion that the soul separated from the body of Socrates is later united and continued with the soul of Plato, and after the death of Plato, with the soul of another man having a complexion similar to the body that belonged to Socrates and Plato. Consequently, such a soul of Socrates passes from body to body by connecting itself with one soul by virtue of the complexion of the body it inhabits, and afterward with another soul existing in another body, as has been said. Thus, according to this opinion, a form of <term>Altenasach</term> is admitted to occur—not in the way the erroneous opinion holds, but according to the manner described in this opinion of the wise.* 

And from the preceding, it is clear how this opinion *differs from the erroneous opinion of <term>Altenasach</term> mentioned above,* which holds that the soul gives existence to every body to which it passes and acts as its substantial form. # ON THE RETURN <note>original: *De Almahad*; this refers to the Arabic term *Al-Ma'ad*, meaning "the place of return" or the afterlife.</note>

...separated from the body of Socrates, it continues and is united with the soul of Plato, and afterward with another soul—not by giving **substantial being** to Plato, but only by assisting Plato’s body because of the conformity of the body's **complexion** <note>In medieval medicine and philosophy, "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a person's physical and mental nature.</note> with the complexion of Socrates. It does this by impressing good or evil upon Plato’s soul and upon Plato himself, or upon another soul existing in another body tempered just as Socrates’ body was. 

With these premises established, the reasoning for this opinion is assigned: namely, that certain souls separated from the body are joined with certain other souls by impressing good or evil upon them. This is because, just as the soul of Socrates emanated from the <term>Intelligence</term> <note>The "Active Intelligence" was thought to be a celestial force that "poured" souls into bodies and thoughts into minds.</note> and was infused into Socrates’ body (which was tempered with a complexion suitable for that specific soul), and because of the suitability between Socrates’ soul and the complexion of his body, the aforementioned soul of Socrates had an inclination and a **bond** <note>original: *colligantiam*</note> with Socrates’ body in this life. 

Similarly, if it should happen—as it is possible—that a complexion occurs in some newly generated human body that is similar or very close to the complexion that was in the body of Socrates, then a specific result follows. Just as Socrates’ soul in this life had a dependency or bond with his own body (due to the suitability of the complexion and the proportion between the soul and body), so too would such a soul of Socrates—assuming it was deficient in the sciences and habituated only to sensory things—have a dependency or some bond with the soul existing in a living body that has a complexion similar to Socrates’ original body.

THEREFORE, because of the cause that existed in the first body from which it was separated—that is, the soul of (for example) Socrates depended on, or had a bond and an inclination toward, the body of Socrates because of the suitability and proportion between that soul and the complexion of Socrates’ body—a similar effect occurs after death. Such a separated soul of Socrates will have a dependency or bond with the body of Plato, or of another person who possesses a complexion similar to the complexion of Socrates’ body. 

For just as there was a suitability between Socrates’ soul and his body because of its physical makeup, and upon the destruction of that makeup the soul was separated from that body, so too there will be a suitability between Socrates’ soul and Plato’s body because of a similar complexion. Because of this suitability, the soul of Socrates is joined to and has a dependency or bond with Plato’s soul and body, "impressing" good or evil upon it, as will be explained below. And although the separated soul of Socrates has a dependency in some way with Plato’s soul and body, as has been said, it is nevertheless impossible for such a soul of Socrates to have a **total dependency** with Plato’s body in the way it previously had with Socrates’ body <note>The author is careful to distinguish this "influence" from actual reincarnation; the soul of Socrates is not "living" as Plato, but merely haunting or influencing him.</note>.

# ON THE RETURN
<note>original: "DE ALMAHAD" — from the Arabic "al-Ma'ād," referring to the "Return" or the afterlife.</note>

...[souls] perfected in some way in the sciences, yet flawed or ignorant, are continued with souls existing in bodies through a spiritual continuation until they are perfected; afterward, they are separated and united with the first intelligence, and thus attain happiness.

**S**OME OF THESE MEN SAID that the cognitive power, etc. That is, some of those who hold the aforementioned opinion: that a certain soul—namely, a soul habituated toward sensible things—is continued with certain [other] souls; and in a certain way, they allow **Altenasach** <note>original: "Altenasach" — the Latinized version of the Arabic "al-tanāsukh," meaning the transmigration of souls or reincarnation.</note> to occur. They said that the **cognitive power** <note>The faculty that combines and divides mental images to form thoughts.</note> of the intellective soul is separated from matter through the corruption of the body and through the separation of the rational soul from the body. And then the cognitive power itself, by this means, apprehends and knows all **intentions** <note>In medieval philosophy, an "intentio" (intention) is the mental representation or "meaning" of an object that the mind perceives beyond its physical form, such as a sheep perceiving the "danger" in a wolf.</note> existing in the sensible and natural world, but it does not apprehend intelligible intentions separated from matter and from sensible things, etc. To clarify what is said by these men, it should be known that those who said the cognitive power is separated hold that the external senses are entirely corporeal and organic; their operations cannot occur without a physical organ. The internal senses, however—although they mostly operate by means of the brain while the soul is in the body—are not, in these internal powers (namely the **imaginative**, **cognitive**, and **memorative**), totally organic, always requiring a corporeal organ for their operations. Therefore, just as the power of the intellective soul, while it is in the body, sometimes requires the body and **phantasms** <note>A "phantasm" is a mental image or representation of a sensory object stored in the mind.</note> in the act of understanding, and sometimes does not—as in the knowledge held concerning things abstracted from the senses and from matter—in the same way, the aforementioned powers (namely the cognitive, imaginative, etc.) sometimes require the body and sometimes do not. This is evident in dreams and in **melancholics** <note>In the medieval medical tradition, "melancholics" were individuals with an excess of black bile, thought to be prone to deep thought, visions, or prophetic dreams.</note>, in whom the cognitive power flourishes most; by them, many things are foreseen and imagined which were not perceived by the external senses, nor previously imagined. And it is clear that in those sleeping, the senses are bound; and in melancholics and those in a **frenzy** <note>The "frenetic" (freneticis) suffered from an inflammation of the brain membranes, leading to delirium.</note>, the **complexion** <note>The specific humoral balance of the body or an organ.</note> of the brain is poorly disposed for the operations of these powers; therefore, such powers do not use the organ at that time. And from this, they hold that just as the intellective power remains in the separated soul, so also do the imaginative, cognitive, **desiderative** <note>The faculty of desire or will.</note>, and memorative powers. But the power of sight, smell, and others which require an organ entirely, do not remain in the soul separated from the body. Therefore, just as the aforementioned powers (the imaginative, cognitive, and desiderative) in this world do not perceive anything except the intentions of sensible things while the soul is united to the body—and do not perceive universal intentions or the intelligible intentions of things abstracted from matter, because that belongs to the intellective power—similarly, in the soul separated from the body, both the aforementioned powers and the intellective power remain. ...they are so situated because they are remote and abstracted from the senses, and the sensible powers and the sensible appetites <note>The physical desires and instincts shared with animals.</note> are asleep; in them, there is only the intellective power, resulting from the continuous contemplation of the intellect regarding those things which are abstracted from the senses. But some men are found in this life who are so immersed and habituated in sensible things <margin>2</margin> that their intellective power is asleep, because such ignorant men are occupied only with things perceived by the senses. And the more the soul is occupied with sensible things, the further it is distanced from the knowledge of God and of abstract substances. And conversely, the more the rational soul in this life is occupied in the contemplation and knowledge of abstract substances, the further it is distanced from these worldly, sensible things.

<margin>
Certain philosophers said that happiness <note>original: "fœlicitas"</note> consists in the consideration of death—that is, just as the soul in death is separated from the body and from these sensible things, so true happiness in this world is the contemplation of things abstracted from this world and from sensible things. Hence, from this kind of contemplation, the soul considers itself to be abstracted as if it were separated from the body, because it considers only divine things and the Intelligences <note>In medieval cosmology, "Intelligences" were celestial beings or minds that governed the movement of the stars and planets.</note>.
</margin>

Therefore, souls in this world are habituated according to the acts they frequently perform. Because of this, souls that were virtuous in this world—and occupied in the sciences and the contemplation of God and the angels, and remote from these sensible things as if they were not even in this world—possess the same habit when they are separated from the body as they previously held in this world. And consequently, just as such souls in this life were distanced from worldly sensations as if they were outside the lower world and occupied in the contemplation of abstract substances, in the same way, after separation from the body, these aforementioned souls are distanced much more than before from this world. They are joined through their intellective power with the divine substance and other abstract substances, and they enjoy true happiness.

Similarly, the souls of men who were occupied during their entire lives with sensible things, and remote from the contemplation of God and of those things which are abstracted from matter and from the senses, preserve after the separation from their bodies the same habit which they previously held in this world. Consequently, because such souls are habituated toward worldly, sensible things, those souls, once separated from the body, are distanced from and ill-disposed to understanding immaterial things and abstract substances in the next life; this is because of their habit toward sensible and material things, which are infinitely distant from non-sensible and immaterial substances. ### CONCERNING THE RETURN
<note>original: "DE ALMAHAD" — A Latinization of the Arabic term *Al-Ma'ad*, referring to the afterlife or "the place of return."</note>

from the knowledge of those things that are withdrawn from matter and sense, the intellective power is dormant <note>original: "sopita" — literally 'put to sleep' or numbed.</note>, for the reason that it has not moved into the actual state of understanding universal concepts and substances separate from matter. Conversely, the sensitive powers <note>The faculties used to process physical sensations like sight, touch, and desire.</note> thrive from frequent actions concerning sensible things <term>sensible things: objects or experiences that can be perceived by the five physical senses</term>. Consequently, because the souls of these people in this life held their intellective power in a dormant state and were distanced from God himself and the knowledge of Him, so too after death in the other life do they possess an intellective power ill-disposed toward the knowledge of divine things. This is due to their habit of focusing on worldly matters, which keeps them distanced from divine knowledge. And just as the souls of these men in this life were occupied, immersed, and habituated only toward sensible things—because only the sensitive powers were frequently active—so too after death these souls will be distanced from the divine essence and from the knowledge of it. They will remain, according to their sensitive powers, immersed in worldly things and sensible objects.

And because it was stated above that the external sensitive power is entirely organic <note>That is, dependent on physical organs like the eyes or ears.</note>, its operation cannot occur without a physical organ. However, the **internal sensitive power**—namely the **imaginative**, the **cogitative**, the **desiring**, and the **memorative**—is not entirely corporeal, because sometimes their operations can occur without a physical organ, as was explained previously. Therefore, souls that were habituated toward worldly, sensible things will, after their separation from the body, remain occupied and immersed in those sensible things. This does not happen through the *external* sensitive powers (since those do not remain in the soul once the body is destroyed), but through the *internal* sensitive powers, which do remain in the soul after death. These powers are those that apprehend and know sensible things only in their particular forms <note>For example, remembering a specific red apple rather than understanding the abstract concept of "redness" or "fruit."</note>, and not as universals.

Therefore, the cogitative and desiring power of these souls—which is separated from matter at the death of the body just as the intellective power is—does not apprehend separate intelligible intentions (that is, universal concepts or the nature of substances abstracted from matter). Instead, it apprehends nothing except the intentions of the natural, sensible things of this world. From this it is clear that the souls of those who in this world were immersed and occupied only with sensible things will, after separation from the body, remain with such a habit. They will neither apprehend nor know God, nor abstract substances, since their intellective power is ill-disposed for this and distanced from the knowledge of divine things, just as they were previously in this life.

And the aforementioned souls will know only these lower, sensible things because of the habit acquired through their preoccupation with such things, mediated by the **imaginative**, **cogitative**, and **desiring** powers. These powers especially thrive in these souls both before their separation from the body and after their separation from it. # ON THE RETURN
<note>original: "DE ALMAHAD" — This refers to Avicenna’s work on the afterlife or "The Return" (Al-Ma'ad in Arabic).</note>

...things in this lower world. And that from the spiritual operations of these spirits, both good and evil, natural operations <note>physical effects or phenomena in the material world</note> occur. And they said that substances separated from matter—such as angels, demons, and souls—have greater power to move from <term>potential to act: the transition from having the capacity to do something to actually doing it</term>, or to move into an action that is fitting and conforms to their quality and "habit" <note>original: "habitui" — here meaning a settled disposition or character acquired through repeated action</note>, whether they be evil or good. 

For if their habits were evil, they more quickly perform evil. And if their habits were good, they more quickly perform actual good; they have greater power to perform that which conforms to their habit and their will than if such souls were still in a body. From this it is clear how humans are troubled by demons and by the aforementioned "domestic spirits," because according to this opinion, the souls of the ignorant and of the wicked wise—who in this world were occupied only with worldly sensory things—are retained in this lower world (as has been said) if they were good or evil, and they continue to be attached to humans. 

Those souls that were habituated to evil habits perform evil, and those habituated to good habits perform good. For it was said that from spiritual operations (that is, from spiritual powers that are not bodily) there come natural, sensible operations. For such separated souls are spiritual powers, and since they have nothing hindering them and they know all causes and all particular motions—and consequently future effects—they have greater power and more easily move into the act of operating than a power existing within a body. 

Therefore, it is not surprising if people in this world see natural, sensible effects caused by these spirits and demons, which a power inside a body could not produce. And for this reason, we see in our experience noises, and the movement of bodies from place to place, and other changes occurring (other than "substantial changes") caused by the aforementioned spirits and demons. I specifically said "except for substantial changes" <term>substantial change: a change that alters the very essence or species of a thing, such as turning a lead bar into gold or a human into a wolf</term> because theologians and philosophers hold that although various local and accidental changes are made by these spirits, a substantial change—for example, a transmutation from species to species or from one individual to another individual of that species—cannot be performed by demons or spirits. 

It is also clear how spirits and demons trouble the bodies of men by inducing evil "accidents" <note>physical symptoms or conditions that are not part of the person's essential nature</note> in them and by entering their bodies. This explains why such people, troubled by spirits, speak in various languages and various idioms, and predict the future, and narrate things they have never seen, and speak in the <note>original: "latino sermone"</note> Latin language concerning sciences which they never learned. According to the aforementioned opinion, all these things are caused by souls separated from the body that were habituated toward sensory things and remained attached to humans and their souls, as was said above. For if any of the aforementioned souls separated from the body were habituated to a certain idiom and were closely united with a person, then that person speaks in that idiom as well as their own idiom, and thus speaks in various languages. If, however, the aforementioned soul was...

-># AVICENNA<-

...habituated in the Latin language, or in some specific conclusion of a science, and that soul becomes united with another person who is ignorant, then that ignorant man speaks Latin and declares scientific conclusions which he never learned. And because such separated souls <note>original: "anime separate" — souls that have left the body after death but remain in the terrestrial sphere</note>, according to this opinion, have knowledge of things past and future (as has been stated), it is therefore no wonder if men vexed by spirits—who according to this aforementioned opinion are souls separated from the body and retained in this world—predict the future. This is because these souls, once separated from the body, understand causes and specific movements, and consequently their future effects. Therefore, such separated souls, when united with the souls of men troubled by spirits, imprint in them a knowledge of future things. Because of this union, many men predict the future; others do not predict or know anything because they do not have a union with a separated soul that might imprint such knowledge of the future.

From these points, it is also clear how, according to Avicenna in the first <term>fen: a term derived from Arabic meaning a specific division or section of a book</term> of his third book, <term>melancolia: melancholy, understood here not just as sadness but as a physical brain disorder causing delusions</term> can be caused by a demon. Avicenna there calls the demon <term>gen: a Latinization of the Arabic 'Jinn'</term>, because from the persistent connection of a separated soul with a living body, various strange imaginings and different types of knowledge are imprinted by that separated soul. Thus, such a person becomes a patient suffering from melancholy and the symptoms of the aforementioned melancholy; yet, along with this, such a person sometimes predicts the future and recounts the past.

And just as according to Avicenna someone may suffer the sickness of melancholy due to a demon, and be vexed by a demon and a spirit, so too according to certain Arabic authors who wrote on philosophy and medicine, it is possible for someone to be <term>epileticus: an epileptic</term> because of a demon. They argue that from the imprinting of "phantasms" <note>mental images or sensory impressions</note> by the aforementioned demon united with a living body, the brain is disrupted and obstructed. Thus, <term>epilentia: epilepsy</term> is caused in paroxysms <note>sudden attacks or fits</note>, occurring to a greater or lesser degree depending on how the passions are imprinted upon the epileptic person by the demon or separated soul.

Through this aforementioned opinion, it becomes clear how men are vexed by demons. It also suggests that the "domestic spirits" commonly called <term>mazaroli: traditional nature spirits or goblins in Venetian folklore</term> in Venice are actually souls separated from the body—not evilly disposed, but retained in this world, as was said above. It further suggests that devils and demons are malicious spirits whom men affirm, through experience, to be the cause of many wonderful operations. 

And although it may be so according to this opinion, nevertheless, according to Christian theologians and according to the truth: the spirits (both good and not good) from whom the aforementioned operations proceed are NOT souls separated from the body wandering in this lower world, as has been said and as many heretics, both Christian and non-Christian, hold in these modern times. For it is written: *The souls of the just are in the hand of God* <note>original: "Iustorum anime in manu Dei sunt" — a quote from the Book of Wisdom 3:1</note>, and the souls of the wicked are detained in hell or purgatory. Instead, such spirits are spiritual, immaterial substances, distinct and different from any intellectual human soul. However, a doubt remains as to how magicians are able to compel these spirits...

-># CONCERNING THE RETURN TO THE AFTERLIFE <note>original: "DE ALMAHAD," from the Arabic *al-ma'ād*, referring to the resurrection or the soul's return to the spiritual world</note><-

*Spirits <note>original: "Edemones," a Latinization of the Greek 'daimones,' referring here to spiritual beings or intelligences</note>, which are intellectual substances more noble than the intellective soul of man. <margin>A</margin> *not because of the servant himself, but because of the authority, power, and name of the King in whose name the servant commands the aforementioned leaders, and not by his own power (since those leaders would not be moved or compelled by the power of that servant on his own). > *At the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. <note>original: "In nomine Iesu omne genu flectatur terrestrium, coelestium, et infernorum," a quote from Philippians 2:10</note>*
*And just as the princes of a city are not compelled by a servant commanding in the King's name and by the King's power unless they know that the servant holds such power from the King, in the same way, spirits are not moved or compelled by just any man commanding them in the name or power of God. They are only compelled and moved by those practitioners of magic whom they know to have received such power of commanding from the Glorious God. Thus, just as the aforementioned princes of the cities do not obey the servant for his own sake, but obey the King himself directly and the servant incidentally <term>per accidens: a philosophical term meaning a secondary or non-essential relationship</term>, so too spirits do not obey or feel compelled by magicians for their own sake, but are compelled by divine power directly, and are compelled incidentally by the practitioners of magic.*

This is because the body and corporeal matter are hindered in all their movements due to the resistance of other bodies which they encounter and which resist them. # AVICENNA

[The soul] needs phantasms <note>original: "phantasmatibus," referring to mental images or sensory impressions stored in the mind</note>, and various senses, and various movements for its knowledge. But when the soul has departed from matter, nothing occurs to it, meets it, or hinders it in its operations. And therefore they are more active: and they have a greater power for performing various operations [different] from our sensory ones than when they were joined with the body. Wherefore, since nothing hinders its operations, and nothing hinders even its knowledge—since all things are present to them—therefore such souls always remain along one path and according to one disposition. Therefore, if such souls were evil, they will always do evil; if truly good, they will do good. The text is clear from what was said before.

<margin>T</margin>
**AND CERTAIN WISE MEN** indeed agree and affirm. The reason for this is that souls perfected in the sciences—because of the habit <note>original: "habitu," a philosophical term for an acquired disposition or stable quality of the mind</note> acquired in this world—are distanced from this lower world, occupied with the contemplation of divine things. Therefore, by such a habit, and because they are also harmless after separation from the body, they enjoy divine knowledge and are distanced from the knowledge of these lower things.

<margin>Δ A</margin>
**AND CERTAIN** wise men have said—here he presents another opinion—that the aforementioned perfect and harmless souls, once separated from the body, will have knowledge of these lower things. This is because in the substance of the aforementioned souls, and of other souls that are not perfect nor harmless, there remains the cogitative power and the imaginative power along with the intellective power. Wherefore, since such souls cannot be entirely stripped of sensory bodily qualities or impressions—especially because the power of memory also remains in them—therefore such souls, separated from the body, through the medium of the cogitative and memory powers that remained in the substance of the soul, know and imagine these lower things. For they imagine the dead person in whom they were previously found before death, and they imagine that person and their body, which they used to inform <note>original: "informabant," meaning the soul gave life, structure, and "form" to the physical matter</note> according to the form and figure it previously had. And then after death, if they are not blessed, they imagine pains: which they used to imagine along the path of the torment of sensory punishment in this life. And they imagine not only these sensory punishments and torments which they felt in this life and knew by experience; rather, they even imagine and know the true punishment and true torment appropriate for them according to their demerits. In summary, souls separated from the body imagine good or evil, pains and delights, according to how they were habituated in this life. For if the souls separated from the body were blessed, then they imagine sensory and non-sensory delights which they used to imagine while in the body. And they also imagine and know true happiness, which they could not perfectly know in this life. If, however, the souls were evil, vicious, and condemned to punishment, then they imagine according to the contrary: for they imagine sensory pains...

REGARDING the title of this book, it should be known that it is called the

book of Rabbi Moses <note>original: "Rabi Moyses," referring to the Jewish philosopher Maimonides</note>, in which the sayings of Galen are collected, is called the Book of Aphorisms. Similarly, this book of Avicenna, in which he makes brief discourses or
brief chapters about the soul, and about its dispositions and operations, can
deservedly be called the Book of Aphorisms, because the chapters are for the
most part separated in their judgment, and express in a brief discourse the
dispositions of the soul and its operations.

<meta>This page continues the "Explanations of the Aphorisms of Avicenna on the Soul" by Andrea of Belluno. # APHORISMS ON THE SOUL

B **potency.** <note>original: "potentia"; referring to the soul's capacity or potential to know</note> And in the soul of an infant or a child, there are inherent **first principles** <note>fundamental truths that do not require proof, such as "the whole is greater than the part"</note> which come to them without the aid of the senses. And the cause of their arrival is a preparation or disposition. And when the soul has been separated <note>this likely refers to the soul's independent operation from the body or its state after death</note>, and has had the preparation or disposition for grasping <term>intelligibles</term> <note>original: "intelligibilia"; objects that can only be understood by the mind, not seen by the eyes</note>, then the arrival of science or knowledge is possible for it without the need for the bodily powers which it left behind or dismissed; rather, knowledge and cognition come to it without intention, and in a way [ <margin>Another reading: that it does not foreknow them, nor does it desire knowledge.</margin> that it is not known how or from where it arrives, ] just as is the disposition in the arrival of first principles in children. And the senses indeed are the ways from which the human soul acquires sciences.

A **KNOWLEDGE** indeed does not belong [to the sense], etc. Note that where "knowledge" is used, in the Arabic it is *al-idrak* <note>original: "aladarech"</note>. And *al-idrak* is the same as apprehension or knowledge. And such apprehension or knowledge primarily belongs to the soul, and not to the instruments of the senses: for we do not say the eye apprehends or knows, except metaphorically and in a broad sense, insofar as the eye and the senses themselves—which are <term>acted upon</term> <note>original: "patiuntur"; literally "suffer," meaning they receive an external impression</note> by sensed things from outside—produce their <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; the mental images or "forms" of objects</note>, and offer or present them to the soul, and are the medium by which the soul knows. For the soul, as Aristotle <note>original: "Ar."</note> said, is the principle of sensing and understanding: therefore, the soul is that which senses and understands. The senses, however, are the instruments and the medium by which the soul understands and senses. Therefore, the aforementioned apprehension or knowledge primarily belongs to the soul. And *al-idrak*—that is, apprehension or knowledge—is defined by Avicenna in his philosophy thus in these Arabic words:

> *That is, al-idrak—that is, apprehension or knowledge—is the arrival of the form or species of the thing apprehended to the one apprehending or knowing, who perceives them by means of that through which he himself apprehends; that is, apprehension or knowledge is the arrival of the form or species of the thing apprehended to the one apprehending, who indeed perceives them—namely, the species and forms—which come to him by means of etc.—that is, by means of the senses. For the senses are that by which the soul apprehends and knows something. And Avicenna said in the "Compendium on the Soul," chapter 2, that the bodies of animals share in this: that they sense and apprehend or know by a certain kind of sensitive apprehension; then they differ, because some of them with this apprehend by an intellectual apprehension.*

From which words it appears that apprehension or knowledge is common to sensory apprehension and to intellectual apprehension, but knowledge properly so called is intellectual knowledge. Knowledge, therefore, whether it be intellectual or sensory, does not belong to anything but the soul. To the sense, however—that is, to the organ of sense—it does not belong, and is not attributed, except as a sensation from the thing sensed, which sensation is nothing but the <term>passive reception</term> <note>original: "passio"; the state of being acted upon by an external object</note> of the sensitive instrument or organ—

<summary>This page discusses the mechanics of how the soul acquires knowledge, distinguishing between innate "first principles" and sensory information. It defines the Arabic term 'al-idrak' (apprehension) as a process where the soul, not the physical organ, is the true agent of knowing.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary by Andrea of Belluno on Avicenna’s "Aphorisms on the Soul." The previous page established that "knowledge" (apprehension) belongs primarily to the soul rather than the physical sense organs. This page explores why we sometimes fail to notice sensations when distracted and how "first principles"—basic truths like "the whole is greater than the part"—are inherent in the human mind from infancy without needing to be learned from experience.</meta>

->OF AVICENNA<-

...of the instrument. The proof of this is: because the eye and the organ of touch are sometimes affected by a sensed thing, yet because the soul is then occupied with another matter, the soul does not receive the <term>form</term> <note>original: "speciem"; in medieval philosophy, a 'species' or 'form' is the mental image or representation of an object</note> of the thing being sensed. Therefore, in such a case, there is something making an impression on the sense organ, yet it is not "sensed" or known by the soul. This is because the form of that which affects the external sense is not imprinted upon an occupied soul, as will be explained below in Chapter 2. The rest of the text is clear.

<margin>A</margin> <margin>B</margin> **AND indeed within the soul of an infant or a child there are first principles.** 
Note that by the "soul of an infant or a child," the commentators in this passage understand the human soul which does not yet possess knowledge or science acquired through art or experience. Because children exist in this state, he used the soul of a child as an example—one who knows naturally that "the whole is greater than its part," and so on for other things that are known through themselves and by nature. These are called <term>first principles</term> <note>fundamental self-evident truths that form the basis of all logical reasoning</note> because they are the first things that the intellect grasps. <margin>A</margin> **AND IT UNDERSTANDS their intelligible forms,** that is, it will understand the <term>intentional forms</term> <note>original: "species intentionales"; the mental meaning or significance of a sensation, such as a sheep perceiving "danger" when seeing a wolf</note> of sensible things, such as the concept of enmity and similar things. **WITHOUT needing the medium of those sensed forms,** that is, without needing the intermediary of the forms of those intelligible things, which are indeed sensed.

<margin>C</margin> **ON THE CONTRARY, knowledge comes to them without intention and without prior knowledge.** 
Note that when science or knowledge is obtained about something through "acquisition," then before it is known, the soul desires and intends to know it, and thus has a confused prior knowledge of it. However, knowledge that is not acquired through the discourse and help of the senses, but is "infused" by God and by the Intelligences <note>in Avicenna's philosophy, "Intelligences" are celestial beings that help impart knowledge to the human mind</note>—such as the knowledge of souls separated from the body—comes to the soul without intention and without desire. This is because such knowledge arrives suddenly; it is the knowledge of things that the soul did not consciously intend to learn. This is similar to the arrival of first principles in children, in whom the knowledge of principles arrives without logical discourse and without them intending to have such knowledge. Children do not know how such knowledge comes to them; it comes to them by nature, not through the logical process and help of the senses, as will be explained below in Chapter 5. The remaining subsequent aphorisms up to the sixth aphorism do not seem to require explanation, therefore, etc.

---

### Second Aphorism

**When a sensed object is not apprehended or is not known by the soul, then the cause of that is because the soul is distracted from it and occupied with the thinking faculty, or out of inattention. And sometimes a sensed form arrives in the <term>common sense</term> <note>original: "sensu communi"; the internal faculty that collects and organizes data from all five external senses</note> but its arrival at the intellective soul itself is not possible. Or the cause is that the soul occupies or exercises the common sense regarding those things toward which it is inclined, so that sensed things do not make an impression...**

### Third Aphorism.

As long as the soul puts on <note>original: "induit"; uses the metaphor of wearing clothes</note> this matter, it does not know the stripping <note>original: "denudationem"; the state of the soul when separated from the physical body</note> of its essence, nor its quality or condition—which belongs to it while it is stripped of matter—nor the state of its arrangements during that stripping. This is because the soul cannot return or turn itself <margin>Another reading: that is, by knowing the property of its essence and...</margin> [ to the property of its essence, and ] to its stripping from that which it has put on. Rather, there exists within it an intermediary by which it is hindered from its "what-ness" <term>quiddity</term> <note>from the Latin "quidditas," meaning the essence or "what" a thing is</note> and from the true knowledge [ of its essence ] and from the consideration of any of its arrangements. <margin>Another reading: by itself.</margin> But when it has been stripped of matter, and this impediment has been removed from it, then it knows its own essence and its arrangements, and the qualities or conditions proper to itself. And it then perceives or knows things without a bodily instrument; it is then excused from the instrument, or rather, it no longer needs it. However, that which the soul imagines now is not its "what-ness" or its essence; it now imagines nothing except the sensed body. And it thinks now <margin>Now: that is, while it is united to the body</margin> that there is no being for anything except for the sensed body itself—which is entirely false.

### Fourth Aphorism.

Bodily powers prevent the soul from the sole, or unique, or pure consideration of its essence, and from its own proper knowledge. This is because it knows "imaginable" things <note>mental images derived from the senses</note> rather than "intelligible" things <note>pure concepts understood by the intellect without physical images</note> because it is drawn toward those sensed, imaginable things due to their dominance over the soul itself. This happens because the soul is not accustomed to the pure intellects or to intelligible things. It knows nothing but the senses, and it is inclined toward them; it even estimates that intelligible things have no existence, and it holds nothing but false opinions.

### Fifth Aphorism.

First principles <note>fundamental truths that require no proof, such as "the whole is greater than the part"</note> come to the human intellect without being acquired <note>learned through effort or study</note>, and the intellect does not perceive from where they come into it, or how they arrive within it.

### Sixth Aphorism.

Whenever there occurs in matter a <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexio"; the specific balance or mixture of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a body</note> suitable for a soul, then a soul occurs or is made without a doubt. Just as when the preparation of matter occurs for receiving a fiery form, or...

AVICENNA'S

...[whether it be] airy, or watery, or earthy: then there happens or is created in it that form, from a separate principle—namely, [a principle separated] from matter. <note>original: "a principio separato. s. a materia"; refers to the idea that the source of life and form is immaterial and exists apart from physical substance.</note> Wherefore the teaching of the *Altenasach* <note>original: "Altenasach"; a Latinization of the Arabic *al-tanāsukh*, referring to the doctrine of the transmigration of souls or reincarnation.</note> is false for this reason.

->To the Sixth Aphorism.<-

<margin>D</margin>
**THEN** there is created in it that form from a separate principle, wherefore the teaching of the *Altenasach* etc. For the explanation of these words, it must be known that according to the opinion of Avicenna and Plato, there resides within every species of thing capable of being generated its own proper Intelligence <note>In medieval philosophy, "Intelligences" were celestial beings or minds that governed the natural world.</note>, which rules and governs that species. This Intelligence induces in matter a complexion <term>complexionem</term> <note>The "complexion" is the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, wet, and dry—that makes a body suitable for a specific type of life.</note>, as well as the outlines and the figure, according to the suitability of this or that form which must be introduced into the matter. Consequently, the Intelligence introduces or "infuses" the specific form <term>forma specifica</term> into that matter, which has been proportioned to the complexion previously induced in said matter. Such an Intelligence governing a species is called by Avicenna the "father of the species" or the "governor of the species."

The reason why Avicenna is moved to posit that in every species there is a proper Intelligence—which rules and governs its assigned species by preparing the matter for the form and then introducing the specific form into it—is because every natural power <term>uirtus naturalis</term> is an "accident" <note>A quality that exists only within a subject, rather than having its own independent existence.</note> lacking its own knowledge. Therefore, a natural power cannot, by itself, outline and shape a body according to the requirements of the form to be introduced. Because of this, it is commonly said by philosophers that nature is directed by an Intelligence that does not err. 

It is therefore necessary to posit in every species of thing that can be generated its own Intelligence, which must preserve and govern its own species by preparing the matter, inducing the outlines and the figure of the body into the matter, and afterward inducing the specific form into it, as has been said. And just as one species is nobler than another, so too is an Intelligence assigned to a nobler species nobler than an Intelligence assigned to a less noble species. All such Intelligences are inferior to the Intelligence moving or assisting the sphere of the moon; and whatever these aforementioned inferior Intelligences do, they do only by the help and influence <term>influxu</term> of the Intelligence assisting the sphere of the moon. Furthermore, that Intelligence itself only acts through the influence and help of God and the Intelligences superior to it. 

Just as the forms of mixed things and the souls of brutes <note>irrational animals</note> come from the outside according to Avicenna (as is clear in Avicenna’s *Compendium on the Soul*, chapter 3), and as souls, according to him, are infused anew into matter that has been prepared and "complexioned" according to the requirements of this or that soul, so too is the intellectual soul <term>anima intellectiua</term> introduced and created anew in matter prepared for the human form. Thus, according to Avicenna, human souls did not exist from eternity, nor do they migrate from body to body, as was the opinion of those called the sect of the *Altenasach*—that is, the sect who believe in the permutation <note>transmigration</note> of souls from one body to another body, just as well...

**T**he human soul has it implanted by nature that it should recognize or know beings; and by nature it knows some of them, wherefore they are present in it always in act <term>in actu</term> <note>To know something "in act" means to have the knowledge actively present and functioning in the mind at this moment, as opposed to "in potential," which is knowledge one possesses but is not currently thinking about.</note> [or because it knows them always in act for the reason that it recognizes them through themselves]; and it knows some of them in potential <term>in potentia</term> through this: that it knows them by acquisition.
