And this is because that which has not yet arrived to it requires a process to arrive. And it seems that that operation or governance of the soul itself—and that which is attributed to the practical part, or the operative part and the bodily powers—is its operation according to nature. But its operation which is attributed to the speculative <note>The "speculative" or theoretical part of the soul is concerned with pure knowledge and contemplation, rather than action.</note> part is its operation in potential. And indeed its operation which is attributed to the bodily powers, although it is present in it according to nature, nevertheless its aforementioned operation which exists within it according to the path of perfection and completion exists through acquisition.

->On the Seventh Aphorism.<-

**T**HE human soul has it implanted by nature, etc. That is, the human soul has by its own nature an aptitude for knowing beings, but the soul itself knows certain beings by its own nature. For it knows by its nature the first principles <note>First principles are fundamental truths that do not need to be proven, such as "the whole is greater than the part."</note>, and it knows them always in act and through themselves. However, it knows certain other things not by its nature, nor always in act, but it knows them in potential and through acquisition <note>Acquisition refers to the process of learning through experience, study, or logic.</note>; therefore it does not know them always in act, because if it knows through acquisition, then before that acquisition it did not know such things. For example, the soul by its nature and in act knows the first principles; however, that it *knows that it knows* these kinds of principles is something it does not know always in act and by nature, but through acquisition and in potential. For before the acquisition of logic and philosophy, it does not know what the first principles are, nor does it know that it naturally knows the first principles. But after the acquisition of the science of logic, philosophy, and metaphysics, it then recognizes the first principles and knows that it knows them through itself and by nature. Before the acquisition of the aforementioned sciences, the soul did not know that it knew or had known these kinds of first principles through itself and by its own nature. And through this, the meaning of the text is clear, which says: AND BY NATURE it knows some of them because they are present in it (that is, in the soul) always in act; just like the knowledge of them through themselves (that is, like the knowledge of those things which the soul knows through itself and by its own nature).

For a human, even if they are foolish and lack all education, nevertheless takes food when necessary and is moved to seek it when they do not have it, just as the other animals do, which are moved by nature. 

Therefore, the operations of the soul regarding the governance of the body—which are practical operations attributed to the bodily powers—are operations of the soul according to nature, which are present in it always in act when necessary. However, the operations of the soul attributed to the speculative part—such as the soul's contemplations and the discourse of reason regarding the speculative sciences—are operations of the soul in potential. For operations of this kind are not present in the soul by nature and in act, but are present in it in potential and come to the soul through acquisition. For by learning in philosophy and in other sciences, the soul acquires knowledge of things which it did not know before, and it acquires the terms or names of things, from which the soul afterwards reasons and performs speculative operations. It is clear, therefore, how speculative operations are present in the soul in potential, and practical operations are present in the soul according to nature. ### Aphorism Eight.

<margin>F</margin> **M**an, in his life, is occupied in the body, or is bound to the body and in those things which follow from it; for this reason he does not verify, or does not affirm anything to exist, except that which he sees with "eye-witness faith" <note>original: "oculata fide," a common expression for believing only what one sees with their own eyes.</note> and which he perceives with his senses. And he believes that whatever is not perceived by them has no essence, nor existence, because of the powerful habit of his soul with its senses. He also believes that the soul itself is ignorant and cannot know those things which are beyond those sensory objects. He believes the soul itself to be immersed in the body and in its powers. All of this arises because the soul does not know by itself—or rather, it does not know its own essence; indeed, the soul is turned away, or distanced, from its own essence and from the knowledge of its essence. But whenever the soul shall have been separated <note>This refers to the separation of the soul from the body, usually at death.</note> and knows through itself, then it apprehends or knows that which seemed false to it in this life, as if it had no essence. Then it apprehends or knows beings through itself and not through a bodily instrument. For this reason, it will know that the instruments <note>The "instruments" refer to the physical sense organs (eyes, ears, etc.).</note> were actually hindering it from its own proper operation.

❧ ...from the composition, or the gathering together of matter with form; for this reason, three things exist there: namely, matter, form, and the gathering—or union—of matter with form. From these points, it is clear that according to Avicenna <note>original: "Auicennam." Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose philosophical works deeply influenced medieval European thought.</note> the heavens contain matter of the same nature as the matter of these lower worlds. This is because he stated that the heaven is composed of matter whose nature is "privation." <note>term: <term>privation</term> (original: "priuatio"). In Aristotelian philosophy, this is the "absence" or "lack" of a form that a piece of matter is naturally capable of having. It is the potential for change.</note> It is clear, however, that the nature of the matter in these lower worlds is privation, which is its own proper condition; therefore, etc.

<margin>H</margin>
...SO THAT ANOTHER specific form may be brought near or joined to it. From these words, it is clear that according to Avicenna, there are two forms within matter. One is the form of the "genus" <note>In logic and biology, a "genus" is a general category, while a "species" is a specific type within that category.</note> which is inseparable from it—for example, the form of "corporeity" <note>term: <term>corporeity</term> (original: "corporeitatis"). The quality of having a physical body or taking up space, regardless of what kind of thing it is.</note>—and the other is the "specific form," which is added on top of the form of corporeity. This is called the "generic form" because it is a common form alongside which various successive specific forms can exist. And just as a genus is narrowed down by this or that "difference," so too is the bodily form narrowed down by this or that specific form. The text is clear. Note that by holding the heaven to be composed of matter whose nature is privation, it follows that the matter in the heaven is of the same nature as the matter of these lower worlds, just as Egidius Romanus <note>Giles of Rome (c. 1243–1316), a prominent medieval theologian and student of Thomas Aquinas.</note> said. However, it does not follow that the heaven is "corruptible" <note>meaning: subject to decay or passing out of existence.</note> because the heavens do not contain the "contrary qualities" of the elements found in these lower regions—which contrary qualities are the causes of decay. Some, however, such as the Arabs called the Sufis <note>original: "Suffi." The author refers to Islamic mystics, noting their belief that knowledge comes through divine inspiration rather than study.</note>—whose knowledge comes through "infusion" from the celestial intelligences rather than the acquisition of doctrine—stated that the heaven is composed of matter and form...

❧ ...from the subtlest parts of the elements in such a proportion that the heaven is either not corruptible, or is only corruptible with great difficulty. For just as gold, because of a certain composition and mixture of elements, is difficult to destroy, so the same—and much more—may be said of the heaven.

This is a famous Avicennian concept describing God as the only Being whose essence is to exist; He cannot *not* exist.</note> For this is His most proper and inseparable characteristic.

<meta>This page continues the examination of Avicenna's philosophy, shifting from the physical composition of the heavens discussed on page 103 to the limits of human epistemology—how we understand the "essence" or true nature of things versus their external properties.</meta>

# AVICENNA

[Avicenna] knows that properties and accidents <note>term: <term>accidents</term> (original: "accidentia"). In medieval philosophy, these are qualities that a thing has (like color or size) which are not essential to what it is. A chair might be blue, but "blueness" is an accident, not the essence of "chairness."</note> exist within things. For we do not know the essence of the highest first being <note>referring to God</note>, nor the essence of intelligence, nor of the soul, nor of heaven, nor of the elements; neither do we even know the essences of accidents. And the illustration of this is that we do not know the essence of substance; <note>term: <term>substance</term> (original: "substantiae"). The fundamental reality that exists by itself, rather than existing as a quality of something else.</note> rather, we only know that it is a thing in which this property resides: namely, that it is a "being not in a subject," <note>original: "ens non in subiecto." This is the classic definition of substance—it doesn't rely on another thing to exist (like a color relies on an object).</note> and this indeed is not its essence. Nor do we know the essence of the body; rather, we know that the body itself is a thing in which this property resides: namely, that it is long, wide, and deep. Nor do we know the essence of an animal; rather, we know a thing in which the property of perceiving—or knowing—and acting resides. 

And because of this, diversity sometimes occurs in the "whatnesses" <note>term: <term>quiddities</term> (original: "quidditatibus"). From the Latin "quid" (what). It refers to the defining nature or "what-it-is-ness" of a thing.</note> of things, because one person sometimes perceives one inseparable thing as different or distinct from what another person perceives. Therefore, he judges according to what that inseparable quality requires, or according to the quality of that inseparable thing. And we affirm nothing except the specific thing; and then we know that it has been made specific to it out of its properties. Then, from this, we know something else specific by means of that through which we knew the first thing. Then we arrive at the knowledge of its essence, as is the case with the soul and with place, and other things besides both of them. We arrive at the knowledge of the essence not through the essence itself; rather, we know it from the proportion that exists in it to other things, or from the accidents that reside in it, or from its inseparable qualities. 

An example of this is in the soul. For we see the body move, then we affirm that matter is present in that motion. And we see a motion different from the motions of the rest of the animals; then we know that a specific mover exists within it, or that a specific condition or quality exists within it,
<margin>Another reading: "in moving things" <note>original: "mobilibus"</note>.</margin>
which is not in the rest [of the movers]. Then we follow from property to property, and from inseparable quality to inseparable quality, and we arrive through them at its essence. 

And similarly, we do not know the essence of the first being <note>God</note>. For we only know that it has "necessary existence." <note>term: <term>necessary existence</term> (original: "necesse esse"). A core concept in Avicenna's thought: God is the only being whose very nature is to exist; He cannot *not* exist.</note> and this is indeed inseparable from it, and not its essence. And regarding Him, by means of this inseparable quality, we know other inseparable qualities, such as the unity of God and the remaining attributes. And His essence indeed, if it is possible to be apprehended, is "being through itself"—that is, that in which "being through itself" resides—and the intention of our discourse (namely, "in which being through itself resides") is pointing toward or signifying something...

<summary>On this page, Avicenna argues that human beings cannot perceive the true "essence" of things directly; instead, we understand the world and the Divine by observing "accidents" and "properties" and reasoning backward toward their nature. He specifically applies this to our understanding of the soul's movement and God's "necessary existence."</summary>

Neither is His essence "being" itself, nor is there any definition among definitions—or rather, the essence of God himself is not found among the definitions or descriptions of God. This is because "being" <note>original: "esse"</note> pertains to those very descriptions, [which is extrinsic to the essence of God himself, namely, He who is the cause of being through Himself.] And indeed, "being" enters into the definition of God himself; it enters either in the same way that <term>genus</term> and <term>difference</term> <note>These are logical tools: "genus" is the general category (like 'animal') and "difference" is the specific trait that sets a thing apart (like 'rational'). Together they create a definition.</note> enter into the definition of simple things, according to what our intellect presupposes or considers about them outside of their essentials (namely, the definitions or descriptions). Therefore, "being" is a part of the definition of God himself, but not a part of His essence—just as we say that genus and difference are parts present in the definitions of simple things, but not in their actual essences. Or perhaps it is because His essence is above being; in that case, "being" is among the inseparable attributes of that essence, and the parts of His simple definition are parts of the definition only, and not of His consistency, or nature, or essence itself. Thus, "being" itself is something presupposed and attributed to Him by—namely—our intellect. And we indeed know of the First Being that He is <term>Necessary Being</term> <note>original: "necesse esse." A central concept in Avicenna's philosophy referring to a being that must exist by its very nature and cannot not exist.</note> through Himself, by primary knowledge without the need for acquisition <note>meaning this is an intuitive truth that does not require a complex logical proof to be understood</note>. And we divide "being" into the necessary and the contingent; then we know that what is necessary through itself must be unique, such that its "species" of being is different from the species of being of any other. And we know the unity of God through that which follows from Him first: and that thing is Necessary Being (or that which is indeed Necessary Being). A definition has parts, but the thing being defined sometimes does not have parts; this occurs when the thing is "simple" <note>in philosophy, 'simple' means not made of parts, like a soul or God, as opposed to 'composite' things like bodies</note>. In such cases, the intellect searches for something to stand in the place of the genus and something to stand in the place of the difference. In a composite thing, [the genus stands in the place of <term>matter</term>, and the difference stands in the place of <term>form</term>.]

...free will, and the movements of the soul itself are also voluntary, just as movements [of the elements] are natural, because these movements of the soul follow intentions and appetites; therefore, the soul wills them and is inclined toward them. Truly, there is a difference between these voluntary movements and natural ones: for voluntary movements are known through the soul's own intentions. A similar arrangement exists in celestial movements, for they are voluntary, although they are not driven by intentions in the same way our own intentions and actions are. Indeed, these actions are called <term>al-ikhtiyariyyah</term> <note>original: "alacthiarie"; a Latinization of the Arabic term for "voluntary" or "chosen" actions.</note>—that is, those which proceed from free will—though in truth this is only fully realized in the First Being [God] alone. THE SOUL is also an agent by necessity, etc. 

For the explanation of these words of Avicenna, <term>Ibn al-Makki</term> <note>original: "Ebenemechi"; a reference to a medieval Arabic physician or commentator.</note>, the foremost physicist among all the Arabs, said that among the <term>Muslims</term> <note>original: "Maumethanos"; the text uses the Latinized "Mahometans."</note> there are three opinions. Some, indeed, say that the actions of man and his soul proceed not from free will, but out of necessity, from the will of God and His operation. Thus, all human actions are attributed to God, who according to their opinion is the principal agent, while man is merely an instrumental agent moved by God. Indeed, an instrumental agent does not move unless it is moved by God, and such an agent does not perform anything of itself, nor does it act freely or contingently, but out of necessity. According to this opinion, man has neither free will nor power in himself, nor does he perform anything by himself; instead, every human action, according to this view, is caused by God, and whatever man does, he does by necessity and not contingently. 

This viewpoint is called the opinion of <term>Al-Ash'ari</term> <note>original: "alhasari"; referring to the Ash'arite school of Islamic theology which emphasizes God's absolute power and predestination.</note>, and it is commonly observed among the people of Damascus and considered the true opinion. Hence, throughout all of Syria, it is commonly held that everything happens by necessity and that all things are "written on a man's forehead" <note>A cultural reference to the concept of a fixed destiny or "Kismet."</note>. And just as the Damascenes in modern times say that God’s attributes are really distinct from His essence, they also hold the aforementioned erroneous opinion, as is evident. 

The second opinion is the opposite of this, saying that whatever man does, he does freely and contingently out of his own pure will, not out of necessity. God does not concur in any human operation as a principal agent (as the first opinion claimed), but man acts as a free, uncoerced principal agent in whatever he does. Because of this, man deserves reward and punishment according to the merits and demerits of the works that were freely performed by the man himself. 

The third opinion was that of **Avicenna** and **Al-Ghazali**, who proposed that God gave man the power and free will to do good and evil. From this, man has the free will to choose virtues and vices, and whatever man performs, he performs from his own free will, without God concurring in the choice man makes or in his operations. Therefore, it is established that if a man performs virtuous works according to the commands of the law, he will receive a reward; and if a man chooses and performs virtuous works, etc., he will receive punishment. However, this opinion of Avicenna differs from the second opinion mentioned above, because although the human soul...

It remains, therefore, to declare how man and the human soul are agents by necessity, from which operations proceed by necessity. To manifest this, it is presupposed that God has known all future things from eternity, and that such knowledge of God is infallible. Indeed, all future things are present to God, and that which is in the future is represented to divine cognition as if it were present. For all things shine in the divine essence as if in a mirror. And the Arab <term>Sufis</term> <note>original: "Suphi"; referring to the mystical branch of Islam whose philosophy often intersected with Avicenna's theories on divine light.</note> say that God knows all things by the radiation and light of His essence; all future things are represented to Him not by being impressed or acting upon the divine essence (as sensible and intelligible things impress their <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; in medieval philosophy, these are the mental "images" or "forms" that represent objects in our minds.</note> and act upon our senses and intellects), but all things are understood and known by the virtue and illumination of divine cognition, to which all things are present and known without any impression and without any hindrance. God, therefore, knows all future things, and His knowledge is certain and infallible, as was stated above. 

<margin>The example of Plato</margin>

In this case, Plato and his soul will steal and be wicked by necessity; because, presupposing that God knew this, it will necessarily be so, just as God knew it. Otherwise, His knowledge would not be certain, as was presupposed. Therefore, Plato’s soul—presupposing the aforementioned divine knowledge—will be wicked by necessity and will perform evil. 

And yet, the aforementioned soul does whatever it does freely and contingently. For Plato’s soul has power and free will; therefore, of itself and out of its own free will, it can steal or not steal, and can perform virtuous works just as well as wicked ones. And the eternal knowledge of God does not take part in any good or bad operation of Plato himself, nor does it force Plato or his soul to choose and want wicked works. Rather, Plato of himself, and his soul out of its own free will, chooses wicked works and wants to steal and do evil. And God indeed knew Plato's will from eternity; He knew that Plato's soul, by its own power and will, would choose wicked works, and because of this, God knew that Plato’s soul will be damned and punished. [The soul] will observe the divine law and will be virtuous, it will be saved and rewarded; and that which does not observe the aforesaid law will be punished, because God gave to the human soul the power and **free will** <note>original: "liberum arbitrium"</note> to observe the precepts of the law. For God does not command anything except that which a human is able to do. Therefore, because God knew that the soul of Plato <note>Scholastic authors often used "Plato" or "Socrates" as generic placeholders for "any person" in logical examples.</note> is able to observe the precepts of the law and yet does not wish to—indeed, it acts against the precepts—for this reason, God from eternity knew that the soul of Plato ought to be damned. This is not because God's knowledge is the cause of the damnation or of the evil works; for, as has been said, evil and vicious operations are caused solely by the soul of Plato and by his own will, and not by the knowledge of God.

An illustration of this is as follows: Suppose a king has a servant whom he commands only to do what is possible, and suppose the aforesaid king has ordained that if that servant observes the commands, he will be rewarded, but if not, he will be punished. Suppose also that the king commands that servant to go outside the city to a distant place to collect money; and so that the servant cannot be excused or refuse the journey assigned to him, the King provides him with a horse and other necessities. However, that wicked servant does not want to go or to observe the king's command. The king himself knows the evil will of his servant; and though the servant is indeed able to ride out of the city to collect the king's money, he nevertheless refuses. Therefore, the king condemns and punishes the servant. 

It is clear that although the king knows the evil will of his servant, the king's knowledge is not the cause of that evil will in the servant, nor does the aforesaid knowledge force the servant to disobey the king's commands. Instead, every evil action proceeds from the will of the servant, not from the knowledge of the king, who commanded the servant to travel and foreknew that the servant would not obey the mandates.

In the same way, it may be said that God, like a king, commanded His law to be observed by men, and God knew those who want to observe the law and those who do not. God’s knowledge is not the cause of one man wishing to observe it and another not wishing to, because every person has free will and the power of observing or not observing the law, as was said above. 

And just as while I see you walking, you walk by necessity, yet the proposition "you are walking" is not <term>absolutely necessary</term> <note>Absolute necessity refers to things that cannot be otherwise by their very nature, like "a circle is round."</note>, but is <term>conditionally necessary</term>—namely, while I see you walking. This is called the <term>necessity of presupposition</term> <note>original: "necessitate præsuppositionis"; a logical term meaning something is necessary only if we assume a certain condition is already met (in this case, the condition of being seen).</note>. That is, presupposing that I see you walking, you must necessarily be walking; and yet my sight is not the cause of your walking. Rather, you walk by your own free will and by your own choice, and in an absolute sense, your walking is <term>contingent</term> <note>Contingent means it could happen or not happen; it is not forced by nature.</note>. 

In the same way, let it be said that if God knew from eternity that the soul of Plato would be vicious, such a soul will be vicious by necessity. I say this is not by *absolute* necessity, but by the *necessity of presupposition*—that is, presupposing that God has known the soul to be vicious. This is because God’s knowledge of future things is certain, just as it is of present things, because all future things are present to the divine cognition. ...certain, divine knowledge is far more certain and infallible. And just as when I see you walking, my sight does not absolutely force you to walk, nor is it the cause of your walking, similarly, if God has known from eternity that the soul of Plato <note>The name Plato is used here as a logical placeholder for "any individual."</note> will be vicious, God’s knowledge does not force the soul of Plato, nor is it the cause of the soul of Plato acting viciously; rather, the soul of Plato acts viciously by its own **free will** <note>original: "libera uoluntate"</note> and of itself, and contingently as was said above. It appears, therefore, how the soul of Plato, in relation to God's foreknowledge from eternity, will be vicious by necessity and will be an agent by necessity, and yet in itself and absolutely it is a free agent. Thus, the soul of Plato is an agent by necessity in its form or in a free disposition—that is, one possessing free will—and just as this is said of the soul of Plato, so it may be said of any human soul. It appears then that the human soul, as Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian philosopher and physician.</note> said, is an agent by necessity in its form or in a free disposition possessing free will; and conversely, the human soul is an agent by free will in a necessary form or one including necessity. This is because the soul, as stated above, is from one perspective an agent by free will and not coerced, and from another perspective, it is an agent by necessity. From the aforementioned points, it appears how, according to Avicenna and Al-Ghazali <note>original: "Algazel"; an 11th-century Persian theologian and philosopher.</note>, the operations of the soul are necessary and how they are voluntary, and how the opinion of Avicenna conforms to the Christian opinion concerning this matter. And although the first opinion states that all things happen by necessity, nevertheless the opinion of the Arab philosophers such as Avicenna and Al-Ghazali—as is clear from what is written above and as my teacher Raysebemechi <note>Likely referring to a Latinized version of a contemporary Arabic scholar or teacher, possibly Abu’l-Khayr ibn al-Khammār or a similar figure.</note> related to me—is in conformity with the Christian opinion.

<margin>L</margin>
**AND THE MOVEMENTS** of the soul itself are also voluntary; that is, just as the movements of the elements <note>The four elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> are natural, so the movements of the soul itself are voluntary and proceed from the free will of the soul. For it is clear according to Avicenna that every movement is either natural or voluntary. Just as the movement of the elements is natural, proceeding from a nature that inclines the elements toward only one end—namely, either upward or downward—so voluntary movement proceeds from the soul by its free will, which moves toward various movements and those contrary to the directions in which the nature of the elements moves. And the difference between natural and voluntary movements is this: voluntary movements are foreknown and intended by the soul before they happen, whereas natural movements are not foreknown by nature, nor are they intended with cognitive intention.

However, the voluntary movements in the celestial bodies are not for the sake of intentions such as our own intentions; for the souls of the celestial bodies cannot choose and intend indifferently between good and evil as our souls do. *...unchangeable toward the good.*

Indeed, the actions of *al-ikhtiyār* <note>original: "Alachiarie"; a Latinization of the Arabic term *al-ikhtiyār*, meaning "choice" or "free will."</note>, that is, those which proceed from free will, are not truly realized in their full sense except in the first being [God] alone. ### Aphorism thirteen.

<margin>Avicenna said that the souls of the celestial bodies are voluntary agents, yet they are not agents acting from free choice. The human soul, however, is an agent acting from choice.</margin>
The soul moves this matter [the human body] just as the souls of the heavens move their own bodies. And just as those souls of the heavens do not move so that something beneath them may come to be, similarly these earthly souls do not move so that a **complexion** <term>Complexion: in medieval medicine, the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a person's physical and mental temperament.</term> or anything other than the complexion resulting from the body's dispositions might arise; rather, they move so that they themselves may exist according to the most noble or worthy state of being possible for them. Therefore, these things—namely, the complexion and the disposition of the body—are consequences, or are ordered toward that which the soul itself seeks, intends, or desires. And because of this, it is said that the soul itself is the intended **end** <note>original: "finis"; here meaning the final cause or purpose.</note>, and the soul moves for its own sake, because it exists for itself and not for the sake of anything else. And its individual end, or that which is proper to it, is that it should exist according to the most noble state of being possible for it.

### Aphorism fourteen.

When the soul perceives or knows something, it then intends and seeks perfection—not for the sake of grasping the essence of the thing perceived, but rather that grasping is a consequence of its quest for perfection.

Thus, the complexion, the composition of the limbs, the forms, the figures, and the dispositions do not arise from the vegetative soul except by its arrival in the body. And these things indeed arrive in the body after motion; therefore, it is not established that these things are final causes, but rather they are among the consequences or things ordered toward an end. # AVICENNA

<margin>
That is, the complexion and composition.
</margin>
...is verified to be in the soul, it is to seek the perfection to which these things are consequent or ordered.

### Aphorism 15.

<margin>Note</margin>
**AND THESE** indeed arrive in the body after movement. Note that this text is explained in three ways regarding the phrase **AFTER** movement. First, after the movement of the intellectual soul. For by presupposing that every intellectual soul has existed from eternity, as Plato holds, then according to this opinion, the soul—before it is united to the body—moves the elements toward a mutual mixture, and toward the generation of a **complexion** <term>complexion: in medieval science, the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a person's physical state</term>, a composition, and a physical form. Therefore, after such movement, the complexion and composition arrive in the body, etc. Finally, the soul is united to the body and resides within it, just as a builder of a house moves the workers to the stones and wood and is the cause for the house being made, and afterward rests in that house. Whether he follows the doctrine of *transmigration* <note>original: "Altenasach"; from the Arabic *at-tanāsukh*, referring to the transmigration of souls or reincarnation.</note> by positing that souls were created from eternity will be discussed below. 

The phrase is explained in another way: **AFTER** movement, meaning after the movement of the intellectual soul that is to be newly created. Although according to Aristotle and the Faith, the soul has not existed from eternity but is created anew, nevertheless, because the soul is the intended "end" <note>The "final cause" or goal for which something is made.</note> before it is created—which is first in intention but last in execution—its goal moves the agent, etc. Given, then, that the soul does not exist before the generation of the embryo with which it must be united, nevertheless, because the soul itself is the goal of the embryo's generation, it moves the elements toward a mixture as a goal intended in the mind of God or the Intelligences. For the sake of such a goal, the complexion and the composition of the limbs are generated. Therefore, although the soul does not pre-exist before the generation of its body with which it must be united, it nevertheless moves as a goal in the mind of God. And after the movement toward this goal, the complexion and composition of the limbs arrive in the body. 

In a third way, it is explained: **AFTER** movement, namely of the **vegetative soul** <term>vegetative soul: the most basic level of the soul responsible for nutrition, growth, and reproduction.</term>. For complexion and composition do not occur except after the vegetative power (which includes within itself the nutritive, augmentative, and generative powers) has moved by attracting or expelling, or has moved by extending or increasing the limbs, or has moved by shaping and composing the limbs. 

And Avicenna’s intention in this chapter is to demonstrate that the vegetative soul does not exist for the sake of the complexion of the composite, etc., as if for its final goal; rather, these things happen, as has been said, after the movement of the vegetative soul, or after the movement of the vegetative power, which in the human body is a power of the intellectual soul. It is clear, moreover, that the complexion and composition of the body exist for the sake of the intellectual soul—namely, so that the intellectual soul may be united to the body by means of a complexion and composition suitable to it, and so that it may be perfected by means of the senses, which are the beginning of the soul's knowledge. Therefore, the complexion and composition which arrive in the body along with the vegetative soul and after the movement of the vegetative soul are ordered toward the vegetative soul, which in the human body is ordered toward the intellectual soul. Consequently, it is not verified that the complexion and composition are the final cause of the vegetative soul; rather, these are ordered toward it.

# APHORISMS ON THE SOUL

...the intellectual soul as if for its final purpose, and you should consider a better explanation. And what has been said is verified in the human body. In plants, however, the **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific balance of bodily qualities—like heat and moisture—that defines a physical organism</term> and composition exist for the sake of the perfection of the vegetative soul itself as its final purpose, as is declared below by **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most influential philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note>: that the soul is both the cause of movement and the end of movement. 

It should be known that according to **Plato**, it is not improper for there to be an infinite number of souls. For granted that the world is eternal, and the souls of all people who have been and who will be exist from eternity, it follows that there is a number of souls without limit. This is not improper in things that lack physical volume, although it is impossible for an actual infinite to exist in physical things. Nor is it improper that souls which are not yet united to a body remain imperfect until that union with the body occurs. Just as it is granted that the souls of dead infants remain continuously imperfect after their separation from the body, so it is not improper for souls that have existed from eternity to remain imperfect, with weak knowledge, until the time they are united with a body and acquire perfection through it. 

And so, according to Plato's opinion, it is not necessary to claim that a transfer of souls <note>A reference to reincarnation or transmigration.</note> occurs from one body to another. Rather, according to Plato, every person possesses their own proper soul which has existed from eternity. This soul is united to this or that specific body according to how well it matches the **complexion** of the embryo suitable for that soul. Whenever there is a proportioned complexion in the embryo for a specific soul, then God or the **Active Intelligence** <term>Active Intelligence: in medieval philosophy, a higher intellect that "illuminates" human minds, allowing them to process abstract thoughts</term> unites that soul with that embryo. According to this opinion, it is said that people love each other in this world because their souls knew each other before their union, even if they had only weak knowledge at that time. 

A certain sect of Muslims called the **Sufis** <term>Sufis: followers of the mystical dimension of Islam, often emphasizing the soul's direct, spiritual connection to the Divine</term> holds the aforementioned opinion. Because of this, the great King of Persia named **Ismail Safavi** <note>original: "Ismael Suffi"; referring to Shah Ismail I (r. 1501–1524), founder of the Safavid dynasty.</note>, following this sect and writing to the most illustrious government of the **Venetians** at the beginning of his letter, confirms the aforementioned opinion with these words, namely:

> *With many greetings, etc. Regarding our intention, we advise you that it is certified and made manifest among us: your love and your benevolence. You are to us like good relatives, for the sake of Christ and the immaculate Virgin, who are the cause of the love we bear for you, etc. We have known that this love was born before the making of the world, from the First Cause, from the day when the spirits gathered before the Lord God before their joining into our bodies which were to come. The Prophet says in the **Alcoran** <note>original: "Alchoran"; the Quran</note> that the spirits were like an army: those who agreed then, now love each other in our bodies; and those who disagreed then, now do not love each other. And the distance of form and body is no reason that there should not be love, etc.* <note>This quote references a famous Hadith: "Souls are like recruited soldiers; those that are similar to each other associate with each other."</note>

And indeed, these aforementioned words and others contained in the letter as above were faithfully translated word-for-word from Arabic into Latin, etc.

It cites a diplomatic letter from the Persian Shah Ismail I to Venice as evidence of this shared mystical belief in souls recognizing one another from a primordial state.</summary>

<page-num>112</page-num>
<header>AVICENNA</header>

### The Sixteenth Aphorism.

Every physical **disposition** <term>disposition: the specific arrangement or state of the body’s parts</term> among the various states of the body is a consequence of its perfection. And that perfection is indeed the soul. <note>In this context, "perfection" refers to the "entelechy"—the realization or functional completion of a living thing.</note>

### The Seventeenth Aphorism.

The soul moves toward the end <note>original: "finem," meaning goal or purpose</note> which it possesses by its own nature or essence. Its goal is to exist in the noblest way possible for it, and the end it holds in its essence or nature is that which it acquires or desires. This end is either in a specific external thing or within the mover itself. It is necessary that every motion has a determined goal toward which something is moved: a goal which is either an external determined thing or within the mover itself.

<margin>On Aphorism 17.</margin>
Note that a goal external to the mover, which exists in an external thing, is like when someone moves in order to go to a house; in that case, the external goal is the house, which is something outside of the person moving. However, a goal which is within the mover itself is like a builder who builds and moves for his own sake—namely, so that he may live in the house and keep himself safe within it, etc.

### The Eighteenth Aphorism.

->Concerning the demonstration that the soul exists; and such a proof<-
->is taken from the purpose of the movement of the elements<-
->toward a gathering, or toward a mixing,<-
->leading toward the existence of the soul.<-

Because motion follows the existence of goals which are either in a specific external thing—such as the boundaries defining an external physical object—or are within the mover itself—as is the case with a builder—it was necessary for there to be a specific existing goal so that the existence of a specific motion could be verified. Therefore, the movement of the elements <note>The four classical elements: fire, air, water, and earth.</note> toward a gathering or a mixture must occur for the sake of another goal different from the simple act of aggregating. 
<margin>Q</margin>
For the aggregation or mixture follows after the motion. And that goal is the **form** or **essence** of the soul, whose existence is verified and perfected through the body. The aggregation, the mixture, the **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific balance of bodily qualities</term>, the composition, the shaping, and the other dispositions that come to the body after motion are all consequences of that goal. 
<margin>R</margin>
That goal is the mover itself: it is both the maker of the motion and its end. Therefore, the "maker" (or efficient cause) and the "end" (or final cause) are one and the same in a human being, and that is the soul.

<meta>Catchword: Aphorism. Vocab: Avicenna, soul, motion, end/goal, mixture, elements, form, essence, aphorism, disposition, perfection</meta>

->Aphorism 18.<-

<margin>Q</margin> **THE GATHERING** and mixing of elements occurs after the movement, namely the movement of the soul, which is the intended goal determined by the "Giver of Forms," <note>original: "datore formarū." In Avicenna’s philosophy, the "Giver of Forms" or "Active Intellect" is a celestial intelligence that bestows forms (like life or intellect) onto prepared matter.</note> as was stated above. Otherwise, this is explained as occurring AFTER the movement of the elements; or alternatively, AFTER the movement of the intellective soul, which pre-exists from eternity. As stated above, this soul moves the elements toward a mixture and a "complexion" <term>complexion: the specific physical balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities in a body</term> that is suitable for itself, so that it may be united with the body and brought to its own perfection.

<margin>R</margin> **THEY ARE AMONG** the things following from that end. That is, they are among those things ordered toward that goal. **WHEREFORE** it is the very thing that causes the movement. That is, the goal itself (the soul) is the efficient cause of the movement and the purpose of the movement. For just as someone building a house for his own sake—namely, so that he may live comfortably in it, etc.—is both the efficient cause of the house and the purpose of the house, so the soul is both the cause and the purpose of movement in a human being. If, therefore, the soul is that which causes movement and is also its goal, then the soul exists. And thus it is clear how the existence of the soul is demonstrated from the perspective of the goal of movement. The intention of Aphorism 19 and Aphorism 20 is also clear from this.

However, regarding whether souls were created from eternity, there is a diversity of opinions. Those holding the opinion of **Altenasach** <note>original: "Altenasach," a Latinization of the Arabic "al-tanasukh," meaning the transmigration of souls or reincarnation.</note>—as seen in the book *On the Return* <note>original: "lib. de Mahad," referring to Avicenna's work *Kitāb al-Ma'ād*.</note>—assert that souls were fixed in number from eternity and are transformed from body to body. Others, however, hold that souls were not from eternity but were created anew according to the mind of Aristotle. Some following this opinion say that souls are created anew in every embryo at the very instant in which the embryo is organized and fit to receive a soul; at that moment, a soul is created anew by God in that embryo, and the Christian faith holds this opinion. <margin>2</margin> The Muslim Sufis, however, hold that all souls were created from the beginning of the world. When a body is generated having a complexion proportional to a certain soul, then the intelligence or "Giver of Forms" pours into and applies that soul to that body. This occurs in every generation of every human being. Nor does the doctrine of *Altenasach* (the transmigration of souls from body to body) follow from this, because according to this opinion, every single soul requires a body with a complexion specifically proportioned to it. The souls that have not yet been united to bodies, but were created from the beginning of the world, wait until a body with a proportioned complexion is generated by celestial influence. Thus, in the generation of a human, a soul which was not previously united to a body is united to it; and in the hour of death, it is separated from the body and is not reunited to a different body other than the first. <margin>2</margin> And if it is argued that an "actual infinity" would then be produced—because humans from the beginning of the world to the end are infinite, etc.—it must be said that although the number of humans who have been and who will be newly generated is not precisely known by us, nevertheless, in reality, the number of humans from the beginning to the end of the world is finite. Thus, souls are finite and do not move from body to body. <margin>R</margin> And if it is argued that souls which are not united to a body until near the end of the world would not acquire knowledge until the end of the world, because the soul...

### Aphorism 19.

Every physical disposition happens after movement: therefore, it is not proven that the disposition itself is the final cause of movement: wherefore the mover itself is the end <note>The "end" here refers to the *telos* or purpose.</note>: and it is the soul.

### Aphorism 20.

If the **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific physical balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities in a body</term> were the soul: then it would be necessary for the complexion to be a being before the complexion existed, since the soul itself is the thing moving the elements toward the mixture.

This power was hindered from its operations during the time of sickness, because the place where the conservative power is established was darkened and veiled by **vapors** and **humors** <note>In medieval physiology, it was believed that physical gasses (vapors) or an imbalance of bodily fluids (humors) could physically cloud the brain, blocking the soul's access to memory and reason.</note>. And as often as the vapors and humors are removed from that place, the hindrance is then removed from it.

*Every apprehension, etc. In this chapter he also proves the soul exists through many arguments. ## Aphorism 22.
The human soul, although it exists through itself, nevertheless does not pass from this body into another body, because every soul has a proportion specifically appropriate to its own body. And the proportion or fitness proper to this soul is different from the proportion or fitness proper to that soul. Indeed, we do not know the exact proportion or fitness that is made appropriate to that body.

### Aphorism 22.
<margin>Text</margin>
**BECAUSE** every soul has a proportion made appropriate to its own body. Note that, beyond the diversity of temperaments existing among individuals of the human species, there is another diversity of proper proportions existing between each body of a human individual and its soul. This proportion results not only from the mixture of the elements, but also from **celestial influence** <note>original: "influxu coelesti." The belief that the positions and movements of the stars and planets influenced the formation and character of earthly bodies and souls.</note>. We are ignorant of this kind of proper proportion which exists in the soul toward its body, and in the body toward the soul. Each soul has a proportion made appropriate to its body, distinct from the proportion that any other soul has toward its own body.

### Aphorism 23.

<margin>Another version of Isaac: and the sense itself is already acted upon during sensation, wherefore they are [distinct].</margin>
**V** The soul is not a temperament, because when the temperament is altered from its health and its balance, it does not then feel its own alteration, and it does not remain in its state of health. Rather, it is sometimes altered or changed. Therefore, that which perceives or understands its own alteration is a stable thing, and that is the soul, which is its **perfection** <note>original: "perfectio." In Aristotelian terms, the soul is the 'first perfection' or 'actuality' that makes a body a living being.</note>. And similarly, when the **continuity** <note>original: "continuitas." Rather, it is a stable thing, which is the soul. And similarly, the powers which are in our bodies, when they move toward the contrary or something different from that toward which they naturally incline, then nothing moves them except a thing other than themselves, and that is the soul. And similarly, when a sense feels something, then that which apprehends it is the sensing soul, which has already been **acted upon** <note>original: "passa est." In medieval psychology, sensation was viewed as a 'passion' or a way the organ is physically affected or changed by the object it perceives.</note> during sensation; for the organ itself does not remain in its original disposition.

### Aphorism 23.

**V** THE SOUL is not a temperament, etc. In this chapter, Avicenna returns to proving that the soul exists through reasons other than those mentioned above, and the text is clear: that which perceives and apprehends is a stable thing, which is the soul. The sense, therefore—that is, the organ of sense—does not [itself] feel, because it is already being altered and acted upon during sensation; wherefore, since the organ itself does not remain in its original state, it does not feel as the primary agent, but is the instrument of the sensitive power. Such a power, and the primary principle of sensation, is the soul.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 115. The previous text ended with the soul described as a "stable thing" and a "perfection." ->A V I C E N N A<-

<margin>Intelligence and the intellectual soul are in reality a particular intelligible thing, and are not a universal concept.</margin>
...[perceiving] the sensible and imaginable things of the mind. However, things stripped <note>original: "denudatæ." In medieval philosophy, this refers to concepts being "stripped" of their physical, material qualities to become abstract thoughts.</note> of matter are apprehended through themselves without a physical instrument. Indeed, instruments were established so that particular and sensed things might be apprehended through them. Universal things, however, and **intelligible** things <note>original: "intelligibilia." Objects or truths that can only be grasped by the intellect, rather than the physical senses.</note> are understood through themselves. And even though the soul itself is an individual thing, it is nevertheless intelligible. For not every intelligible thing is a **universal concept** <note>original: "intentio vniuertalis." A "universal" is a general category (like "humanity") rather than a specific individual (like "Socrates").</note>, just as intelligence and the soul are not.

### Aphorism 24.

<margin>X</margin>
THAT WHICH UNDERSTANDS anything is stripped of matter.
*Note that the souls of **brutes** <note>original: "brutorum." A standard term for non-human animals.</note>, because they are not stripped of matter, do not understand their own essence, as Avicenna says below in Aphorism 26. And they only know through the **estimative power** <note>original: "uirtutem existimatiuam." In medieval psychology, this is the faculty that allows an animal to "estimate" or sense non-physical intentions, such as a sheep sensing that a wolf is dangerous.</note>, which holds the place of the intellect in animals. Therefore, the human soul does not understand its own essence with true intellection unless it is stripped of matter. And this is the proof that demonstrates that the human soul remains after separation—that is, after the death of the person. For if the human soul is stripped of matter, it does not depend on matter; and consequently, when it is separated from the body and matter, it then remains in its own being.*

FOR NOT every intelligible thing is a universal concept. For intelligence and the intellectual soul are, in reality—setting aside the operation of the intellect—something intelligible, and they are not universal concepts, as is evident.

### Aphorism 25.

THE BODY is a thing presupposed in the being of the soul. *This text is explained in two ways: one way is "in the being of the soul," meaning in the body, because the soul cannot be understood to be in the body unless a body is presupposed; and this explanation is valid according to the opinion of those who hold that souls have existed from eternity, or that souls were created at the beginning of the world. BUT IN the remaining of the soul, that is, in the remaining of the soul after death. Otherwise it is explained: "the body is presupposed in the being of the soul," that is, in the creation of the soul anew. For the soul is not created anew unless a body disposed for the reception of that soul is presupposed. AND IT IS possible for it when it is separated, etc. Concerning this there is a doubt: for if a soul that is not perfect can be perfected without the body itself, then why is the intellectual soul united to the body to acquire perfection? It must be said that the intellectual soul, through its union with the body, acquires a disposition and a preparation for receiving the **emanation** <note>original: "emanationem." The flow of knowledge or being from a higher divine or celestial source to a lower one.</note> and knowledge infused by the Intelligence, or by the **Active Intellect** <note>original: "intellectu agente." The "Active" or "Agent" Intellect was seen as a light that allows the human mind to turn potential thoughts into actual knowledge.</note>. ...it is possible for perfection and preparation from God and the **agent intellect** <note>original: "intellectu agente." In the Aristotelian and Islamic philosophical traditions, this is a celestial intelligence that acts as the "light" allowing the human mind to move from potential thought to actual understanding.</note> to come to the soul. Thus, it is possible for a soul that was not completely perfected in this world to be perfected in the other world without a body, as will be explained below. However, before it is united with the body, the soul possesses no perfection or preparation. Therefore, the souls of infants and the simple-minded <note>original: "stultorum." This likely refers to individuals who, through disability, lacked the use of reason.</note>, since they do not have such preparation, are not naturally fit to possess **blessedness** <note>original: "beatitudinem." Supreme happiness or the state of salvation.</note> in the next life; instead, it is said that they go to **limbo** <note>original: "limbum." In medieval theology, a place on the edge of hell for those who, while not condemned for personal sins, died without baptism or the development of reason.</note>. Supernaturally <margin>s</margin> however, and through divine power, the souls of those who die in infancy can, through baptism, receive the knowledge of God and attain blessedness. And if it is held that all souls were created from the beginning of the world, then it must be said that before they are united with the body, souls remain unformed and without any perfection until they are joined to bodies. They possess nothing but a certain confused natural knowledge, and through their union with the body and the mediation of the senses, they acquire knowledge and the preparation to receive infused knowledge and the knowledge of God from the agent intellect.

### Aphorism 25.

The body is a condition, or a conditional thing, or a thing presupposed for the **existence** <note>original: "in esse." Literally "in being."</note> of the soul, without a doubt. But in the **survival** <note>original: "remanentia." Referring to the soul's continued existence after death.</note> of the soul, the soul itself does not need the body. It is possible for the soul, when it is separated from the body and is not yet perfected, for perfections to come to it without the body itself. For the body is not a thing conditioned or presupposed for the soul's perfection, even though it is a thing conditioned for its being or its existence.

### Aphorism 26.

The souls of **brute animals** <note>original: "brutorum animalium." Non-human animals.</note> are different from man or the human soul because they are not stripped <note>original: "denudatæ." In this context, "stripped" means abstract or separated from physical matter.</note> of matter; therefore, they do not understand their own essences. Even if they were to apprehend their own essences, <margin>y</margin> they would only apprehend them through the **estimative power** <note>original: "virtutem existimatiuam." An internal sense described by Avicenna that allows animals to perceive "intentions" (like a lamb sensing the danger of a wolf) without intellectual reasoning.</note>. For this reason, their essence is not "intelligible" to them, and in them, the estimative power takes the place of the intellect.

### Commentary on Aphorism 26.

<margin>Y</margin>
FOR THIS REASON their essence—that is, the essence of brutes—is not intelligible to them—meaning to the brutes themselves. One should add: not intelligible with **true intellection**. This is because, as was said above, the souls of brutes are not stripped of matter. Therefore, they do not have true intellection, but rather a certain kind of knowledge produced by the estimative power. This is not an intellectual power, but in them, it stands in place of the intellect and the intellectual power. Consequently, the essence of brutes is not intelligible, or fit to be understood with true intellection by the brutes themselves, because they do not possess an intellect, as has been stated.

### Aphorism 27.

When we see certain things in a dream, we understand them first, and afterward, we imagine them. The cause of this is that the **agent intellect** <note>original: "intellectus agens." In the Aristotelian and Islamic philosophical traditions, this is a celestial intelligence that acts as the "light" allowing the human mind to move from potential thought to actual understanding.</note> pours those intelligible things into our intellect, and from there they are poured into our imagination, or our phantastic power. However, when we learn things, we imagine them first, and afterward, we understand them—this is the opposite of the first case. <margin>Z</margin> And when we wish to learn something and we arrange or prepare the soul to receive it by removing the obstacles that prevent the soul from reaching this desired goal—so that its preparation is appropriate—then we usually strive to occupy or exercise the imaginative power away from the things that occur and interfere with it. For example, when we wish to know a solution in **mathematics** <term>mathematica: here referring specifically to geometry or the study of shapes and lines</term>, we occupy the imaginative power with linear figures so that it does not wander to other things and become obstructed. Indeed, human souls are perfected when they have received the principles of their sciences from the imaginative power in such a way that they no longer need to take principles from the imaginative power for the things they wish to know. But when souls are **separated** <note>original: "separatæ," referring to the state after death when the soul is freed from the body</note>, they possess a disposition appropriate for receiving the **emanation** <term>emanationem: the "flowing forth" of knowledge or existence from a higher divine or celestial source to a lower one</term>, or the knowledge infused by the agent intellect. For the agent intellect operates its work continuously and does not hold back or delay its operation for anyone, provided that the receiving matter <note>In this context, the "matter" is the human soul or mind</note> has the appropriate preparation to receive the aforementioned emanation. Because of this purpose, it is necessary for a person to strive in this world to attain this perfection, or this most excellent preparation.

### Aphorism 27.

<margin>Z</margin> **THE OPPOSITE of the first case**: that is, the opposite of the type of knowledge first mentioned, namely the knowledge of things seen in sleep. For those things are understood first and imagined afterward; but when we learn, we imagine first and afterward we learn <note>original: "addiscimus." In this context, it implies the final step of grasping a concept intellectually through study.</note>.

### Aphorism 28.

Dreams and visions of this kind are signs that the human soul is naturally joined with the first intelligence without having to acquire it...

### Aphorism 29.

When branches of knowledge have been grasped, it is possible for them to be strengthened in the mind through **imagination** and **sensory perception**. Examples of this include mathematical figures and other concepts that depend in some way on the imagination. 

However, **pure concepts** <note>original: "intelligibilia." These are abstract truths or universal ideas that exist beyond physical shapes.</note> are different from these; because the imaginative power can actually hinder or block them, these concepts must overcome or surpass the faculty of imagination that gets in their way. 

Indeed, we do not necessarily need to draw mathematical figures on a tablet when we want to learn a demonstration, except to keep the imaginative power occupied with them as a middle ground. This ensures the **intellect** is not harmed or weighed down by boredom while it is busy acquiring or completing the proof. By keeping the imagination busy with something related to the subject being studied, we prevent it from becoming a hindrance. Thus, the teaching or acquisition of knowledge is completed by occupying the imagination and the senses with something relevant to the subject under consideration, so that the soul is not distracted from what it seeks or desires.

### Aphorism 30.

Consideration or **contemplation** occurs when the soul occupies its powers with something related to what it seeks or desires. This process perfects the soul’s preparation to receive the **forms** or essences it seeks from the **Giver of Forms** <term>dator formarum: In medieval philosophy, this refers to a celestial intelligence (often the Active Intellect) that "pours" specific essences or knowledge into the human mind once it is ready.</term>.

### Aphorism 31.

When a virtuous and moral soul that has performed good deeds is **separated from the body** <note>a common euphemism for death in this philosophical context</note>, the active intelligences pour a "perfection" into it. This results in the immediate grasp of pure concepts. Consequently, all things are represented to the soul instantly, and it no longer requires a physical body to understand them.

### Aphorism 32.

There is no logical proof that imperfect souls, once separated from the body, possess the things that would make them perfect—though some have believed that the **souls of the planets** <note>In ancient and medieval cosmology, the planets were often thought to be governed by their own divine or semi-divine souls.</note> possess their own source of perfection. Similarly, there is no proof that perfect souls, once separated, lack the things that continue to perfect them after their departure.

APHORISMS ON THE SOUL

...we suppose <note>completing the word "existimamus" from the previous page</note> that the body attains a perfection which is not within its own limits, or which is not suitable to its essence—specifically, that the body itself is made into an intellective being—then that would be an error of the **estimative faculty** <note>the mental power that perceives non-sensible intentions, like fear or utility, but can sometimes be misled by physical appearances</note>. And it would be erroneous to think that the disposition of souls that are not perfected at the time of their separation from the body would immediately reach the degree of perfection of perfected souls; for this would exceed their limits and their own essence or nature.

### Aphorism 35.

<margin>
Another reading: To understand the soul through its essence is essential to it.
</margin>
While the soul is joined to matter, it does not understand its own **essence** <term>the fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing</term>. For if it did understand its essence, then its perfection would be equal to the perfection of the **Intelligences** <term>higher celestial beings or pure intellects that exist without physical bodies</term>, which do understand their own essences. If it were possible for the soul to understand its own essence, then its act of understanding itself would be essential to its being; but the soul does not even understand that it understands its own essence. This is because it only gains such knowledge through acquisition and **stimulation** <note>original: "excitationem"</note> within it, or through the manifestation <margin>Another reading: through exercise</margin> of it, or by turning its attention toward it.

### Aphorism 36.

Every soul possesses a preparation or suitability specifically for receiving the **emanation** <term>the "flowing" of knowledge or existence from a higher source to a lower one</term> or infusion of the knowledge of truths. However, one type of soul possesses a "remote possibility," and therefore requires an appropriate external preparation; while another type of soul possesses a "proximate possibility," being prepared by its own nature. This latter soul has its own specific preparation to receive the emanation or infused knowledge.

### Aphorism 36. b

CONCERNING THE APPROPRIATE EXTERNAL PREPARATION. External preparation consists of things such as fasting, prayers, and a moral life. All of these prepare the soul for the knowledge infused by the Intelligences.

### Aphorism 37.

A soul separated from the body is not assigned to a specific place, nor to a body. Nor is there any doubt that every separated soul retains a specific "appropriation of disposition" or quality which it acquired from the human individual in which it resided before its separation. However, we do not know the nature of those specific appropriations or qualities.

Souls separated from the body are distinguished numerically, according to **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian philosopher whose work blended Aristotelianism and Neoplatonism</note>, through the various habits and various inclinations acquired from their bodies; and although it has been illustrated in this way, nevertheless we do not know the essence of the aforementioned qualities acquired from the body.

### Aphorism 38.

Because human individuals are created beings and not eternal, they were diverse or distinct—and this is not to be denied—for which reason it is necessary that the aforementioned individuals be diversified, even in the health of their **complexion** <term>the specific balance of the four physical humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which was thought to determine health and personality</term> and its corruption, and in the **temperament** <term>the "mixing" or proportion of the primary qualities of hot, cold, moist, and dry</term> of their composition, or its distance from the ideal balance and its deficiency. And this is not **forced** <note>original: "violentum"; in medieval philosophy, a "violent" motion or state is one imposed from the outside that goes against a thing's natural inclination</note>, and because of this it is necessary that individuals be diversified also in the rest of their dispositions: in good and evil, in sharpness of wit and speed of understanding, and in ignorance and dullness of wit.

### Aphorism 38.

<margin>A</margin>
AND THIS IS NOT FORCED. That is, that unequal physical complexion and composition is not forced; it is not "preternatural" <note>outside the normal course of nature</note> to this or that individual. Rather, it is natural from the beginning of their generation, following the proportions of the elements to one another.

### Aphorism 39.

#### Concerning the nature of reward and punishment, or concerning the nature of bliss, or happiness, and unhappiness.

<margin>B</margin>
**Beatitude** <note>bliss or supreme happiness</note> or the reward of beatitude is the arrival of that perfection of the soul which it desires; or, it is when the perfection the soul desires comes to it. Indeed, punishment, or the penalty of unhappiness, is when a soul that is not perfect contemplates perfection, or realizes that it was capable of being perfected. From this follows a sense of harm or punishment because of its own ignorance and its own diminishment, which it recognizes to exist within itself. Its condition in this state is similar to the condition of a sick person while they are being treated <note>suggesting the "pain" of the soul is a realization of its own lack, much like the discomfort of a medical cure</note>.

### Aphorism 40.

<margin>B</margin>
The sense of touch, so long as its physical complexion is not altered, does not apprehend—or does not feel—as is the case with the hand, for example. And that which is altered is not permanent; or, the altered complexion is not permanent. How then can that which is not permanent apprehend or feel? Therefore, the perceiving subject is something that exists, and it is distinct from the **complexion** <note>the physical, elemental makeup of the body</note>.

# APHORISMS ON THE SOUL

...complexion <note>completing the word "complexione" from the previous page</note>. Even the **radical complexion** <term>the innate balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—established at birth</term>, or natural complexion, does not perceive its own essence. How then could a newly arriving or accidental complexion, which is not natural, perceive its own essence? And furthermore, the motion of a trembling limb requires two "motors" <note>in Aristotelian physics, a 'motor' is the source or cause of a motion</note>, since we know that natural motion follows a continuous path or a single inseparable path. And since a 

<margin>a</margin>
trembling of a limb consists of two contrary motions, it follows that for each of these two motions there are two motors: one of which is the **complexional form** <term>the physical nature or "blueprint" of the body's humors</term>, and the second motor is another **intention** <note>original: "intentio"; here meaning a directed power or purpose</note>, and this is undoubtedly the soul. And again: because the movement of the **spirits** <term>the "pneumata" or vital vapors believed to travel through the nerves and arteries to facilitate life and thought</term> is diverse, and the causes of its diversity are various—which are distinct from the complexion—therefore the cause itself is the soul. And again, if the motor 

<margin>a</margin>
in animals were merely the complexion, then **fatigue** <note>original: "lassitudo"</note> would not be caused. For it is not possible that one and the same thing should both move and prohibit that very motion. Indeed, fatigue is the sensation of injury or pain following an alteration of the complexion toward the opposite of what that complexion requires.

->Aphorism 40.<-

<margin>B</margin>
**WHILE** *it is not altered (that is, by a tangible thing),* **IT DOES NOT** *sense (that is, the tangible thing).*

->Aphorism 41.<-

<margin>C</margin>
A thing does not "suffer" <note>in the sense of being acted upon or receiving an impression</note> from its own like, just as it is not affected by a heat that is similar to it. For the hand does not feel heat unless that heat has surpassed or overcome the hand's own heat, being added to it or being more intense than it. For if it were exactly like its own heat, then the hand would not feel it, because a thing does not arrive in another thing twice.

->Aphorism 41.<-

<margin>C</margin>
*THE HAND, etc. Note that if a warm hand felt a heat similar to itself, then heat—being one in number or one in degree—would arrive in the hand twice, which is false. For similar heat, which is felt by the hand, happens to the hand (as is evident), and thus there would be two heats of the same degree in the hand, and one heat of that degree would have happened to the hand twice.*

->Aphorism 42.<-

Those things which are generated and come to pass are imprinted or known in the **souls of the planets and the heavens** <note>the medieval belief that celestial bodies possessed rational souls that directed their movements and influenced earthly events</note>, [otherwise] generation would not occur. And if our own souls could imagine using the **imaginative power** <term>the faculty that processes sensory images</term> of the planets and the heavens, then they would see, or know, all things that happen and come to be.

# AVICENNA

### Aphorism 43.

**Man** perceives imagined things and senses them by means of external objects. The planets, however, in their own perception or cognition, do not require external things. Rather, knowledge arrives in their imaginative faculty from the **Intelligences** <term>in medieval cosmology, these are non-physical, divine beings that govern the movement of the celestial spheres</term>. For the Intelligences pour knowledge into the intellects of the planets themselves, and 
<margin>D</margin>
thence knowledge arrives in the imaginative faculty of those planets, just as occurs in those who are sleeping. In us, however, when we are awake, nothing arrives unless it first arrives in our senses; then it is elevated from them to our imaginative faculty, and then to our intellects.

->Aphorism 43.<-

<margin>D</margin>
JUST AS occurs in those who are sleeping, etc. Just as in a dream knowledge is first poured from the Intelligences into our intellect, and then from the intellect to our senses, so the higher Intelligences pour knowledge into the intelligence of the planets; then from the intelligence assigned to the planets, which is something external to them, such knowledge is poured into the **imaginative faculty of the souls of the planets** <note>Avicenna, following Aristotle, believed planets were living beings with their own souls and intellects</note>, which soul is intrinsic to the planets.

### Aphorism 44.

The human **Soul** is a substance existing through itself, not immersed in matter. Rather, it is separate from it. And the human soul indeed does not require this body, except so that through it the soul might acquire some perfection for itself.

### Aphorism 45.

->Concerning the knowledge of the cause for which some prayers are heard, and others are not.<-

The **cause** for which prayers are heard is the agreement, or gathering together of causes along with divine wisdom. And it is required that they agree, or be gathered together, with the cause of the man’s prayer. For example, in that which he himself prays for: and the cause of that thing being brought into existence by the Creator. If it were asked whether it is possible 
<margin>E</margin>
for the existence of that thing to be realized without prayer, and without the agreement of the thing itself with that prayer, we would say no. For the cause of it is one: and it is the Creator most high. And it is He who ordains that the cause of that thing being brought into existence is prayer, just as He ordains that the cause of health in this sick man is the drinking of medicine. ### Aphorism 46

Impressions from the souls of the planets upon our souls do not occur except through action and passion <note>In medieval philosophy, "action and passion" refers to the process of one thing acting upon another and the second thing being "passive" or receiving that influence.</note>, just as they occur through movements. And sometimes the aforementioned souls of the planets apprehend the **species** <term>species: here meaning a mental image, form, or the essential "idea" of a thing</term> of a thing, and that becomes the reason why we apprehend the species of that thing, whereby we are moved to perform it. And this is because those souls imagine, or apprehend, or see what we pray for; and they know that there is nothing prohibiting it, which is why the fulfillment of our prayers follows. Those souls apprehend, or see us, and they apprehend those things that are necessary for us. And among the things necessary for us is that we pray. Therefore, fulfillment follows our prayer when there is no obstacle; and for this reason, prayer is commanded of us, so that fulfillment may follow.
