->On description<-

A complete description is a discourse composed of the genus of a thing and its inseparable accident <term>accident: a property that a thing possesses but which is not essential to what it is, such as a person being "tall"</term>. This is done so that the description is made equal to or interchangeable with the thing itself. A description, taken absolutely, is a statement by which a thing is known through non-essential knowledge. Truly, it is a specific statement; or it is a statement by which something is distinguished from that which it is not, though not through its essential qualities.

## EXPOSITION.

### What GOD is.

<margin>Another reading: [He is not multiplied] by integral parts, nor by parts of a definition, nor by parts that are relative. And he is not altered either in essence, nor in those things that follow the essence which are not relative, nor in those which follow a relation, or which include the intention of a relation.</margin>
**God** the glorious creator, etc. The text is clear up to the point where it says that he is not multiplied by number, nor by quantity. That is, he is not multiplied by number, nor by quantity—meaning continuous quantity—that is, not by continuous quantitative parts. **NOR** by integral parts <note>integral parts: the individual components that make up a whole, like bricks in a wall</note>—that is, nor by the parts of which something consists or is composed. **NOR** by parts of a definition <note>original: "partes diffinitionis"; in logic, a definition is composed of a genus (a general category) and a specific difference. Avicenna argues God is too simple to be divided into such logical categories</note>, because God has no definition, as was said above. And although the name of God may be described in some way—saying that God is all-powerful, most wise, etc.—nevertheless, whatever is fitting and attributed to God is the same as God himself. **NOR** by parts that are relative. It should be noted that God is called "Lord" and is called "Creator." It is clear, however, that both "Lord" and "Creator" imply a relation <note>original: "relationem"; a term describing God's connection to created things rather than his internal nature</note>, and these are parts of the total sum of those things which belong to God, and along with this, they imply a relation. **AND HE IS NOT** altered in essence. That is, God does not vary, nor is he changed in his essence, nor in those things which follow the essence. It should be known, according to Avicenna, that God’s wisdom, and his power, and his justice, and similar things follow the essence of God, and are the same as the essence of God; they are not "relative," nor do they imply a relation in the way that "Lord" and "Creator" do. God, therefore, is not altered or changed in wisdom and power, which follow his essence, nor is he even changed in those things which follow a relation, or which imply a relation, such as mercy, piety, and generosity. For although things of this kind are not expressly relative—as "Lord," "Creator," "Father," and "Son" are—nevertheless they follow a relation, or have within themselves a certain intention and relation, as is clear; and in such things, God also does not change or vary. It should be noted that Avicenna proposed that the wisdom, power, and justice of God are the same as the essence of God, as was seen above. But nevertheless, the leading Muslims of Damascus—namely the judges and scribes who are the *Alfachi* <term>Alfachi: from the Arabic "al-faqih," referring to experts in Islamic jurisprudence or legal scholars</term> in the Muslim sect—hold that the power of God is something added-on, and outside the essence of God, and they say similarly regarding...

### Definition of the intellect.

<margin>Another reading from Isaac: [concerning] a sound radical or natural genius.</margin>
**Intellect** is a name common to many distinct meanings <note>original: "intentionibus"; in medieval logic, an "intention" refers to the way the mind grasps or intends a specific concept</note>. For "intellect" is used to describe a sound constitution, or a radical creation within a human being. Its definition is this: it is the power <note>original: "virtus"; in this context, it refers to a mental faculty or capacity</note> with which things that are shameful are perfectly discerned from things that are good or praiseworthy. Intellect is also spoken of as that by which a human acquires knowledge or learns through experience from universal judgments; therefore, the definition of intellect in this sense is as follows: namely, that it is the collection of concepts in the mind which serve as premises, from which those things that are suitable and intended are concluded or drawn out. Intellect is also used according to another meaning, the definition of which is this: it is a praiseworthy quality or disposition in a human, seen in their movements and rest, in their speech, and in their choices. These three meanings are those <margin>Another reading from Isaac: which the common people attribute [to it].</margin> which the common people assign to the name "intellect."

However, that which is signified by the name "intellect" among the philosophers is divided into eight meanings. One of these is the intellect of which the Philosopher <note>The "Philosopher" almost always refers to Aristotle</note> spoke in the *Book of Demonstrations* <note>Aristotle's *Posterior Analytics*</note>: he places a distinction between it and science <note>original: "scientia"; here meaning systematic, proven knowledge</note>. The meaning of what the Philosopher said there is this: namely, that intellect consists of the intelligible forms or species and the propositions whose knowledge comes to the soul from natural talent or natural cognition. Science, however, is the knowledge that comes to the soul <margin>through acquisition, that is, through the discourse of reason.</margin> through acquisition.

<margin>B</margin>
There is also the intellect of which it is spoken in the book *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's *De Anima*</note>, stating that one kind of intellect is speculative and another is practical. The **speculative intellect** is the power of the soul by which it grasps the forms of universal things, insofar as they are universal. The **practical intellect**, however, is the power of the soul that exists as a principle of motion, by which the desiring power is moved toward that which is chosen from things heard, for the sake of an intended end. Furthermore, "intellect" is spoken of in relation to several powers of the speculative intellect, for from those <margin>from those, namely, powers.</margin>

# ON DEFINITIONS AND QUESTIONS
### DE DIFFINI. ET QVESI.

The **intellect in act** <note>original: "intellectus in actu"</note> truly, according to Avicenna, exists when the soul is perfected by the knowledge or "intentions" <note>original: "intentionibus"; in medieval philosophy, an 'intention' refers to the mental representation or concept of an object</note> of intelligible things. It is in such a state that whenever the soul wishes, it can perform the act of understanding and make those concepts present to itself in actuality. This is like a trained philosopher who, when he wishes, can understand philosophical propositions; so it is with other sciences. A soul so perfected and disposed is called the "intellect in act." There is also an intellect called the **infused intellect** <note>original: "intellectus infusus"</note>, or the intellect possessing infused knowledge and science, such as is found in the intellect of prophets and saints. 

Furthermore, "intellect" is used to describe those intellects or substances entirely separate from matter, which are called **agent intellects** or **agent intelligences**. The definition of the **agent intellect**—or agent intelligence—regarding its nature as an intellect or a thinking being, is this: it is a formal substance whose essence is a form stripped of matter <note>original: "forma denudata"</note> by its own nature, not needing anything else to strip it of matter or from those things which depend on matter. 

Indeed, this intelligence is the form of all beings in this lower world <note>The sublunary world, or the earthly realm below the moon</note>, because within its own mind and concept are the forms of all beings of this lower world. From these intelligences flow the forms of the aforementioned things; as soon as matter is disposed for a certain form, this intelligence infuses the form proportioned to it. Thus it is clear how the separate intelligences, which are called **agent intellects**—and especially the intelligence moving the sphere of the moon—are the form of all things. 

However, in the sense that the aforementioned intelligence is the agent intellect, it is defined as follows: it is a formal substance whose essence is a form stripped of matter by its own nature, and which does not depend on matter or things dependent on matter through any other thing. The power of such an intelligence is to draw the **possible intellect** <note>The human capacity to learn</note> from potentiality into actuality by means of an "irradiation" <note>A symbolic light or flow of divine knowledge</note> cast upon it. From this it appears that the agent intellect, according to Avicenna, is not a power of the human soul, but is a separate substance moving the sphere of the moon, as will be declared in the following chapter. Such an agent intellect, of which Avicenna speaks, relates to the human intellect just as light relates to sight, as Avicenna says in his *Compendium on the Soul*.

->**Definition of the Soul**<-

<margin>C</margin>
**Soul** <note>original: "Anima"</note> is a common name applying to the concept shared by humans, animals, and plants, as well as to the concept shared by humans and the angels who rule the celestial bodies. The definition of the first concept is this: namely, that the soul itself is the **perfection** <note>original: "perfectio"; meaning the "fulfillment" or "actuality" that makes a body alive</note> of a natural organic body having life in potentiality. The definition of the soul according to the other concept is that the soul, an incorporeal substance, is the perfection of a body, moving it by will...

...ity] from a spiritual principle <note>original: "a principio spirituali"</note>, that is, an intellectual one, either in **act** or in **potency** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "potency" is the potential for something to happen, while "act" is its realization or operation.</note>. And that which is in potency is the distinguishing feature <note>original: "differentia"</note> of the human soul. That which is said to be in act, however, is the distinguishing feature of an angel.

And these terms are spoken of, or found: namely, the **universal intellect** <note>original: "intellectus universalis"</note>, or "intellect in the universal"; and **understanding the whole** <note>original: "intelligens totum"</note>, or "the all," or the "intellect of the total." There is also the "soul in the universal" and the "soul of the whole."

The **universal intellect**, or the intellect in the universal, is an **intended concept** <note>original: "intentio intellecta"; in medieval philosophy, an "intention" is a mental representation of an object</note> which is spoken of in relation to many individual intellects in number, such as those within individual human beings; it does not have a real existence <note>as a physical object</note>, but exists as a mental representation or a concept.

However, **understanding the whole**, or the "intellect of the total," or the "intellect of all," is spoken of according to two meanings, because "the whole" or "all" is used in two ways. The first is that by "whole" or "all," the entire world is understood. The second is that by "whole" or "all," one understands the body of the **highest sphere of heaven** <note>The outermost celestial sphere that encompasses all others in the medieval model of the universe</note>, which, because of its vast size or capacity, is called the "body of the whole"; and with its movement, the whole moves—or all things move—since everything is subject to its motion.

Therefore, if the "whole" or "all" is considered according to the first meaning, then the explanation of this name—namely, "understanding the whole" or "intellect of the total" or "intellect of all"—is the sum of those **substances stripped of matter** <note>original: "substantiarum expoliatarum a materia"; these are pure spiritual intelligences</note> in every way. These are not moved by themselves, nor by accident; they are moved only by desire <note>original: "appetitu"</note>. And the last in number of this sum is the **agent intellect** <note>original: "intellectus agens"</note> that acts upon human souls. Indeed, this sum is the principle of all things after the **First Principle** <note>God</note>. The First Principle is therefore the author of all things.

But considering the "whole" or "all" according to the second meaning, "understanding the whole" or the "intellect of the total" is the intellect that is a substance entirely denuded of matter, and it moves all things by its own motion along the path of its own desire; its being is the first being to **emanate** from the **First Being**.

Regarding the **soul in the universal** and the **soul of the whole**, let us say that the "soul in the universal" is the concept used to describe many souls differing in number, when one asks what the specific soul belonging to an individual is. The **soul of the whole**, however, in comparison or proportion to the "intellect of the total" or "that which understands the whole," is the sum of **incorporeal substances** <note>beings without bodies</note> which are the **perfections** governing bodies...

->Chapter on the definition of the soul.<-

<margin>But the **DEFINITION** according to another perspective—that is, the definition of the soul shared by both humans and angels—is as follows.</margin> *The soul is an incorporeal substance; it is the perfection of a body, moving it voluntarily in act or in potency from a spiritual (that is, an intellectual) principle.* To clarify this definition, it must be understood that according to Avicenna, the celestial bodies <note>The stars and planets</note> are animate and possess a soul, just as human bodies do. And just as the human soul is an incorporeal substance and the perfection of the human body, moving it voluntarily, so too the soul of the celestial bodies is an incorporeal substance and the perfection of the celestial body, moving it voluntarily. There is, however, a difference between the human soul and the soul of heaven: the human soul moves its body voluntarily **in potency** <note>potentiality; the human soul does not move the body at all times, such as during sleep</note>, because it does not move it always; but the soul of heaven is always **in the act** of moving. **FROM A** spiritual principle, that is, an intellectual one. This is explained in two ways: in one way, that the human soul and the soul of heaven have their existence and are the perfection of a body, etc., not from themselves, but they have their being from a spiritual principle from which they proceed. For, as will be explained below, from God the glorious proceeds the first universal intellect, or first intelligence; and from this intellect proceed three things: namely, an intellect, a soul, and a celestial body; and so on successively down to the intelligence of the sphere of the moon. One intelligence proceeds from another, and possesses its knowledge and its operation from the other. Similarly, the being of the human soul proceeds from a certain universal intelligence which moves the sphere of the moon, as will be shown below. In the second way, "from a spiritual principle" is explained to mean that the voluntary motion of the human body by the soul, and the voluntary motion of the celestial body by the soul of heaven, proceeds from a spiritual principle—that is, from a superior intelligence. Just as the intellectual operations of the human soul depend on the universal intelligence, so the voluntary motive operations performed by the celestial soul and the human soul depend on the universal intelligence.

AVICENNA

These terms—universal intellect or intelligence, intellect of the whole, universal soul, soul of the whole, and similarly universal spirit—are used here. So that they may be understood correctly, Avicenna provides a definition and explanation for each of them. The text is clear.

<margin>
It should be known that some Muslims <note>original: "maumethani"</note> of the Sufi sect <note>original: "secta Sophi"</note> hold that the First Intellect, of which we speak here, took on the body of Adam; afterwards the body of Moses, then the body of Jesus, and finally took on the body of the prophet Muhammad. Thus, they hold that Muhammad was the First Intellect. Just as Christians hold that the person of the Son of God took on human flesh in Christ, so the substance of the First Intellect took on the body of Muhammad.
</margin>

# WHY IF the whole is considered according to the first intention,
that is, if the entire world is understood, then just as the whole world includes many primary things within itself and is characterized chiefly by its most noble things, so by this name "intellect of the whole"—or "the all-understanding," or "the intellect of all"—is understood the sum of the substances separated from matter <note>These are the Intelligences, celestial beings that exist without physical bodies.</note>. These are the universal intelligences which, with appetite and will, move the celestial bodies. There are nine such intelligences, the last of which—that is, the one that moves the sphere of the moon—is called the **active intellect** <term>intellectus agens: the cosmic force that enables human beings to think and perceive universal truths.</term> in human souls. That is, it is the intelligence that is present in the human intellectual operation, behaving just as light behaves toward sight. Avicenna speaks of this intelligence in his *Compendium on the Soul*, in the final chapter. Such an intelligence, which flows knowledge into the souls of men, is the last in the order of intelligences moving the lunar sphere; it is more closely related to this lower world, and for that reason, the moon has a greater influence than the other spheres. Similarly, the intelligence moving the sphere of the moon influences these lower things more by infusing the forms of things into prepared matter, and also helping the human soul toward knowledge of them, leading the **possible intellect** <term>intellectus possibilis: the human mind's capacity to receive knowledge, which is "potential" until activated by the Active Intellect.</term> from potentiality into act. However, whatever this last intelligence performs, it only does so from the influence, knowledge, and help emanating from a higher intelligence. **AND THIS** sum indeed is the principle of all. For the explanation of this text and of what has been said above, it must be known that the order of beings is as follows, according to the school of those who follow Avicenna. For first there is God the Glorious, who, since He is one being, from Him proceeds only one thing. Therefore, according to Avicenna, from God proceeds only the first intellect or the first intelligence, which is an abstract intellectual substance more noble than all other separate substances and closest to God the Glorious. And because in such an intellect many diverse things are considered—namely, that the intellect knows itself, knows its own principle (or knows its substance proceeds from God), and insofar as the substance of the aforementioned intellect is both a possible and a necessary being—therefore, several things proceed from the aforementioned intellect, not just one. For from this intellect proceed these three: the second intellect (or second intelligence), the soul, and the supreme sphere. And from the second intellect proceeds the third intellect, and the soul of the second heaven, and its sphere. And from the third intelligence proceeds the fourth intelligence, the soul of the third heaven, and the substance of that third heaven. And so it continues in succession, descending down to the intellect or intelligence moving the sphere of the moon, and to the soul of the lunar sphere itself.

...and the substance of the sphere of the Moon itself, which three things—namely, the sphere of the Moon, its soul, and the intelligence moving that same sphere of the Moon—proceed from the intellect, or from the intelligence immediately above it in the hierarchy: namely, from the intelligence moving the sphere of Mercury, which contains the sphere of the Moon. It must be understood further that, just as the first intellect (or first intelligence) proceeds immediately from God, so its knowledge and power proceed from <note>Large space in original</note> immediately. And just as the power, knowledge, and being of the first intelligence proceed and emanate immediately from God most high, so the being, knowledge, every power, and every action of the second intelligence proceed from the first intelligence. The knowledge and action of the third intelligence depend on the second, and so on descending successively down to the lowest intelligence moving the sphere of the Moon. It is clear, therefore, that the knowledge, motion, and every operation of any of the intelligences moving the celestial bodies emanate and depend on a higher intelligence, as was said above.

The intelligence moving the sphere of the Moon is that which is called the **active intellect** <term>intellectus agens: the cosmic "agent" or "provider of forms" that illuminates the human mind</term>. According to Avicenna, this intellect brings the **possible intellect** <term>intellectus possibilis: the human capacity for thought, which is "potential" until activated by the higher intelligence</term> of man from potentiality into act; it relates to the human intellect just as light relates to the sense of sight. And such an active intellect, moving the sphere of the Moon by the power of God flowing into it through the mediation of the higher intervening intelligences, pours the forms of things into the matter prepared in this lower world. It does this in such a way that it not only pours in the forms of inanimate bodies, but also of animate ones, and it pours the **intellective soul** into the human body.

This is not surprising, because just as the being and knowledge of the second intelligence emanate from the first intelligence (as has been said), and the being and knowledge of the lowest intelligence moving the sphere of the Moon emanate from the higher intelligence moving the sphere touching the Moon's sphere, so—because the human soul is lower in order than the intelligence moving the sphere of the Moon—it must be said that the being of the human soul and its knowledge proceed and emanate from the intelligence moving the sphere of the Moon, which is called the **active intellect** by Avicenna.

And although the higher intelligences are also called "acting" intellects or "active" intelligences—because the first intelligence impresses or flows into the second, and the second into the third, and so on for the others, and even the celestial bodies moved by higher intelligences impress themselves upon these lower things—nevertheless, because the body of the Moon is closest to these lower things, it impresses upon them more strongly and more clearly. Therefore, the intelligence that moves and governs the motion of the Moon through power flowing from God by the mediation of the intervening intelligences is specifically called the **active intellect**, and this name is more properly attributed to it. 

Since, therefore, this lower world depends on the celestial bodies and the intelligences moving them, it is true what Avicenna said: that the sum of the essentially ordered intelligences is the principle of all things. And if elsewhere in Avicenna’s writings it is found that the "universal soul" or "universal intelligence" is a principle aiding the understandings of man...

### ON DEFINITIONS AND QUESTIONS

...by the **intellect of the whole** <note>original: "intellectum totius," referring to the collective or universal intellect that encompasses all separate substances</note> we understand the second intelligence; then it can be said that the existence of this second intelligence emanates from the first being—that is, from the first intelligence, which is the first being and emanates immediately from God the Glorious.

**ON THE SOUL** in the universal, etc. In this section, he compares the soul in the universal (or the universal soul) to the intellect in the universal. For just as "intellect in the universal" is spoken of and predicated of many individual intellects, so "soul in the universal" is a concept <note>original: "intentio," a technical term in medieval logic for a mental concept or representation</note> that is predicated of many numerically distinct souls. And just as the "intellect of the whole"—by understanding the whole (the entire world, as was said above)—is the sum total of substances separated from matter, so the "soul of the whole"—by considering the whole as has been said (namely, the entire world)—is the sum total of incorporeal substances which are the perfections <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, a "perfection" (entelechy) is the formal cause that makes a thing complete or actual; here, the soul is what makes the celestial body a living, moving thing.</note> governing the celestial bodies, and so on. Such substances are indeed the souls of the celestial bodies. Therefore, the sum of these souls is called the "soul of the whole," just as the sum of beings existing through themselves, or substances stripped of all matter, is called the "intellect of the whole." 

And just as the "intellect of the whole"—by understanding the whole according to a second intention—is an intelligence and a stripped substance upon which all lower things depend (just as all celestial bodies depend on the body of the highest sphere and are contained by it), so the "soul of the whole" is an incorporeal substance which is the first perfection of the body of the highest sphere, moving all things along with the motion of that same sphere. Thus, the soul of the whole is the soul of the highest heaven. It is therefore clear that just as by the "intellect of the whole" we understand either the sum of substances entirely stripped of matter, etc., or we understand the intelligence moving the highest sphere, so by the "**soul of the whole**" we understand either the sum of incorporeal substances which are the perfections and forms of the celestial bodies (that is, either the sum of the souls of every heaven), or we understand the soul of the highest heaven, which is the perfection and form of the highest sphere. This soul moves that highest sphere according to the path of intellectual will, and by the motion of the highest sphere, it moves all things, and so on. 

It should be noted that between the intelligences moving the celestial bodies and the souls of the celestial bodies, there is a twofold difference. 

First, because the substances of the intelligences are entirely abstracted from matter and from the body, <margin>C</margin> because they are not the "forms" of the celestial bodies; but the souls of those same celestial bodies, although they are incorporeal, are nonetheless not entirely stripped of the body, because they are the substantial forms <note>A "substantial form" is the internal principle that gives a thing its essential properties; here, the soul is what makes the celestial sphere a specific kind of living entity.</note> of the celestial bodies, just as the human soul is the form of the human body. 

The second difference is because the intelligences moving the celestial bodies move them with appetite, or love, or delight, because such an operation is their own perfection; therefore they move with desire and love, or with delight. But the souls of the celestial bodies move with **intellectual will**, because their will is not sensory, but rational. With this will, they obey the intelligences and move according to their command and according to the power flowing down from them.

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of Avicenna’s cosmology and metaphysics, specifically focusing on the hierarchy between the "soul of the whole" and the "intellect of the whole." **AVICENNA**

**AND THE COMPARISON** indeed, or the proportion or likeness of the soul of the whole to the intellect of the whole, etc. This text is explained in two ways. In one way, it is just as our human souls depend on the agent intellect <note>original: "intellectu agente"; in medieval philosophy, this is the "active" power of the mind that allows us to understand abstract concepts</note> in the act of understanding. This agent intellect leads our possible intellect from potentiality into actuality, acting much like light does for our sense of sight. In the same way, the "soul of the whole"—that is, the sum total of the souls of the celestial bodies—relates to the "intellect of the whole"—that is, to the sum total of the intelligences that move the celestial spheres. This is because every action and power of the aforementioned souls depends on and emanates from the aforementioned intelligences, as has been said. In another way, it is explained thus: the "soul of the whole"—that is, the soul of the highest heaven—relates to the "intellect of the whole"—that is, to the second intelligence moving the highest sphere—because the power and action of the soul of the highest heaven emanates from that second intelligence.

**AND THE SOUL** of the whole indeed, etc.—that is, the sum of the souls of the celestial bodies, whose power and operation emanate and proceed in an orderly fashion from the "intellect of the whole" (the sum of the intelligences). I say that such a sum of souls is the "proximate principle" <note>The most immediate cause or starting point.</note> of the very being of natural bodies. And its order—that is, the order of the soul of the whole in causing the existence of these lower things—follows after the order of the intellect of the whole. This is because the intellect of the whole is prior in the order of causing existence than the soul of the whole. And its being—that is, the being of the soul of the whole—emanates from its being—that is, from the being of the intellect of the whole.

### Definition of form.

<margin>Another reading of the text: concerning many in the response "what is it" regarding shared nature.</margin>
<margin>Without that, namely, that in which it exists.</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
"Form" is a common name used in several "intentions" <note>original: "intentionibus"; here meaning different conceptual applications or definitions of a word</note>: namely, regarding "species" and the essence of a thing, in whatever way it may be. It is also used to refer to "perfection," by which a species is completed in its "secondary perfection" <note>In Aristotelian thought, "first perfection" is the form or soul itself, while "secondary perfection" refers to the functioning or activity of that thing.</note>. It is also used for the essence through which a recipient possessing it exists or consists by itself. And it is used for the essence through which a species is established or constituted. Now, the definition of form according to the first intention, which is "species," is that it is predicated of many in the response to the question "What is it?" <note>original: "quid est"; a technical term in logic for defining the essential nature of a thing.</note> And it is said in another way [in response to "What is it?" in which something communicates or shares] with another. But the definition of the second intention is that form is every being in something that is not like a part of it, and the substance or existence of that thing cannot be verified without it, in whatever way it occurs. And the definition of form according to the third intention is that it is a being in something, not as a part of it, nor is its existence verified without it; and the thing exists because of it—such as the sciences and the nobilities or "perfections" which are attributed to a human being. Finally, the definition of form according to the fourth intention is that it is a being in another thing, not as a part of it, nor is its existence verified as being separate from that thing.

And the intention of what I have said—that it is a "substance"—is that its being exists in it in actuality through itself. therefore, etc. **IT IS THAT** its very being belongs to it in actuality by itself. It should be known that just as prime matter <note>original: "materia prima"; the most basic, characterless "stuff" that underlies all physical reality.</note> is a substance in its own right, so too does it possess actual being in a substantial and real sense. However, as was stated above, it does not possess actual "formal" being <note>original: "esse in actu formali"; the state of having a specific identity or shape, such as being "water" or "gold."</note> through itself, but rather achieves that formal state through a "form." That prime matter exists as a substantial reality is proven thus: it is either a real being, or it is not. If one argues the latter, it could not be a "subject" <note>original: "subiectum"; the underlying foundation that supports properties.</note>, nor could it receive any form. If it is a real being, it must be either a substance or an accident. It cannot be called an accident, because an accident cannot serve as the foundation for a substantial form. Therefore, prime matter is a substance; and consequently, by the very fact that it is a substance, it possesses substantial being in actuality through itself.

### Definition of the subject.

<margin>F</margin>
The word "subject" is used for that which we have already discussed: it is any thing whose nature is such that it may possess some perfection which it currently holds. "Subject" is also said of everything that is "placed under" <note>original: "subijcitur"; the Latin root of 'subject', meaning to be thrown or placed underneath as a support.</note> by itself—existing and providing being or stability to that which is founded upon it or inheres within it. In this way, <term>hyle</term> <note>original: "hyle"; a Greek term for "matter" or "timber," referring to the raw material of the universe.</note> is called a "subject" that does not exist by itself, but exists through that which inheres in it. Finally, "subject" is used for every logical intention <note>An "intention" in medieval logic is a concept or mental representation of a thing.</note> about which a judgment is made, whether an affirmation or negation is being asserted.

### Definition of the subject.

<margin>F</margin>
**JUST AS IT IS CALLED** *hyle* in relation to the subject. Note what was said above: that the underlying substance of prime matter is called *hyle*, and it is called "subject" according to different perspectives. It is called *hyle* in relation to the perfection and form which it *lacks*; but it is called "subject" in relation to the form which it *actually possesses*. Therefore, "subject" is used in many ways: it refers to a thing existing by itself that gives being to a property within it, and *hyle* refers to a subject that does not exist on its own, but through the form dwelling within it—because the substance of matter does not exist by itself in a finished ("formal") state, but only through the form that completes it. From this, it is clear that the term "subject" applies both to prime matter and to a composite being <note>A "composite being" is a physical object made of both matter and form, like a tree or a stone.</note> already existing in actuality. Thus, matter is called both *hyle* and "subject."

### Definition of matter.

<margin>G</margin>
"Matter" is sometimes used as a synonym for *hyle*. Matter is also said of any subject that receives perfection through the gathering of another thing to itself. Its arrival occurs "little by little," just as sperm and blood relate to the eventually developing form of an animal. For sometimes that which is gathered or associated with it is of its own species, and sometimes it is not of its own species.

<margin>G</margin>
**MATTER** is sometimes said, etc. From the words of Avicenna, it is clear that

Matter is used synonymously with *hyle* <note>original: "hyle"; the Greek term for raw wood, used by philosophers to denote the fundamental "stuff" of the universe.</note>, and for every subject which, together with another thing of the same species or a different species, receives some perfection or form.

### Definition of *al-unṣur*.

<margin>H</margin> *Al-unṣur* <note>original: "alhanſor"; a Latinization of the Arabic word *al-unṣur*, meaning "the origin," "root," or "element."</note> is the name of the primary root in subjects. And *al-unṣur* is said of the primary subject which, through its own alteration, receives the form by which the thing made from it—either absolutely or specifically—is defined. This is "prime hyle," or "prime matter," or matter considered with the condition of corporeality <note>being a physical body</note>; it is the primary subject among bodies, from which all other bodies are made, precisely because it receives their form. <margin>from it; namely, from the subject.</margin>

### *Definition of al-unṣur.*

<margin>H</margin> *This name "al-unṣur" among the Arabs is the name assigned to the thing which is the first root-subject. Therefore, this name "al-unṣur" is used for the first subject which, by means of its alteration, receives a specific substantial form, through which the thing made from it is granted its species. And such a first subject is of two kinds: for such a first subject either receives the aforementioned form insofar as it is a corporeal thing—and in this sense "al-unṣur" is the first subject of bodies, and according to this consideration the primary elements are called "al-unṣur," because from them the remaining bodies are made, and the elements themselves, through their alteration and their mixing with one another, receive the specific form of mixed things. If, however, the first subject receives the aforementioned form absolutely insofar as it is pure substance, then hyle, or prime matter, is called "al-unṣur." Thus it is clear how this name "al-unṣur" is said of prime matter and is also said of the four elements. And there is a difference between "subject" and "al-unṣur": because "al-unṣur" is said only of a subject that receives a specific substantial form, but "subject" is said of any subject receiving either an accidental form or a substantial form; for "subject" is used for that which is hyle, and for that which is an actual being, or a simple body, or a mixed body. But this name "al-unṣur" is used only for the subject that receives a specific substantial form.*

### Definition of *al-ustaqus*.

<margin>I</margin> *Al-ustaqus* <note>original: "alaſtachos"; a Latinization of the Arabic *al-ustaqus*, which is itself derived from the Greek *stoicheion*, meaning "element" or "first principle."</note> is the primary body which exists from its aggregation with other primary bodies that differ from it in species; and it is called *al-ustaqus* because the composition [of things] is made from it and from them. Because of this, it is said that it is the smallest part of those things reached by the resolution <note>the process of breaking a complex thing down into its basic parts</note> of bodies; and no division is found in it, except into parts that are similar or homogeneous.

<meta>This page continues the technical ontological analysis of Avicenna's metaphysics, moving from the definition of "prime matter" to the specific distinctions between different types of "elements" and "subjects." # .122. AVICENNA ON THE DIFFERENCES

Every element is a primary body, from which—along with other elements in an aggregate—a composition is made, which generates a mixed body; this body is later resolved back into those same elements as into its smallest parts, etc. Note that elements, insofar as they are parts of some mixture, are called *alastachos* <note>original: "alastachos"; a Latinization of the Arabic *al-ustaqus*, which itself comes from the Greek *stoicheion*, meaning "component element" or "building block."</note>; however, insofar as they are parts of the world in themselves and are fit to receive form, they are called *alhanfor* <note>original: "alhanfor"; the Latinized *al-unṣur*, meaning "the root," "source," or "elemental matter."</note>.

## Definition of *al-rukn*.

<margin>K</margin> *Al-rukn* <note>original: "alrachen"; Latinized from the Arabic *al-rukn*, meaning "the pillar," "foundation," or "fundamental part."</note> is a simple body which is an essential part of the world, such as the planets and the elemental matter (*alhanfor*). Indeed, a thing is called *al-rukn* in relation to the world; and in relation to that which is composed from it, it is called *alastachos* (component element). And in relation to that which is made from it—whether its generation occurs through composition and alteration together, or through alteration from it alone—it is called *alhanfor* (elemental matter). For example: air is the *alhanfor* of clouds through its own thickening <note>the process of condensation</note>. Yet air is not an *alastachos* (building block) of clouds <note>Because a cloud is seen as just "thickened air" rather than a mixture of multiple distinct elements.</note>. However, air is both the *alastachos* and the *alhanfor* of plants. Plants themselves are *al-rukn* (fundamental parts of the world). Their forms do not have an *alastachos* or an *alhanfor*. Their forms do have a subject <note>a substrate or underlying reality</note>; yet they do not have an *alhanfor*, <margin>H</margin> nor do they have *hyle* <note>original: "hyle"; the Greek term for raw matter.</note>. And it is true that the forms of the planets have a subject, if by "subject" one understands the "subsistent" of a thing which is in it in actuality; and if by that "subject" one does not understand a thing existing as a self-subsistent entity. In this context, *hyle* is understood as the subject or the subsistent. And by *alhanfor*, one also understands the subject which is in potentiality toward something that is made from it. In this place, *hyle* should not be understood as a substance perfected with the perfection that inheres in it. And these sorts of things—which are *hyle*, subject, *alhanfor*, matter, *alastachos*, and *al-rukn*—are related in such a way that one of them may be said or taken in place of another.

## *Definition of al-rukn.*

<margin>K</margin> **A PART** that is essential to the world, such as the planets and the *alhanfor*—that is, the elements in the act of composition, meaning mixture. **SINCE** air is the *alhanfor* of clouds, that is, since air is the matter or the subject receiving the form of clouds. <margin>I</margin> For air, when it is altered and thickened, receives the form of clouds. And thus air is not the *alastachos* (building block) of clouds, because an *alastachos* is a body which receives a form not from itself alone, but through the aggregation or mixture of itself with other primary bodies that are different from it in species. But it is clear that air receives the form of a cloud through alteration or thickening alone, without the mixture of another element; therefore, etc. Nevertheless, we say that air is the *alastachos* of plants, because plants are composed of air together with other elements. And air is also <margin>L</margin> the *alhanfor* of plants, because air is the matter and the subject receiving the form of plants.

# .129. ON DEFINITIONS AND QUESTIONS

...of plants, **AND THE PLANETS** are pillars <note>original: "alrachen"; from the Arabic *al-rukn*, meaning a fundamental pillar or foundation of the world's structure</note>, that is, the celestial bodies are called "pillars" because they are essential parts of the world. And the forms of these celestial bodies do not have component elements <note>original: "astachos"; from the Greek *stoicheion*, the smallest building blocks</note>; that is, they do not exist in a subject that is called a "component element." They are not grounded or situated in a mixture of elements as if in a subject, nor do they have elemental matter <note>original: "alhansor"; from the Arabic *al-unṣur*, meaning the source or root matter</note>. By "elemental matter," we mean a subject or recipient that is in "potentiality" <note>the capacity or possibility to become something else</note> for something to be made from it, as will be explained below. And the forms of these planets do have a subject, and yet it is not true to say that they have elemental matter or prime matter <note>original: "hyle"; the Greek term for the most basic, formless matter</note> as their subject. **AND IT IS TRUE** etc. In this section, Avicenna <note>the 11th-century Persian philosopher Ibn Sina</note> explains in what way it is true that the forms of celestial bodies have a subject and in what way it is not. For if by "subject" one means that which sustains a thing that is currently in existence <note>in "actuality"</note>, then in this way it is true: the forms of celestial bodies have a subject and are in a subject. This is because a certain substance that possesses quantity <note>extension in space</note> but is without material is the "subject" for the forms of the celestial bodies; for the celestial bodies are composed of such a "quantified substance" and the form that dwells within it. However, if by "subject" one means something that exists independently on its own—like natural bodies which exist by themselves and stand beneath "accidents" <note>temporary qualities like color or heat</note>—then the forms of celestial bodies do not have a subject in that sense, because the quantified substance in which the celestial form dwells is not a being that exists by itself. **AND BY** matter (*hyle*) etc. Since it was stated that the forms of plants do not have matter (*hyle*) or elemental matter (*alhansor*), he clarifies what is meant by matter here: "matter" refers to a subject or recipient that does not exist by itself and is in a state of potentiality. Similarly, "elemental matter" refers to a subject in a state of potentiality. According to this intention, the forms of celestial bodies do not have matter, nor a subject that is in potentiality for something else, because if they did, the heavens would be "corruptible" <note>subject to decay or change into a different substance</note>. If, however, by "matter" one means a substance perfected by a specific form that dwells within it, then we can say that the forms of the heavens *do* have matter, because they possess a quantified substance perfected by their own form. Thus, "corruptibility" does not follow, as it does when a form has matter that is a substance merely in potentiality for something else. Therefore, when it is said that the forms of plants do not have matter, it is not meant in this second sense, but in the first. **AND OF THIS KIND** of thing, etc. Although these aforementioned terms have their own proper meanings as stated, they are often used interchangeably, and one is taken in place of the other.

Regarding these terms *alrachen* (pillars), *alhansor* (elemental matter), and *alastachos* (component elements) which were discussed above: insofar as a body is a part of a composite whole, such a body—as Casseroni <note>likely referring to a commentator on Arabic philosophy</note> said in his commentary on the *Mugerzi* <note>likely the *Mujiz* or a similar summary of philosophical principles</note>—is called a **pillar** (*alrachen*). When considering that body as the material starting point of a composition, it is called **elemental matter** (*alhansor*). But when considering it as the final point of resolution <note>the smallest part you get when you break a thing down</note>, it is called a **component element** (*alastachos*). Doctors <note>medical authorities of the time</note> have specifically assigned the name *Alrachen* (Pillar) to each of the four elements. Hence, the elements are called *Alarchian*.

### Definition of Nature.

Nature is the first principle of motion and rest in the thing in which it exists inherently <note>original: "per se"; meaning by its own essence rather than by accident</note>. In short, it is the principle of all change and stability or permanence by itself. Some who have added to this definition—claiming that nature itself is a power diffused through a body that acts as a principle in one way or another—have erred. This is because the definition of "power" used in this context is simply "the principle of change in the thing being altered." Thus, they are essentially saying nature is "the principle of change that is the principle of change," which is a foolish error, for it defines a thing by itself. The term "nature" is applied to <term>alhansor</term> <note>original: from the Arabic *al-unṣur*, meaning the fundamental source or root matter from which elements arise</note>, to essential form, and to the motion that is produced by nature (from which the name "nature" is derived or takes its denomination). Physicians, however, use this name "nature" to mean the "complexion" <note>the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determines a person's health</note>, and for natural heat, the forms of the limbs, movements, and the **vegetative soul** <note>the most basic level of the soul, responsible for biological functions like growth and nutrition</note>; we will provide a definition for each of these in turn.

### Definition of *althabha*.

<margin>L</margin>
<term>Althabha</term> <note>original: from the Arabic *al-tab'ah*, referring to the specific "disposition" or "character" of a thing</note> is every quality or form by which any of the species is perfected, whether it be active or passive. It is a more general term than "nature." Sometimes something arises from nature and yet is not according to <term>althabha</term>, such as an extra finger <note>referring to polydactyly, a natural growth that deviates from the standard "type" of the species</note>. It appears that such a thing arises from <term>althabha</term> according to an individual or particular nature, but not according to a universal nature.

### *Definition of althabha.*

<margin>L</margin>
> *Note that the property of a thing, and the quality following its specific nature—whether that quality or property be active or passive—and in summary every perfection arriving at a composite thing is called <term>althabha</term>. Everything that is from "nature" is also from the thing called <term>althabha</term>, but not the other way around: therefore, <term>althabha</term> is more common than nature. And although there may be something from nature, such as a sixth finger, which is not from <term>althabha</term> according to the universal nature, nevertheless that added sixth finger, which is from nature, is said to be from <term>althabha</term> according to the individual nature.*

### Definition of Body.

<margin>M</margin>
"Body" is a common name, and it is used according to several different intentions. For a "body" is spoken of as a continuous quantity <note>a mathematical or physical entity that is not broken into discrete parts</note> that is bounded and measured by three dimensions in potentiality <note>meaning it has the inherent capacity to be measured by length, width, and depth</note>. A thing is also called a "body" in terms of the form in which it is possible, as I shall presuppose...

<header>CONCERNING DEFINITIONS AND QUESTIONS</header>

...dimensions may be produced or made in whatever way you wish—in length, width, and depth—having determined boundaries. And "body" is spoken of regarding a substance composed of <term>hyle</term> <note>original: *hyle*; the Greek term for "prime matter," the formless "stuff" that underlies all physical things</note> and the aforementioned form, or described in this way. The difference between quantity and this form is this: just as a piece of water or wax is changed or varied in its shape, so too are the determined, measured dimensions varied within it. No single dimension remains the same; not even one remains numerically identical. Instead, what remains is the form that receives these various arrangements, and this is "corporeity" <note>the state or quality of being a body</note>, which is numerically one and remains without change or variation. Similarly, when an object is thickened or thinned, the form of its corporeity is not altered, but its dimensions are altered. There is, therefore, a difference between the form that belongs to the category of quantity and the form that belongs to the category of substance.

### Definition of the body.

<margin>M</margin> ***BODY** is spoken of as a continuous quantity. It should be known that the "quantity" of which <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose philosophical works deeply influenced Medieval European thought</note> speaks here is quantity in general, abstracting from this or that specific dimension. For this reason, quantity in general is limited and dimensioned by three dimensions potentially; in its actual state, it does not include any specific dimensions, but is in potentiality and indifferent to any dimensions whatsoever. And "body" is spoken of regarding form—that is, regarding the substantial corporeal form, etc. But the form remains—that is, the form belonging to the category of substance. Therefore, there is a **DIFFERENCE** between form in the category of quantity and form in the category of substance, because form in the category of quantity varies, while form in the category of substance remains.*

### Definition of substance.

Substance is a common name. For "substance" is used for the essence of any thing, such as a human or whiteness <note>While "whiteness" is a quality, Avicenna notes that in common speech, people use "substance" to mean the "essence" or "what-it-is" of any thing</note>. And "substance" is used for every being whose essence does not need another essence to be associated or joined with it in order to exist in actuality. According to this meaning is the phrasing of those who say that a substance is a "being existing through itself" <note>original: *ens per se existens*; a thing that does not need to "inhere" in something else to exist, unlike a color which needs a surface</note>. "Substance" is also said of that which fits this description or condition and, additionally, has a nature that can receive "contraries" <note>opposite qualities, such as hot and cold, or black and white</note> within itself, one after the other in succession. "Substance" is also used for every essence whose being is not in a recipient. And "substance" is used for every essence whose being is not in a subject. The ancient philosophers have agreed on this from the time of **Aristotle** until now,

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the metaphysical definitions of substance, specifically refining the distinction between a "subject" (which supports accidents like color) and a "receptacle" (which receives the very form of a thing). It builds on the previous page's discussion of the physical body by looking at the logical categories that define existence.</meta>

<page-num>14</page-num>
<header>AVICENNA</header>

...in the use of this word "substance." We have already established <margin>N</margin> before this the difference between a "subject" and a <term>Mahal</term> <note>original: *Mahal*; an Arabic term used in Latin translations of Avicenna to mean a "receptacle" or "place of stay," distinct from a logical subject</note>, that is, a "recipient." Therefore, the intention of their speech when they say "a being not in a subject" <note>original: *ens non in subiecto*; the classic Aristotelian definition of a substance—something that exists on its own and is not just a property of something else</note> is understood to mean a being whose existence is not associated with a recipient that exists through itself in actuality and gives being to that thing. And it is not inconsistent for a substance to be in a recipient without which that recipient would not exist in actuality; for although it is in a recipient, it is nevertheless not in a subject.

Therefore, every being—even if it is like whiteness, heat, or motion—is nevertheless a substance according to the first intention <note>In medieval logic, an "intention" refers to the way a concept is understood or directed toward an object</note>. And <margin>The first principle, namely God.</margin> the first principle is a substance according to the second, fourth, and fifth intentions; but God is not a substance according to the third intention. <term>Hyle</term> <note>original: *Hyle*; Greek for "matter"</note>, however, is a substance according to the fourth and fifth intentions, but it is not a substance according to the second and third intentions. And the form is indeed a substance according to the fifth intention, but it is not a substance according to the second, third, and fourth intentions; and there is no diversity in the names.

### The Definition of Substance.

<margin>N</margin> *The **DIFFERENCE** between a "subject" and a **Mahal** (that is, a recipient): for by "subject" is properly understood a being existing in actuality that supports an <term>accident</term> <note>a property that is not essential to a thing's nature, like being "blue" or "sitting"</note>. By **Mahal**, however, is understood a being that of itself is not in actuality but in potentiality, such as "matter," which is the subject of "form." And although sometimes this term **mahal** (the recipient) and this term "subject" are used as if they were the same, nevertheless, what each of them signifies is what has been stated. Some, however, understand **Mahal** or "recipient" in this place to mean "place," and you should consider which is the better explanation. **WHEN** it is called "a being not in a subject," it is understood as a being not associated, etc. For whiteness, or any accident, is a being associated with the existence of a recipient (that is, a subject) existing through itself, which in actuality gives being to that whiteness. For an accident does not have being of itself, but its being depends on the subject in which it exists; therefore, an accident separated from its subject has no being, but its being depends on the subject. And so, an accident is an "associated being," or one depending on the existence of the recipient subject existing through itself, which subject indeed gives being to the accident itself. And because a substance is not in a subject that exists in actuality and through itself, nor does it depend on it for its existence, therefore a substance is not in a subject existing in actuality, nor is it a being associated with the existence of a recipient (the subject existing through itself) in the way an accident is. And although it is the case that a substance is not in a subject existing through itself like an accident is, as has been said, it is nevertheless not inconsistent for some substance—namely, a "substantial form"—to be in a recipient.*

->Definition of an accident.<-

"Accident" is a common name that is used for every being that exists in a recipient. And "accident" is used for every being that exists in a subject. And "accident" is used for a simple universal intention that can be predicated of many things in a universal sense, which do not exist through themselves, and which are accidents. And "accident" is used for every intention existing in something outside of its own nature. And "intention" is used for every intention which is predicated of something because its very being is in another thing with which it is associated. And "accident" is used for every intention whose being was not present at the beginning of the thing.
<margin>o</margin> Therefore, "form" is an accident according to the first intention only. And "white"—that is, a thing having whiteness, which is predicated of camphor and snow—is not an accident according to the first and second modes, or according to the first and second intentions; rather, it is an accident according to the third mode. ### *Definition of planets or the heavens.*

<margin>Q</margin>A planet is a simple, spherical substance that does not undergo <term>generation and corruption</term> <note>The Aristotelian idea that celestial bodies are eternal and do not change, decay, or "rot" like earthly matter.</note>, moving naturally above the medium which it encompasses or contains.

### *Definition of planets or the heavens.*

<margin>Q</margin>Moving above—that is, above the earth, which is contained by the celestial bodies.

### *Definition of a star.*

<margin>R</margin>A star is a simple, spherical body whose natural place is the planet itself, or the heaven itself; its nature is to shine; it does not undergo generation and corruption; it moves above a medium without encompassing or surrounding it.

### *Definition of stars.*

<margin>R</margin>Moving above a medium—that is, above the earth, without encompassing it. This is because a star, in relation to the celestial body, is like a <term>knot in a wooden board</term> <note>A common medieval analogy: just as a knot is fixed in wood and moves only when the whole board moves, stars were thought to be fixed in their celestial spheres rather than flying through space independently.</note>. For this reason, the star, which is a part of the celestial body, does not encompass the earth on its own.

### *Definition of the sun.*

The sun is a star, and it is the largest body of all the stars, and of the most powerful light. And its natural place is in the fourth sphere <note>In the geocentric model, the spheres were ordered: Moon, Mercury, Venus, and then the Sun in the fourth position.</note>.

### *Definition of the moon.*

<margin>s</margin>The moon is a planet, or a star, whose natural place is the lowest heaven. And its nature is such that it receives light from the sun according to various shapes. And its essential or natural color inclines toward blackness.

### *Definition of the moon.*

<margin>s</margin>And its essential color—that is, the color that belongs to it by itself as far as our sight is concerned, when the light of the sun is excluded—is a color inclining toward blackness.

### *Definition of <term>jinn</term>, or spirits.*

A <term>jinn</term> <note>original: *gen*; the Latinization of the Arabic *jinn*. In this context, they are treated as physical, though "airy," entities.</note> or spirit is a rational, airy animal having a transparent body, whose nature is such that it can be formed into various shapes. And this is not actually a description of its essence, but rather the meaning of the name.

### *Definition of fire.*

<margin>From the center—namely, of the world, that is, from the earth.</margin>Fire is a simple body whose nature is such that it is hot and dry, moving naturally away from the center <note>In medieval physics, fire's "natural place" was upward, toward the edge of the sublunary world.</note>, so that it remains beneath the sphere of the moon.

### Definition of water.

Water is a simple body, whose nature is to be cold and humid, transparent, and moving in the place which is beneath the sphere of air and above the earth.

### Definition of the world.

<margin>T</margin>
The world is an aggregate of all simple natural bodies. And the word "world" is used for the entire sum of <term>homogeneous</term> <note>Beings that share a common nature or substance.</note> beings, just as their discourse speaks of the "natural world" (or the world of natural things), the "world of souls," and the "world of intellects."

### Definition of the world.

<margin>T</margin>

The "world of souls"—that is, the aggregate of souls—is called a world. ### Definition of motion.

<margin>V</margin>
Motion is the <term>first perfection</term> <note>A classic Aristotelian definition: the realization or "actuality" of a possibility while it is still in the process of becoming.</note>, or the first act of a thing or being in <term>potentiality</term> <note>The capacity of a thing to become something else; for example, a cold stone has the "potentiality" to become warm.</note>, insofar as it is in potentiality. And if you wish, it may be said that motion is the exit from potentiality to act, not occurring in a single instant. The "motion of the whole," however, is the motion of the highest celestial body above the center, encompassing all motions that are above the center, and it is faster than them.

### Definition of motion.

<margin>V</margin>
*The "motion of the whole," etc. Note that the motion of the highest sphere is called the "motion of the whole" because the remaining inferior things are moved by its motion. Therefore, the motion of the highest sphere is called the motion of the whole because it encompasses all inferior motions and is faster than all inferior motions.*

### Definition of aldhar <note>original: "aldhar," a Latinization of the Arabic term "al-dahr," referring to absolute time or eternity.</note>, that is, of the age or eternity.

The "age" or "eternity" is attributed to the Creator or the Craftsman. And eternity is a concept understood concerning the fixed attributes toward the soul throughout all time.

### Definition of time.

Time is attributed to craftsmanship, and time is the measure of motion.

### Definition by Alan <note>original: "alan."; likely referring to Alan of Lille (Alanus ab Insulis), a 12th-century scholar</note> of the "now," that is, of the instant.

The "now" or the instant is an imagined extremity in which the past and future time share a connection. And sometimes it is said that it is a time of small measure or quantity in the imagination, continued through a true instant from its two sides.

### Definition of the term, or the extreme.

A term <note>In this context, "term" refers to a boundary or limit (Latin: *terminus*).</note> or end or extremity of a thing is that by which a thing possessing quantity reaches its "where" <note>A reference to the Aristotelian category of *Ubi* (Place).</note>, in which nothing of that thing exists beyond it.

### Definition of the infinite.

<margin>X</margin>
The infinite is a quantity of which, no matter what parts you have taken, there still exist things of it outside of them that are not repeated. Or otherwise: the infinite is a "how much" <note>Latin: *quantum*; a quantified thing.</note> of which, whatever parts were taken, there still exist or are found things of it not repeated, which are outside of them or are different from them.

### Definition of the infinite.

<margin>X</margin>
<margin>In Book 3 of the *Physics*, chapter 6, on the infinite and numbers.</margin>
*Of which whatever parts you have taken, etc.*—that is, that thing is called infinite from which, although you have taken whatever parts you wish, there still remain things of it (that is, other parts of that same infinite) which are different from the parts previously taken. And such parts remain "not repeated"—that is, without a repetition of the parts previously taken occurring. For if a number of things is taken which are parts of something—suppose the number one thousand—after such a number of a thousand, there are still found and still remain other parts different from the preceding ones, which are not repeated or counted among the previous ones; and beyond these parts, others still remain different from the prior ones, and so on into infinity.

### Definition of the point.

<margin>Y</margin>
A point is an indivisible essence having position, and it is the boundary of a line.

### Definition of the point.

<margin>Y</margin>
*And having position*—add "by accident" <note>In medieval philosophy, "by accident" (*per accidens*) means a property that is not part of a thing's essential definition but happens to be true of it; here, the point's position is defined by the position of the object it belongs to.</note>, because it is situated according to the situation of that in which it exists.

### Definition of the line.

<margin>Z</margin>
A line is a quantity which does not admit division except from one part <note>Meaning it has only one dimension (length).</note>. And again, a line is a quantity which is not divided in any way in the direction of its extension, and it is the boundary of a surface.

### Definition of the line.

<margin>Z</margin>
*EXCEPT from one part*—that is, except transversely in the direction of its extension.

### Definition of a Surface.

A surface <term>superficies; the two-dimensional boundary of a solid</term> is a quantity in which it is possible for divisions to occur that intersect one another directly <note>original: "directe"; here meaning at right angles or in straight lines</note>. And it is the boundary <note>original: "terminus"</note> of a body.

### Definition of Space.

Space <term>spacium; in this context, it refers to the interval or distance between points rather than outer space</term> is everything that exists between two boundaries that do not meet when they are approached. And its nature is such that other boundaries of the same kind as those boundaries may also be imagined within it. And the difference between space and the three dimensions is that sometimes there is linear space without a line, and superficial space without a surface. An example of this is if two points are presupposed within a body that is not actually divided internally; then between them there will be a space, but there will not be a line between them. And similarly, if two opposing lines are imagined within it, then there is a space between them, and yet there will not be a surface between them. 

<margin>Another reading: these lines themselves do not have a surface unless they are separated.</margin>

For the thing itself does not possess a surface except when it is separated by some act or mode of division. And indeed, there are no lines in it unless there are surfaces in it. Therefore, there is a difference between length and a line, and between breadth and a surface: because the space between the two aforementioned points is length, but it is not a line. And the space between the two aforementioned lines is breadth, and yet it is not a surface; although every line possesses length, and every surface possesses breadth.

### Definition of Space.

*Space is everything that, etc. That is, that is called space which is enclosed between two boundaries—for instance, between boundaries "a" and "b" which do not meet or approach one another when they are accessed. That is, when things move toward those boundaries (namely "a" and "b"), then such things moving or moved toward those boundaries do not meet each other. AND ITS nature—that is, it is possible that in it (namely the aforementioned space) other boundaries similar in kind to the aforementioned boundaries "a" and "b" may be imagined. For example, in a square body, there is a space enclosed between boundaries "a" and "b." Similarly, we can imagine within the aforementioned space another space enclosed between "c" and "d," and likewise another space enclosed between "e" and "f," and so on successively, as in this square figure.*

<meta>This page concludes the discussion on the distinction between mathematical lines/surfaces and the physical "spaces" they occupy within a solid body, based on Avicenna’s physics. It then transitions into a formal definition of "place" (locus), distinguishing between the Aristotelian definition (the boundary of the surrounding body) and the concept of an empty void or vacuum.</meta>

<page-num>134</page-num>
<header>ON DEFINITIONS AND QUESTIONS</header>

An example of this, etc. In this section, Avicenna <note>original: "Auicenna"; the Latinized name for Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician and philosopher whose work "The Cure" heavily influenced medieval European science</note> explains through examples how there can be a linear space <term>spacium lineale; the distance or interval between two points as opposed to the mathematical line itself</term> without an actual line. For if two points are presupposed and marked within a continuous body that has not been actually divided, there will be a linear space between those two points, and yet there will be no line. This is because, according to Avicenna and the geometers, a line is only created when two points in a body that is actually divided touch each other and are in close proximity. Similarly, a surface <term>superficies</term> is not created unless two lines in an actually divided body touch each other.

If, therefore, two points are marked in a continuous body that is not actually divided, there will not be a line between them, but there will be a linear space—namely, a space in which a line is imagined—and yet there will be no line. Similarly, if two opposing lines are marked and presupposed in the aforementioned body, there will be a space between them, but it will not be a surface. This is because the body itself in which the opposing lines are marked does not possess a surface unless that body is actually divided and no longer continuous. Furthermore, there are no true lines in it unless there are surfaces. Therefore, the difference is, etc. The space between two marked points in a continuous body is a longitudinal space similar to a line, but it is not a line; likewise, the space in the said body between the aforementioned lines is a breadth <note>original: "latitudo"</note>, and yet it is not a surface.

## Definition of Place.

Place <term>locus</term> is the inner surface of a surrounding body that touches the outer surface of the body it contains. Place is also defined by the lower surface upon which a heavy body rests. Furthermore, "place" is spoken of according to a third meaning <note>original: "secundum intentionem tertiam"</note>. In truth, place in this third sense is not a real entity. It consists of dimensions equal to the dimensions of the place where the space of the location enters. If it were possible for such a place to exist without something occupying it, then it would be a vacuum <term>vacuum; a space containing no matter</term>. If, however, it is not possible for it to exist unless a body occupies or fills it, then it is a space distinct from the space of a vacuum. Nevertheless, this particular meaning of the word "place" does not exist in the actual nature of things <note>This reflects the Aristotelian view that a true vacuum is impossible in nature; "place" must always be filled by something.</note>.

### Definition of the vacuum.

<margin>?</margin>
A vacuum is a space or dimension in which it is possible for us to presuppose the existence of three dimensions existing by themselves, not within a matter whose nature is such that it fills a body, even though the vacuum is free from it. <note>Avicenna is exploring the hypothetical concept of a void—a space containing length, width, and depth but no physical substance.</note>

### Definition of the vacuum.

<margin>?</margin>
NOT IN matter: that is, not in a subject, or in real actuality, because such a dimension is not a real being, but a being of reason <term>ens rationis; a concept that exists in the mind to help understand a principle</term>, or an imaginable being.

### Definition of the full.

The full <term>repletum; also known as a plenum</term> is a body insofar as its dimensions prevent another body from entering into it.

### Definition of privation.

Privation, which is one of the principles <note>referring to the three Aristotelian principles of nature: matter, form, and privation (the absence of a form)</note>, is the absence of the essence of a thing in something whose nature is to receive it and for that essence to be within it.

### Definition of rest.

Rest is the privation of motion in that which is capable of being moved, such that it remains in a single disposition of quantity, quality, place <note>original: "vbi"; literally "where," one of the ten Aristotelian categories</note>, and position for some time; and this aforementioned disposition is found in it for two hours, or two instants, or two small intervals of time.

### Definition of the fast.

The fast is local motion over a long space in a short time.

### Definition of the slow.

The slow is when local motion occurs over a short space in a long time.

### Definition of inclination and support.

Support <term>sustentatio</term> and inclination <term>inclinatio; the internal tendency or force that drives a body toward its natural place</term> is the quality through which a body repels that which prevents it from its motion toward a certain direction.

### Definition of lightness.

Lightness is a natural power through which a body is moved away from the center <note>in the medieval geocentric model, "the center" refers to the center of the Earth/Universe</note> by nature.

### Definition of heaviness.

Heaviness is a natural power through which a body is moved toward the center by nature.

### Definition of heat.

Heat is an active quality moving that in which it exists toward the higher region, because it causes lightness to occur. And there occurs from it
