Coldness is an active quality that causes the gathering together of things that are both of the same kind and of different kinds, binding bodies together through their thickening and coagulation; this belongs to the genus of quality.

->Definition of moisture.<-

Moisture <note>original: "humiditas"</note> is a passive quality that easily accepts gathering and foreign shapes, but does not preserve them. Instead, it returns to those very shapes and to the position that follows the natural motion of its body.

->Definition of dryness.<-

Dryness is a passive quality that accepts gathering and foreign shapes only with difficulty, and gives them up with difficulty, returning instead to its natural shapes.

->Definition of the rough.<-

The rough is a body whose surface is divided into parts that occupy different positions <note>i.e., an uneven or jagged surface</note>.

->Definition of the level, the equal, or the polished.<-

The polished or the level <note>original: "planum"</note> is a body whose surface is divided into equal parts.

->Definition of the hard.<-

The hard is a body that does not allow its surface to be pressed inward toward its interior, except with great difficulty.

->Definition of the yielding.<-

The yielding <note>original: "lene"; often meaning smooth or soft in this context</note> is a body that accepts such pressure with ease.

->Definition of the loose.<-

The loose or the supple <note>original: "laxum seu molle"</note> is a yielding body that undergoes rapid separation of its parts.

->Definition of the fragile.<-

The fragile <note>original: "frangibile"</note> is a hard body that undergoes rapid separation.

->Definition of the transparent.<-

The transparent is a body that possesses no color in its own essence. It is its nature that, through its mediation, colors which are located behind it may be seen.

<summary>This page provides formal Aristotelian definitions for the fundamental physical properties of matter, categorized into active qualities like coldness and passive qualities like moisture and dryness, alongside mechanical properties like hardness and transparency.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotelian physics, qualities, coldness, moisture, dryness, texture, transparency, Avicenna, natural philosophy</keywords>

### The definition of rarity.

Rarity <term>raritas; in this context, it refers to the thinness or porousness of a substance rather than its scarcity</term> is a common name. For it is used to describe the motion of a body from one quantity to a larger quantity. From this, it follows that the substance of the body becomes more subtle <note>original: "subtilior"; thinner or less dense</note> while its continuity remains intact. Rarity is also used to describe the quality of that very substance. Furthermore, rarity is used to describe the motion of the parts of a body as they move from being close together to being far apart. In this case, a body that is more subtle than they are enters into the spaces between them. This last motion is a change in position, whereas the first motion mentioned is a change in quality. Finally, rarity is used to describe the form of the arrangement of parts according to this manner.

### The definition of density.

<margin>And the fourth, that is, the form of the position of the parts in a dense thing, is position.</margin>
Indeed, from the definition of rarity, the definition of density <note>original: "densitas"</note> is known or understood. For density is a common name that covers four concepts <note>original: "intentiones"; technical scholastic terms for specific ways of understanding a concept</note> opposite to those other concepts: one of which is motion in quantity, another is quality, the third is motion in position, and the fourth is the position itself.

### The definition of gathering.

<margin>b. A single concept, just like the word "army."</margin>
Gathering <note>original: "congregatio"; a collection or assembly</note> is the state of many things being present which a single concept ᵇ contains under itself.

### The definition of separation.

Separation <note>original: "separatio"</note> is the opposite of gathering.

### The definition of the contiguous.

Things that are touching or contiguous <note>original: "contigua"</note> are any things whose extremities are together in position, such that it is not possible for anything else possessing a position to fall between them.

### The definition of things that enter into one another.

Things that enter into one another <note>original: "ingredientia ad se invicem"; referring to total interpenetration</note> are those where one encounters the other entirely, so that a single place suffices for both of them.

### The definition of the continuous.

The continuous <note>original: "continuum"</note> is a common name that is used for three concepts. One of these is that which is said of continuity itself, which is one of the distinct ways of measuring quantity. The definition of the continuous according to this concept is that thing whose nature is such that a single common boundary is found between its parts. The description of the aforementioned continuous is that it is infinitely divisible. There are also a second and a third concept of the continuous. Indeed, the first of these two refers to the accidents of continuous quantity...

...in the first sense <term>intentio; a technical scholastic term for a concept or a way of understanding a term</term>, regarding continuous quantity <term>quantitas continua; a mathematical or physical extension that can be divided infinitely, like a line or a body</term>, it occurs when there are two continuous things whose final boundaries are one and the same. The second sense of the continuous relates to motion in position, but it is considered alongside position. For anything whose final boundary and the final boundary of another thing are one in actuality is said to be continuous. An example of this is the two lines forming the angle of a triangle. The third sense of the continuous concerns the "accidents" <note>accidents are properties that can change without altering the core essence of a thing</note> of continuous quantity as it exists in matter. In this sense, two things are continuous when the boundary of each is joined and adhering to the boundary of the other during motion, even if they remain distinct in actuality. Examples include the continuity of limbs with one another, the continuity of ligaments with bones, and the continuity of those things that are attached to or joined within the neck.

### The definition of the continuous.

<margin>☞ It concerns accidents, because it is accidental to continuous quantity that one point should be the boundary of two parts of a continuum more than another point; or, put another way, that the first sense relates to accidents. That is, that such a sense applies to the continuous "how much" <note>original: "quanto continuo"</note> within the category of quantity; for continuous quantity, insofar as it exists in matter, is the same as a body within the category of substance <note>original: "praedicamento substantiae"</note>.</margin>

### The definition of unification.

Unity, or the "one," or unification <term>vnificatio</term>, is a common name. For "unity" is used to describe a community of things that share a single inherent quality or an essential or accidental predicate <note>a "predicate" is a property or characteristic asserted about a subject</note>. Examples include the unity or shared quality of *alcachones* <note>original: "alcachones i. canforæ"; a Latinization of the Arabic word for camphor</note> (that is, camphor) and snow in their whiteness. Or the unity and shared quality of a donkey and a human in their "animal-ness" or nature as living creatures. Unity is also used to describe a community of inherent qualities or predicates within a single subject, such as the unity of flavor and scent in an apple. Unity is also used to describe an aggregate composed of a subject and what is inherent to its single essence, such as how a human is made of body and soul. Furthermore, "unity" or the "one" is used to describe an aggregate made of many bodies, whether by similarity (such as a city), by contact (such as a bench or a litter <note>a portable bed or seat</note>), or by connection and continuity (such as the limbs of an animal). What is more truly meant in this chapter by the name "unity" or "one" is that unification or unity occurs when one body is formed, numerically speaking, from an assembly of many bodies because their individual properties have been destroyed <note>meaning they lose their individual identity to form a new whole</note>. This happens because their common boundaries have been removed or lifted through a genuine destruction of their previous limits.

### Definition of *al-tatalī* <note>original: "altheteli"; a Latin transliteration of the Arabic *al-tatalī*, referring to "adjacency" or "contiguity" where things are next to each other without anything of the same kind in between</note>.

*Al-tatalī* is the existence of things having a position, between which there is no other thing of their own kind.

### Definition of *al-tuwālī* <note>original: "althuali"; the Arabic term for "succession" or "sequence," where things follow a specific order</note>.

*Al-tuwālī* is the existence of one thing after another in relation to a fixed starting point. And there is nothing between them of their own kind or category.

### Definition of cause.

<margin>of this, namely the cause, to that, namely the thing caused.</margin>
A cause is any thing from whose existence in actuality <term>actuality; "in actu," meaning something that is currently real and active, not just a potential</term> follows the existence of another thing in actuality. And the existence of the first in actuality does not arise from the existence of the second in actuality.

### Definition of the caused <note>the effect</note>.

The caused is any thing whose existence in actuality comes from the existence of another. And the existence of that other does not arise from its own existence. And the intent of our speech when we say "from its existence" is different from the intent of our speech when we say "along with its existence." For the intent of the speech when we say "from its existence" is that it becomes an essence which, by consideration of itself, is "possible" in existence. Its own existence is not "necessary" in itself in actuality; rather, it is because from the existence in actuality of another thing or another essence that the existence of this thing or this essence follows.
<margin>it, namely the essence of the caused thing, is the possibility, namely of existing.</margin>
And the thing according to itself has possibility. Wherefore, in itself or within itself without any condition, there is possibility. But in itself or according to itself with the condition of a cause, it has the necessity of existing. And in itself, with the condition that it does not have a cause, it is "possessing a hindrance," or is impossible. <note>Avicenna is describing his famous metaphysical proof: things in the world are "possible" on their own, but become "necessary" once a cause acts upon them.</note> And the difference between our speech when we said "without condition" and our speech when we said "with condition" is not like the difference between saying "white wood" and "wood that is not white." The intent, however, when we say "along with its existence," is that when we presuppose any one of two things to be an existing entity, it follows that we know the other is also an existing entity. And when we presuppose it to fail or not exist, it follows that the other fails or does not exist. And indeed, the cause and the caused are
<margin>by 'cause' here is understood the total or perfect cause, not a partial or diminished cause.</margin>
simultaneous in the sense that these two are following one another, although the ways in which they follow each other are different. For when we presuppose one of them to be an existing entity, it follows that the other is already an existing entity by itself, whenever this is found. But the other...

...the cause, that whenever we assume that it exists, it follows that the existence of the caused <note>the effect</note> follows from its existence. Indeed, if the caused is removed, it is necessary to remove the cause; however, when we remove the cause, it is necessary to remove the caused by necessity, because by removing the cause, the caused itself is removed.

### Definition of *al-ibdāʿ* <note>original: "alabedha"; a Latin transliteration of the Arabic *al-ibdāʿ*, meaning primordial innovation or bringing into being from nothing</note>, that is, of first origination.

<margin>A</margin> *Al-ibdāʿ*, or first origination, is a common name for two understood things. The first of these is the intention of a thing, or the arrival of a thing not from anything else, nor through any medium. The second understood thing, or the second intention of this term, is that something has being absolutely from a cause without a medium. And in its own essence, it holds that it is a non-being; and yet it is now deprived of that non-being which it has in itself by a complete privation <note>meaning it has been fully brought into existence, leaving no trace of its inherent "nothingness"</note>.

->Definition of *al-ibdāʿ*<-

<margin>A</margin> *IN ITS essence, that is, considered in itself without the condition of the cause, as was said above, it does not have actual being, but it has possible being <term>possible being; "possibile esse," a state where something can exist but does not yet have reality on its own</term>.*

*AND IT IS NOW deprived of that, that is, because it is now "in act" <term>in act; "in actu," meaning currently real and existing</term> from the existence of the cause in act. Therefore, when it is in act, it is deprived of that possible or potential being which it has when considering the thing in itself and in its own essence without considering the cause.*

### Definition of creation.

Creation is a common name. For creation is spoken of as the emanation <term>emanation; "emanatio," the philosophical concept of reality flowing out from a source, similar to heat from a fire</term> of being, in whatever way it occurs. And it is spoken of as the emanation of being arriving out of matter and form, in whatever way it occurs. And creation is also spoken of regarding this second intention of a thing: that after it exists, no "being in potential" precedes it because of the conjunction of matter and form in its being. Or, put another way: no being in potential precedes it, which potential being would follow upon matter and form in existence.

### Definition of the made or the occurring.

Things made or occurring <note>original: "facti seu euenientis"</note> are spoken of according to two modes: one of which is temporal, and the other non-temporal. And the intention of a temporal "made thing" or "occurring thing" is that something is made or becomes, or occurs, after it did not have being in a preceding time. But the intention of a non-temporal made thing is the emanation of something into being, where the thing does not possess that being through itself.

->**Definition of the eternal.**<-

The **Eternal** is spoken of in several ways. For a thing is called eternal by comparison or in respect to another, and it is also called eternal in an absolute sense. That which is eternal by comparison is a thing whose time in the past is greater than the time of another thing. In this way, it is called eternal in comparison to that other thing. However, that which is absolute eternity is also spoken of in two modes: according to time, and according to essence. That which is eternal according to time is a thing that has existed for an infinite time in the past. But that which is eternal according to essence is a thing whose essence <note>the fundamental nature of what it is</note> does not have its being from a principle <note>a source or cause</note> that causes it. Therefore, the eternal according to time is that which has no temporal beginning. And the eternal according to essence is that which has no causing principle upon which it depends; and this kind of eternal is the **glorious God**.

WHAT is the essence of *al-tabīʿa* <note>original: "Altabha"; the Latin transliteration of the Arabic word for "nature"</note>? And what is the intention of the discourse regarding "nature" among physicians? The response is that among philosophers and physicians, *al-tabīʿa* <note>nature</note> is a common name applied to several different meanings. For nature is spoken of as the work of the **Supreme Craftsman** <note>original: "summi opificis"; referring to God as the Creator</note>, who devised the nature which we describe as being in the matter of the body, so that action and motion may proceed from that nature we describe. And nature is also spoken of as everything which requires something else—whether that requirement comes from nature or not from nature, or whether it possesses a nature or does not possess a nature. And because of this, it is said that the **soul** loves reason, or reasoning, by nature, and that **man** is a social being <note>original: "ciuilis"; literally "civil" or "political," referencing the Aristotelian idea that humans naturally live in organized societies</note> by nature. Indeed, nature <note>original: "Althabia"</note>, or "the natural," in the discourse of the philosophers, is spoken of as that in which an **order** is found. And when they say that something is proceeding in an orderly fashion in this or that way, it is known that it comes from nature; and thus it is known among us that it is not through nature...

...they want, or they do not understand the nature which we shall describe. Rather, by it they understand a stable and permanent mode or quality in an orderly state. And **nature**—called *Thabia* <note>original: "Thabia"; a Latin transliteration of the Arabic *al-tabīʿa*, meaning "nature"</note>—is spoken of as a power existing in bodies, from which proceeds movement and rest, occurring in a consistent way in that which exists by itself. Truly, some say that nature is a "complexion" <term>complexion: in medieval science, the specific mixture of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines the character of a body</term>. Yet nature, when defined as a complexion, is not found in simple bodies <note>the four primary elements: earth, water, air, and fire</note>, because a complexion exists only through composition or mixture. Indeed, it appears after the composition itself: when the contrary powers <note>the opposing qualities like heat and cold</note> have acted upon each other, been acted upon, and have been stabilized at a single point. 

Physicians also say that nature refers to the **form of composition**, just as they say there are certain bodies whose nature is such that "obstructions" <note>original: "oppilationes"; medical blockages in the vessels or pores</note> are multiplied within them. This refers to the narrowing of their pores. They also say that nature refers to every corporeal power that moves without the use of will: thus, they might say or name the **vegetative soul** <term>vegetative soul: the most basic level of life, responsible for growth and nutrition, shared by plants, animals, and humans</term> as "nature."

Philosophers, however, say that the soul of plants is "nature," since it moves with contrary motions toward different parts—spreading and lifting many branches, while sinking and thickening the roots. It works by means of organic instruments, and this distinguishes it from the definition of nature that applies to non-living things.

It is asked whether the sun, the moon, and the remaining planets are **living beings** or not, and whether they move while being dependent on something or fixed in something, or whether they move without being dependent on anything. The response is that a body, insofar as it is a body, is not living at all. Rather, it is not called living unless there is within it a principle of voluntary movement and knowledge. And the principle of such movement and governance within it is the **soul**, which is a **spiritual substance**. 

Now, those following the faith and the ancient wise men have agreed: that every body has a specific office and operation assigned or committed to it by an **angel**, so much so that even the rain and the wind have this. Indeed, no one has denied this except those departing from the foundations and firm roots of faith, and from the truth founded in the sciences or in philosophy. For the founders of the faith—namely, the **prophets**—delivered and taught this by inspiration...

Therefore, it is manifest and true from this consideration and demonstration—after diligent consideration has been held—that the mover of the celestial bodies, specifically the proximate or immediate mover, is a **spiritual substance** moving with will. And every body whose governance and mover is a spirit is a **living thing**. Therefore, celestial bodies, according to this summary or in this manner, are living beings.

It is asked whether there are more eternal beings than one. And if there is one eternal being, whether it is eternal through itself, or through another. And if there are more eternal beings than one: it is asked what commonality exists between them in this regard.

The answer is that everything whose being depends on another—which is the principle of its being—is "later" <note>secondary or posterior</note> by its own nature or in its essence. And everything that is "later" by itself or in its essence is not eternal, unless by "eternal" one understands that which is not preceded by time. And this is understood either absolutely or by comparison. That which is **absolute** is that before which there was nothing existing in time in which the thing itself was not already present. That, however, is **eternal by comparison** which is such that the "later" thing has no time in which that which is...

Or otherwise, that is truly **eternal by comparison**, which is such that what follows it does not have a time in which such an eternal thing does not enter first. But this kind of eternity and priority is already within time, in which the posterior thing does not enter. 

However, taking "eternal" according to the first mode of these two divisions: then the **body** and **universal motions** and **time** itself and all things that are not exhausted by or released from time, nor is time released from them, are said to be **eternal**, although their existence has a beginning. 

But taking "eternal" according to the second division: then everything that is more preceding, or prior or more ancient, is "eternal" in comparison to that which is closer to the time of its generation. But our intention is not concerning "eternal" understood in this sense. Rather, by **eternal** we understand that which nothing precedes in being. And that which nothing precedes in being is that which possesses **necessary existence** <note>original: "necesse esse"; a core scholastic concept meaning a being that must exist and cannot *not* exist</note> not from another that precedes it in being, but possesses necessary existence through itself. 

Therefore, an **eternal substance** is a being that is necessary through itself, or a being that possesses necessary existence by its own nature. And it is **one**, since a being that has necessary existence does not tolerate multitude or multiplication. For if "necessary existence" comes to or belongs to something, it must adhere to it or belong to it through itself by necessity, and not from another. Otherwise, it would be possible for "necessary existence" to happen or come to it by chance. And it would be possible for it *not* to come to it, and then it would not be "non-necessary"—or rather, it would be something other than necessary—if the "necessary existence" itself came to it from outside. And then its coming would not belong to each thing because the thing itself was necessary through itself, but it would be necessary only because of a cause.

# ON THE DIVISION OF THE SCIENCES

[Theo]retical or speculative science <note>original: "speculativa"; science concerned with knowledge for its own sake rather than for practical application</note> is divided into these parts only because the things under consideration or speculation are not exhausted without being one of three types. First, there are things whose being and definition depend on corporeal matter and on motion. These include the celestial bodies, the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water, the building blocks of the physical world in medieval science</note>, and those things generated from them. These are found with the dispositions proper to them, such as motion and rest, change, alteration, generation and corruption, growth and decay, and old age or thinning, as well as the powers and qualities from which these dispositions proceed, and other things similar to these. This, therefore, is one part.

Or, secondly, there are things whose existence depends on matter and motion, but whose determination or definition does not depend on both of them. Examples include **four-sidedness**, **roundness**, **sphericity**, and **pyramid-shape**, as well as number and its properties. For you can understand a sphere without it being necessary for your understanding to include whether it is made of wood, gold, or iron. 

A human being, however, cannot be understood by you unless you necessarily know and understand that his form exists in flesh and bone. Similarly, **concavity** is understood without it being necessary to understand the specific thing in which the concavity exists. But the **snub-ness** of a nose <note>original: "simitas"; a classic philosophical example illustrating that some qualities cannot be defined without the physical body they inhabit</note> is not understood without the necessity of understanding the thing—the nose—in which that snub-ness exists. Yet, despite all this, four-sidedness, roundness, concavity, and a twisted or humped line do not exist in reality except in some subject among the sum of bodies in which motion occurs. This, then, is the second part.

Or, thirdly, there are things whose existence, definition, and knowledge are neither joined to nor associated with matter and motion. An example of essences—those things which exist through themselves—is the essence of the unique truth of the **Creator of the world**. Examples of things attributed to another are concepts like essence-ness, unity, <margin>Another reading: plurality and cause.</margin> [multitude and scarcity], that which is caused, universality, particularity, completion, diminution, and things similar in this regard.

And because beings are categorized according to these three divisions or parts, theoretical or speculative sciences also have three divisions. Therefore, the science proper to the first part is named **natural science**. The science proper to the second part is named **rihadi science** <note>original: "scientia rihadi"; from the Arabic 'riyāḍī,' meaning mathematical or disciplinary</note>, which is to say the exercise of the intellect, or mathe[matics]...

f 4

->On the divisions, or parts, of practical science.<-

Because human governance is either restricted to a single individual or it is not. And that which is not restricted to one is that which is not completed except through companions. These companions are grouped either according to a family gathering or according to a civil gathering <note>meaning a city or state</note>. Therefore, there are three practical sciences. One of these is assigned to the first division, and through it one learns how a human being ought to be in his morals and his actions, so that his life—both here and hereafter—may be a <term>blessed life</term> <note>original: "vita beata"; the ultimate goal of ancient and medieval philosophy, often meaning "human flourishing" or "happiness"</note>. This part is contained in Aristotle's book on morals <note>The *Nicomachean Ethics*</note>.

The second science from those mentioned above is assigned to the second division, and through it one learns how a man’s governance ought to be in his common home, between himself and his wife, his children, and his servants. This is so that his household may be well-ordered, leading to the possibility of acquiring blessedness or happiness. This part is contained in the book on household governance <note>often called "Economics" in the classical sense of *oikonomia* or "house-management"</note>, about which some others have also written.

The third science of the practical sciences is assigned to the third part, and through it are known the types of civil governance and the governance of the republic, and the dignity of princes. Through it, the conditions of a republic—whether it is governed well or poorly—are known. One also learns the method or the cause by which a good or bad government persists in a republic and in cities, and the way and cause through which each of these is removed or changed from one state to another. That which pertains to kings among these matters is contained in the two books by Plato and Aristotle on political or civil governance. 

That which pertains to prophets and to laws, however, is contained in the books of the <term>nuamis</term> <note>original: "nuamis" or "namus," derived from the Greek *nomos*, meaning "law." In this context, it refers to divinely revealed law</note>, that is, concerning divine laws. Philosophers do not understand by *nuamis* what common people think—namely, that the *nuamis* or *namus* is a form of tyranny or the unjust seizure of another's property. Rather, according to the philosophers themselves, the *namus* is that which ought to be observed in a law that has been revealed from God for a long time. The Arabs call the angel who descends from God, or who reveals [truth] miraculously...

### The principal divisions, or parts, of natural science.

Of natural science, there is one kind that acts like a root or a governing science <note>literally "subalternating," meaning it provides the principles for other branches</note>. And another kind acts like a branch, or a subordinate science, or like branched-out parts. Indeed, there are eight parts of that which acts like a root. In the first of these, one learns about universal things, or those common to all natural things, such as matter, form, motion, nature, causes, the finite, and the infinite. One also learns about the dependency of motion upon a mover, and its arrival or termination, or its state [reaching] toward a first, single, unmoved mover <note>the "First Mover" or God in the Aristotelian tradition</note>, who does <term>not</term><gloss>not</gloss> have finite power—or who is not a finite power—<term>nor</term><gloss>nor</gloss> is a body, nor exists within a body. This part is contained in the book *Alchian* <note>original: "Alchian," from the Arabic *al-Kiyān*, referring to Aristotle's *Physics*</note>, that is, the book of physics.

Through the second part of the aforementioned science, one learns the dispositions of bodies which are the Elements <note>original: "Alarchan," from the Arabic *al-arkān*, meaning the primary components or "pillars" of the physical world</note>, that is, the parts that compose the world. These are the heavenly bodies and what is within them, and the four elements, their nature, their motions, and their places. One also gains knowledge of the judgment as to what end they were made and ordered, and how they touch each other in a spherical manner. This part is contained in the book *On the Heaven and the World* <note>Aristotle's *De Caelo*</note>.

Through the third part, one learns the nature of generation and corruption, and generation <term>without</term><gloss>without</gloss> seed <note>referring to "spontaneous generation," a common medieval belief that some life forms arose from decaying matter</note>, and generation with seed (namely, procreation). One also learns the nature of growth and decay, and alterations in an absolute sense, <term>without</term><gloss>without</gloss> distinction. And among the number of the aforementioned sciences is the science of alchemy; and the intention in it is to strip a mineral substance of its own properties and to induce in it the properties of others, so that those things mixed with one another may pour their properties into each other, so that gold and silver may be made from bodies different from either of them.

### On the division of divine science.

<margin>
Another reading: they will predicate of him.
Another reading: diversity.
</margin>
The radical or principal parts and divisions of **divine science** <note>original: "scientiae divinae"; this refers to Metaphysics, the study of existence itself and of God as the First Cause</note> are five. The first of these is the speculation on the knowledge of the **intentions** <note>original: "intentionum"; in medieval philosophy, these are the fundamental concepts or logical ways the mind understands things</note> common to all beings, such as **essence**, **unity**, **plurality**, **agreement**, **diversity**, **contrariety**, **potency**, **act**, **virtue**, **operation**, **cause**, and **the caused**. The second part, however, is the speculation on the roots and principles of subjects such as natural science, mathematical science, and dialectical science, and it teaches how to refute corrupt or erroneous opinions within them. In the third part is the speculation on the affirmations of **God**, the **First Truth**, and on His unity, and on the demonstration of His **simplicity** <note>the theological concept that God is not composed of parts</note> in His essence, His rank, or His order. It also treats the impossibility of Him sharing His essence with any other being. His being is **necessary being by itself** <note>original: "necesse esse per se"; a core concept in Avicenna's philosophy meaning God's existence is essential to His nature and requires no outside cause</note>. And the existence of that which comes from Him must exist through Him. Furthermore, this part includes the speculation or consideration of His **attributes**, or of those things which are predicated of Him, and in what manner they are His attributes. It asks: what is that which is understood from the expression of each of His attributes? For the expressions used regarding His attributes include "the One," "Being," "the Eternal," "the Wise," and "the Powerful"; and each of these signifies a single intention. It is not possible for multiple intentions—each being different from the other—to be caused within a single being in which there is no plurality. One learns how it is necessary to understand these attributes of His, or these predications of Him, in such a way that nothing <insert>other than Him</insert> is caused in His essence, nor any plurality, nor any conflict within His true essential unity.

<margin>
Another reading: the assistance that depends on each of these for completion or perfection of the whole.
</margin>
In the fourth part, there is speculation and consideration of the affirmations or demonstrations of the existence of the **substances** which are the effects of God and His creatures closest to His throne; and concerning the demonstrations of their plurality, the diversity of their orders, and their ranks. And [the necessity that depends on each of these for the perfection or completion] of the whole. These substances are the **angels** and **cherubim**. Afterward, it considers the affirmation of the existence of the **secondary spiritual substances**, which in sum are different from the sum of those first ones; and their dwellings are known, <note>original: "mansiones"; often referring to the celestial spheres or ranks of spiritual existence</note> and...

-># ON THE DIVISION OF THE SCIENCES<-

The angel Gabriel, and the sanctified spirit, and the spirit **alamin** <note>original: "spiritus alamin"; from the Arabic *Rūḥ al-Amīn*, meaning the "Faithful Spirit," a title for Gabriel in Islamic tradition</note>—that is, the angel Gabriel—belong to the second order of spiritual substances. And the sanctified spirit is from the order of the **Cherubim** <note>traditionally the second highest rank of angels in the celestial hierarchy</note>. Among the aforementioned sciences subordinate to divine science is the science of **mahad** <note>original: "mahad"; from the Arabic *ma‘ād*, meaning "the return" or the place of the afterlife</note>, which is the science of the state of the **rational soul** <term>rational soul: the part of the human spirit capable of reason and intellect, which philosophers argued was immortal</term> after its separation from the body. Such a science encompasses the knowledge that even if the human body were not to rise again after death—for example—then his spirit would still remain after death, either rewarded or punished, deserving of merit or demerit. This is distinct or different from what is confirmed in faith, or in the laws, or in the divinely revealed theological scriptures. Therefore, the perfect spirits—who are the virtuous souls, truly believing in the truth and performing good works as faith, law, and intellect require—shall possess a **happiness**, joy, and delight that are above all other happiness, joy, and delight; and these shall be more intense or more worthy than those things which are confirmed in faith or in the scriptures of faith. Nor does the intellect oppose the idea that such things might also be present in or suitable for their bodies. Indeed, God the Glorious, the remunerator of His perfect servants, has through the tongue of the **prophets** promised the gathering together of two happinesses at once: namely, the **spiritual beatitude** which belongs to the soul remaining after death, and the **corporal beatitude** which belongs to the body that will rise after death. This happiness shall indeed come according to the measure God wills, and when He wills it.

<margin>
In the same way, consider that just as spiritual happiness is known—because the intellect has a path and a reason to affirm and demonstrate it—so it must be said of spiritual torment. And just as corporal happiness is not affirmed except through faith and revelation, so also corporal torment is not affirmed except through faith and revelation.
</margin>

And from the aforementioned science it is made clear how that spiritual happiness comes to be, because the intellect alone has the path to knowing such beatitude. But corporal happiness cannot be described or affirmed except by divine revelation and faith, or the scriptures of faith. In the same way, the nature of **spiritual torment** is known, which belongs to vicious souls; and such torment will be of more vehement injury and harm than the torment which is proclaimed through the scriptures or through God's chosen ones to happen to the vicious after the resurrection of the bodies. It is also known in whom that torment shall remain continuously, and from whom it shall be removed. Truly, the torment which is assigned to the body through faith or through the scriptures of faith is certified for them, or affirmed according to its truth, without independent speculation or intellect; for in order to prove that there is spiritual torment...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of human happiness and the afterlife, specifically how the intellect and prophecy interact regarding the fate of the body. It marks the transition from the "Divine Sciences" (metaphysics and theology) to Logic, which Avicenna defines as the essential tool for all scientific inquiry.</meta>

->AVICENNA<-

...spiritual <note>The word "spiritualem" begins on the previous page and concludes here as "tualem."</note> [happiness] is indeed accessible to the intellect by way of speculation, argumentation, and demonstration. But the existence of bodily torment is verified through the prophets, who have been verified and approved by the intellect; and their existence is necessarily demonstrated through signs that certify the intellect. For whenever the intellect does not arrive at affirming, or cannot affirm, the existence of a thing or its necessity through a sign or demonstration, and it possesses nothing but the possibility of that thing; then the prophets teach or speak of its existence or its absence with determination or certainty. Moreover, the certainty of those prophets and the truth of their words are verified within the intellect itself. Therefore, through the sayings of the prophets, the knowledge of that thing—in the knowledge of which the intellect was deficient—is completed. 

Since, therefore, we have now considered the fundamental parts and the branched <note>original: "partes radicales et partes ramosas"; a common medieval metaphor where the primary principles are "roots" and the sub-disciplines are "branches"</note> or subordinate parts of science, it now remains for us to know the parts of that science which is the instrument or **organ** <term>organ: from the Greek 'organon' (tool), referring to logic as a tool used to build other sciences rather than a subject studied for its own sake</term> of man, leading him to acquire the speculative and practical sciences, and protecting him from fallacy and error in considerations or examinations. Indeed, the study of the knowledge of such a science leads man to the path he ought to walk in every consideration, and to the knowledge of the essence of a true definition, and the essence of true argumentation or demonstration (which is demonstrative), and the essence of inductive argumentation (which is closest to demonstration), and the essence of probable or persuasive argumentation (which falls short of both), and the essence of erroneous or sophistical argumentation (appearing similar to both), and the essence of argumentation which proceeds through the similarities of things or through metaphorical imaginings. And such a science, which teaches the aforementioned things, is called **logic**.

### On the division of logic.

The parts of logic, which is the instrument of the sciences, are nine. For in the first part, the terms and **intentions** <term>intentions: mental concepts or the "pointing" of the mind toward an object of thought</term> are made manifest according to how they are simple universals; and this part is contained in the book **Isagoge** <note>original: "ysagoge"; an introduction to Aristotle's logic written by Porphyry in the 3rd century, which became a standard textbook in the Middle Ages</note>, composed by Porphyry, and it is an introduction or beginning. <meta>This page continues Avicenna’s introduction to Logic. The previous page ended with the definition of logic as the "organ" or tool for acquiring science and avoiding error. Here, he begins to categorize the specific books of Aristotle’s logic (the Organon) according to their function in human reasoning.</meta>

### ON THE DIVISION OF SCIENCE

->AVICENNA<-

...universally all beings, insofar as they are those intentions <note>original: "intentiones"; in medieval logic, an "intention" refers to a mental concept or the way the mind grasps an object as opposed to the object itself.</note> without the condition of whether they exist in reality or only in the intellect. And this part is contained in the book of Aristotle named the *Categories*, that is, the *Predicaments*. And in the third part, the composition of simple intentions with affirmation or negation is revealed or taught, so that it becomes a statement or enunciation that is true or false; and this part is contained in the book named *Perihermenias*, that is, *On Interpretation*.

In the fourth part, the composition of enunciations or statements is taught, so that from them is composed a significance contributing to the knowledge of that which was unknown; and such is argumentation or demonstration. And this part is contained in the first book of the *Analytics*, <note>original: "analetichorum"; usually referring to the Prior Analytics, which deals with the structure of the syllogism.</note> that is, of *Resolutions* by conversion or conversely.

<margin>Another reading: knowledge which is demonstrated through it, or...</margin>

From the fifth part, indeed, the conditions of argumentation are known—both in its composition and in its statements, which are premises—when [that which is affirmed through it] is certain knowledge in which there is no doubt. And such is demonstrative argumentation, and this part is contained in the book named the second *Analytics*, and *Fulchatachi* <note>original: "fulchatachi"; a Latinized version of the Arabic title "Kitāb al-Burhān" (The Book of Demonstration), which corresponds to Aristotle's Posterior Analytics.</note>—that is, *Of Demonstrations*. 

The sixth part contains the knowledge of argumentations contributing to persuading in every matter those who cannot understand and learn those things which are demonstrated through demonstrative argumentation. It also contributes to those things which are necessary in disputations, in which the intent is to reach a laudable conclusion, or to defend oneself so as not to be cornered or attacked by an adversary. And the aforesaid part includes the "places" <term>places: from the Latin 'loci' (Greek 'topoi'), these are standard "pigeonholes" or strategies of argument used to find points of proof in a debate.</term> by which argumentation is acquired, contributing to probable speech or argumentation, and in questions and answers. This part is contained in the book named the *Book of Topics*, that is, the *Book of Places*. And sometimes it is also named the *Book of Dialectics*, that is, of *Probabilities*. And in sum, in it are known the probable or persuasive argumentations in universal practical matters.

The seventh part, however, comprises the knowledge of errors that occur in argumentation and discourse, the knowledge of the path or "place" of fallacy and error within them, and the total count of all fallacies, however many there may be. It also covers the manifestation of the modes or ways of defending oneself from them. And this part is contained in the *Book of Elenchi*, that is, of *Sophisms*. And the eighth part indeed comprehen...

--- Page 289 ---
<meta>This page concludes Avicenna’s division of the sciences, focusing on the final two parts of logic: Rhetoric and Poetics. The previous page outlined the books of Aristotle’s logic dealing with Categories, Interpretation, and the Analytics (Demonstration). This section completes the "Long Organon" and offers a concluding defense of the harmony between philosophy and faith.</meta>

# AVICENNA ON DIALECTIC

<margin>
<unclear>...al-shi'ri</unclear> <note>Likely a reference to the Arabic title for the Poetics, *Kitāb al-shi'r*.</note>
</margin>

[it provides] the knowledge of persuasive arguments that contribute to speeches, or to the sermons delivered to the public or the common people. This includes those made in the style of debaters or litigants, as well as those used for the praise or blame of an individual. It also encompasses the skills and methods used for denouncing vices, pursuing virtues, and for refining or magnifying matters. Furthermore, it includes the methods for excusing someone from a crime they have been accused of and defending them from an imposed punishment. It also covers the ways of organizing speech in any narration or persuasion. This part is contained in the book named the *Rhetoric*, <note>original: "rethoricorum"</note> which is the book of persuasions.

The ninth part, however, encompasses speech that proceeds by analogies, <note>original: "similitudines"; in the context of medieval logic, this refers to the metaphorical and imaginative comparisons central to poetic reasoning.</note> explaining how one should proceed through various analogies in any given subject, and what the types of such argumentation are—whether they proceed through analogies that are humorous or even those that are repulsive. This part is contained in the book named *Chuabisthichi*, <note>A Latinized transliteration of the Arabic *Kitāb al-shi‘r*, "The Book of Poetry" (Aristotle's Poetics).</note> and it is also called *Al-Fakhri*. <note>original: "alfahari"; likely a corruption of an Arabic term or a reference to a specific commentary.</note>

Thus, we have now demonstrated the divisions of the sciences. It is manifest that there is none among them that contains anything opposing or resisting the faith or divine laws. And although some may be called "wise men" or "philosophers" who later wander from the path of faith and divine law, they indeed err and sin of their own accord—out of their own deficiency and malice—and not because science itself causes this. For science is separate from them and cut off from their wicked deeds.

Now, as we bring this work of ours to its conclusion, let us give infinite thanks to God Most High, to whom be honor and glory forever. Amen.

->T H E  E N D.<-
